#6823. Alfonso Ribeiro and Julianne Hough’s Exact ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Salaries Revealed by Show Source

Ever wonder how much Alfonso Ribeiro and Julianne Hough make for hosting Dancing With the Stars every season? Well, some interesting information just dropped, and by that I mean we now know their exact (alleged!) salaries, including a pretty big pay discrepancy.

An insider tells The Sun that Alfonso makes $1.75 million per season for hosting the show. Meanwhile, Julianne makes $1.25 million. If you’re wondering why Alfonso is earning $500,000 more than Julianne, apparently it’s because he’s been hosting for longer, is the “head host,” and has presumably had more time for salary negotiations and raises.

“Alfonso has also been hosting since 2022 and brings his own history with the show, having won Season 19,” the source says. “His experience in Hollywood, his admiration from viewers and his established relationship with the franchise support the substantial hosting fee.”

The source adds that Julianne “brings a different kind of value to the show than Alfonso. Her value comes from her being a two-time DWTS champion and a former judge. She also has a lot of Hollywood credits under her belt. But Alfonso is considered the ‘main host’ so he gets more than Julianne.”

Meanwhile, Alfonso and Julianne’s predecessor Tom Bergeron was reportedly earning $150,000 per episode according to Celebrity Net Worth, which is about $1.8 million per season.

Alfonso and Julianne haven’t confirmed their salary details (obviously) and Dancing With the Stars keeps these things under wraps, so take all this with a grain of salt but...they’re clearly earning a lot!

#6820. The Fall Winter 2026 Fashion Trends to Know and Shop Now

If recent seasons have been defined by understated dressing, the fall-winter 2026 trends mark a shift toward a more expressive approach to style. However, there’s still a piece of the cake for every aesthetic to cut into. Across the runways, designers embraced the art of contrast. By pairing clean, minimalist silhouettes with rich textures—and reimagining classic wardrobe staples with unexpected details like a peplum or a voluminous shape—they proved that practicality and personality can coexist. The result is a season that feels both wearable and exciting.

Leading the conversation this season are six standout trends that capture fashion’s evolving mood. The Updated Lady introduces a fresh take on suiting for the modern woman, complete with feminine touches and softened structures. (Take a look at Chanel, Balenciaga, and Jil Sander for fresh inspiration, for starters.) Elsewhere, collections at Khaite, Kallmeyer, and Conner Ives nodded to the golden age of the 1920s, incorporating elegant Art Deco touches throughout. An unexpected take on proportions has entered the chat, too, with Tory Burch and Celine reconfiguring preconceived notions of size and shape. Designers, from Prada to Loewe, leaned on the power of styling, too, showcasing how layering and a close attention to detail can transform a wardrobe. For a more alluring take on the season, Alaïa and Valentino celebrated the female form through body-hugging silhouettes and delicate sheer pieces. Meanwhile, Dries Van Noten and Erdem embraced the spirit of fall with down-to-earth palettes of green and brown, punctuated by dark floral patterns.

Discover a shoppable first look at the key fall winter 2026 fashion trends before they fully take over. Don’t forget to come back to this story for more.

Unlike past seasons, there wasn’t one definitive silhouette for tailoring this fall. Let’s start with suiting. Designers don’t want you to stay within the lines. Many jackets were shown with mismatched trousers and skirts; lapel linings were exposed; traditional collared shirts were left undone and wrinkled; collars were turned up and styled with one in and one out. Some blazers shrank; some went long and lean. Others were cropped, nipped in, or even made sculptural.

In autumn’s sea of black coats and navy sweaters, choose color. This season, designers made it simple, showing a slew of head-to-toe looks in vivid monochrome hues. Take your pick! The runways offered a spin around the contemporary color wheel with splashes of color-drenched leather bags and footwear. From knits to denim, dresses to outerwear, we can’t think of a reason not to try this kind of energetic dressing.

This isn’t your grandmother’s lace! On the fall runways, designers from Altuzarra and Colleen Allen to Bottega Veneta, Dior, and Gabriela Hearst embraced a more dramatic kind of romance, with cascading layers, frothy ruffles, and sheer, sweeping silhouettes. Get the look with a delicate lace blouse paired with a tiered black skirt, or go all in with a floor-length lace dress. The effect is romantic, but anything but prim.

Photos: Courtesy of Kallmeyer, Khaite, Rabanne, Chanel, and Loro Piana

Although F. Scott Fitzgerald’s 1925 novel, The Great Gatsby, predates the height of the design style, its themes of 1920s luxury have permanently associated the story with the movement’s signature geometric patterns and overt opulence. From Khaite to Colleen Allen, designers embraced the era with richly detailed texture, glamorous shapes, fringe, gloves, and velvet. To quote the iconic host himself: “Can’t repeat the past? Why, of course, you can!” For 2026, the era returns with a modern, streamlined touch—ready for daily wear to elegant soirées.

Photos: Courtesy of Chanel, Stella McCartney, Givenchy, Jil Sander, and Chloé

The fall-winter 2026 runways showcased a sense of whimsy through bold proportions, featuring oversized designs, cropped styles, and exaggerated silhouettes. Cocoon-like tailoring, dramatic hemlines, and billowy pants and dresses create an expressive and eye-catching approach to fashion. This trend embraces a bit of drama (because that’s life!) while also maintaining a sense of balance. Unconventional silhouettes might feel daunting to incorporate into your daily lineup, so start with small touches. Destree’s jacquard blouse balances voluminous shoulders with a fitted waist that pairs easily with jeans, while Aflalo’s tapered white balloon pants feel airy and light—just add a layered knit and coat for transitional dressing.

Photos: Courtesy of Ferragamo, Loewe, Prada, Johanna Parv, The Row (middle)

Primarily inspired by the fall/winter 2026 Prada runway, the power of styling was a reminder that great style isn’t about owning more—it’s about seeing familiar pieces, like cardigans and tailored trousers, in a new light. Everyday wardrobe staples were transformed through unique pairings, layered basics, and unexpected accessories to create ensembles that demand a second glance. Styling, too, becomes a vessel for self-expression, allowing you to make each piece your own through personal touches and a careful attention to detail.

Photos: Courtesy of Dior, Chanel, Givenchy, Balenciaga, Proenza Schouler, Kallmeyer

Current, confident, and sophisticated, the Updated Lady emerged as one of fall-winter 2026’s defining archetypes, with houses like Chanel, Givenchy, and Balenciaga reimagining power dressing through a contemporary lens. Rather than rigid corporate suiting, the season favored softened structures, explored through gently sloping waists, sculpted jackets, and rich textures that balance strength with ease. The modern woman is multifaceted and full of contradictions, balancing polish with her own distinct edge—shouldn’t her wardrobe follow suit?

Photos: Courtesy of Gucci, Gorunway.com, Khaite and Alaïa

Bodies, bodies, bodies! The fall 2026 runways were an homage to the female form. From the second-skin dresses at Alaïa—some of which actually walked in flesh-colored nude—to Khaite’s sheer layers and Valentino’s lingerie-inspired slips, little was left to the imagination. Translating the trend into your own fall rotation may seem far-fetched, but by embracing it piece by piece, you can achieve an alluring look without going full naked dressing. Imagine Jil Sander’s knit bustier top with a slim trouser, Gucci’s cut-out leggings grounded by a crisp white tee, or one of Saint Lauren’s lace mini dresses beneath a sharp tailored blazer. To bring it back to one of the season’s strongest show notes—and one we outlined above: It all comes down to the styling.

It’s not unusual for fall trends to find inspiration in the countryside—whether it’s heritage plaids, khaki barn jackets, or some kind of cozy knit variation. As grounding as the source material may be, this season’s expression is more elaborate than ever. Nowhere is that more apparent than in the floral prints peppered throughout the collections: they’re richer, deeper, and even moodier than in years’ past. Par for the course, intricate floral brocades appeared at Dries Van Noten on everything from outerwear to midiskirts. Simone Rocha and Erdem also showcased their fair share of flora and fauna, from draped dresses to blouses, proving that the look can move between moods and occasions.

#6819. Inside the Lavish Estates Where The Gilded Age Was Filmed

These locations are straight out of 1880s high society.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE Decor editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Why should the Brits have all the fun? The writer of Downton Abbey, Julian Fellowes, went stateside with the HBO series The Gilded Age, which tells the story of New York City high society in the 1880s amid the halcyon days of the industrial boom. The series explores the tension between old-money elites and their escalating feud with the nouveau riche neighbors who threaten the established social order. Meanwhile in real life, powerhouse families like the Vanderbilts and the Carnegies left their opulent footprints on Newport, Rhode Island, in the form of their famously ostentatious and absolutely gargantuan “summer cottages.” Circumstances which lend themselves to set-design magic.

In honor of season four of The Gilded Age, which premiered November 1, we’re revisiting the real-life settings that have helped bring the series to life. The social alliances may shift, but the architecture remains a dependable scene-stealer. Below, tour 21 properties that rank among the East Coast’s architectural crown jewels, from historic house museums to lavish mansions.

Features as: Bertha Russell’s ballroom and George Russell’s bedroom, as well as the billiard room.

These so-called dollar princesses and their families lived in Manhattan and spent their summers in Newport, Rhode Island. Of course, these industry magnates didn’t consider their infrequent visits (some only came a few weeks in a year) as a reason to exercise restraint. The mammoth Breakers mansion is one of four so-called summer “cottages” (read: castles) that were completed just blocks from each other in a building boom between 1892 and 1902. The mansion was designed by Richard Morris Hunt in the Renaissance Revival style, as a less-than-subtle symbol of the Vanderbilt family’s social and financial preeminence in the Gilded Age. It was architectural one-upmanship that is considered the grandest of all the manses, featuring ornate ballrooms, extensive art collections, manicured gardens, and the latest (then) in modern technology, including electric lights. It has 70 rooms, an interior using marble imported from Italy and Africa, and a library mantel purchased from a château in France.

“When you walk into the dining room of The Breakers, with its painting of the goddess Aurora on the ceiling 50 feet above you or see 500,000 cubic feet of marble in a variety of different hues, you can’t help but be awestruck by the incredible wealth of these Gilded Age tycoons,” says Trudy Coxe, the chief executive officer and executive director of The Preservation Society of Newport County, which has under its stewardship six of the grand mansions featured in the series.

The preservation society worked closely with the filming crew to ensure the safety of the objects and spaces. “We had long discussions about the billiard table at The Breakers,” she explains. “It could not be removed, but it was important to the scene being filmed. Rather than moving it, we worked with their props department to put an alternative covering on the table to simulate an actual game of pool.”

In the series, the Breakers’ neo–Italian Renaissance great hall and music room are featured as Bertha Russell’s (played by Carrie Coon) ballroom, which we see in the final ball scene. George Russell (Morgan Spector) also discusses business while playing billiards in the mansion’s massive billiard room.

Features as: Bertha Russell’s bedroom in the Russell residence

Marble House was built from 1888 to 1892 as a summer cottage for Alva and William Kissam Vanderbilt. It was also designed by Richard Morris Hunt, but in the Beaux-Arts style. For an American house, it was unparalleled in opulence, with a temple-front portico resembling that of the White House, which had been completed 92 years earlier in 1800 (lofty, no?).

Mrs. Russell’s bedroom, built on a soundstage in Bethpage, New York, was inspired by real-life socialite Alva Vanderbilt’s bedroom in the Marble House. The French Louis XV bed was painted and reupholstered in salmon-pink velvet, and the custom bedding used 300 yards of fabric that have been draped, cinched, and swagged.

And that’s just the textiles. Most of the room’s furniture is refurbished antique and everything in the room has been painted to match. Sometimes, Shaw notes, it was difficult to paint a lovely wooden antique piece. “The scenic artists would look at us and say, ‘You really want me to paint over the chestnut? Are you sure?’” says Shaw. “Yes.”

Consuelo Vanderbilt’s (Alva and William’s child) monochrome red bedroom in the mansion also serves as George Russell’s bedroom in the show.

Features as: The exterior of Sylvia Chamberlain’s house

Rosecliff was built for Nevada silver heiress Theresa Fair Oelrichs, whose father, James Graham Fair, was one of the four partners in the Comstock Lode. The famed architectural firm McKim, Mead & White was commissioned to design the mansion, which was modeled after the Grand Trianon, the garden retreat of French kings at Versailles. The French Baroque Revival gem was designed for entertaining at a grand scale—and it certainly fulfilled its purpose. Fair Oelrichs would become known as one of the three great hostesses of Newport.

The white front facade of this mansion, which recently got a $7.4 million renovation, is a stand-in for Sylvia Chamberlain’s (played by Jeanne Tripplehorn) house. You’ll see it in Episode 7, when Tom Raikes (Thomas Cocquerel) pays a visit.

Features as: The servant kitchen and the real-life Sarah Berwind’s bedroom as parts of the Russell residence

The Elms is a Classical Revival dwelling that was completed in 1901. Architect Horace Trumbauer designed it for the coal baron Edward Julius Berwind, taking inspiration from the 18th-century d’Asnières French château. It also houses an impressive collection of paintings and tapestries, as well as the latest technology of its age.

In The Gilded Age Seasons 1 and 2, The Elms stands in as part of the Russells’ lavish residence, including scenes in the kitchen and Bertha Russell’s bedroom. But it truly steps into the spotlight in Season 3, when it hosts a dazzling ball. And as a long-awaited confession of love looms (we won’t spoil from whom), the opulent Newport mansion proves to be the perfect setting for high drama and high society.

Each guest is granted a cinematic entrance, illuminated by a golden glow that bathes the grand façade—a new addition this season, as electricity is now becoming available. “The house’s interiors would not have been electrified yet, but people were beginning to use it for parties,” Shaw says. “That would mean they would have to have their own generator installed somewhere on the property to light up those lights.” To accomplish this, the crew went to specialty shops that make reproduction bulbs. “The original bulbs were much bigger than what we have in a household today,” Shaw adds. “Some of the lightbulbs we used were 10 inches in diameter, which is how big they were then.”

Features as: The exterior is used for Caroline Astor’s Beechwood house; the boardinghouse is used for a scene with Oscar van Rhijn; and another room serves as Agnes van Rhijn’s bedroom

Completed in 1852, Château-sur-Mer is one of the first grand Bellevue Avenue mansions of the Gilded Age in Newport, built by architect Seth C. Bradford for William Shepard Wetmore. Its interiors were designed by Ogden Codman Jr., who co-authored Edith Wharton’s Decoration of Houses. The mansion was host to many major parties, including the Fête Champêtre, an elaborate country picnic for more than 2,000 guests in 1857, as well as a debutante ball for Edith Wetmore in 1889. Wetmore’s son, George Peabody Wetmore, went on to have a distinguished political career as the governor of Rhode Island and, later, as a U.S. senator.

In The Gilded Age, the home’s exterior was used for Caroline Astor’s (Donna Murphy) Beechwood House. The hallway, dining room, and ballroom were used during Mamie Fish’s (Ashlie Atkinson) doll tea party. Several bedrooms serve as Agnes van Rhijn’s (Christine Baranski) bedroom, Oscar van Rhijn’s (Blake Ritson) bedroom, Anne Morris’s (Katie Finneran) bedroom, and Patrick Morris’s (Michel Gill) office. There’s also a scene filmed at the boardinghouse with Oscar van Rhijn, according to Patch.

Features as: The office of Brook family lawyer Tom Raikes

Hunter House was constructed in 1748 at the harborfront near the north end of the Newport Historic District at a time when the city was a bustling seaport in the British empire. The house was owned by wealthy merchants and overlooked the wharves that serviced their trading ships. It’s one of the finest examples of Colonial architecture in Newport, according to the Preservation Society. Inside, its resident families furnished the house with decorative arts produced by expert craftsmen, much of which has been preserved today. Such a luxurious lifestyle, however, depended upon the labor of enslaved people of African descent; recent research by the Preservation Society has identified at least 13 enslaved individuals who lived and worked at Hunter House. Today’s Hunter House honors their perseverance and incalculable contributions to Newport’s past.

One of the sitting rooms in Hunter House functions as the office of Brook family lawyer Tom Raikes, and is set fictitiously in Doylestown, Pennsylvania.

Features as: The Astor family summer home

Belcourt was completed in 1894 for Oliver Hazard Perry Belmont, a prominent American socialite and coachman who served in the U.S. House of Representatives. Like many of the Newport mansions, the Château-esque structure was completed by architect Richard Morris Hunt; it was designed to mimic the hunting lodge of Versailles, built for Louis XIII of France, but with a special ask to accommodate Oliver’s collection of horses and automobiles. In 1896, Oliver gave the house to his second wife, the former Alva Vanderbilt, who designed the neighboring Newport mansion Marble House. Alva used Belcourt as a gathering place for the elite of society, hosting lavish parties and balls and attracting notable figures in politics, business, and the arts.

In The Gilded Age Season 1, Belcourt shows up in Episode 8 as Mrs. Astor’s lavish new Newport home, which Mrs. Russell sneaks inside and is forced to flee to avoid a less-than-pleasant meetup.

Features as: The social gathering scene where Caroline Astor and George Russell meet

Built in 1867 by prolific Boston tea and china merchant Robert M. Cushing, the Ledges was originally the summer home of the Cushing family. This majestic oceanfront pile is perched on one of Newport’s most desirable peninsulas, overlooking Bailey’s Beach. It was built by architect John H. Sturgis, who designed a large, Stick-style cottage that was equal parts comfort and elegance. Today it features original furnishings, papered walls, and unique artwork, including a studio that was added to the side of the house for Robert’s artistic children.

Today, the estate remains in the hands of the Cushing descendants, who occasionally open the house up to film crews. It was featured a few years ago in the film Evening, starring Glenn Close and Meryl Streep. “Working at the Ledges was pretty extraordinary,” Gilded Age location manager Lauri Pitkus told The Providence Journal, “because I don't think I’ve ever been in a home with spectacular views out of every window.”

This historic house was built in 1864 for John Noble Alsop Griswold, an Old China Trade merchant and diplomat. The house is the work of Richard Morris Hunt; it was one of the earliest buildings in the American Stick style of architecture. The house has a complex roofline with a main mansarded section that is pierced by numerous gable and dormer sections. It boasts a number of balconies sheltered by deep eaves, with gable ends decorated with woodwork. Today, the house is a gallery location for the Newport Art Museum. In the series, the house features in Season 1 Episode 1, and again in Episode 5.

Features as: Mingling with the other elite scene

The International Tennis Hall of Fame and its perfectly preserved grass courts are in the Newport Casino, a National Historic Landmark property. The historic seven-acre estate was commissioned by New York Herald publisher James Gordon Bennett as a social club for the elite summer residents of Newport. The Newport News boasted three days after it opened in July 1880: “It is doubtful if a livelier place can be found.” Today, the space is recognized as the official hall of fame for the sport of tennis globally. Since 1955, 262 distinguished inductees representing 27 countries have been enshrined in Newport.

In the eighth episode of The Gilded Age Season 1, the characters are seen promenading around the piazza that overlooks what is known today as Horseshoe Court. A few characters are even playing tennis. “It was fitting to have that history depicted here, given The Gilded Age’s look into that time period,” the hall of fame’s Megan Erbes tells ELLE DECOR. “Several of our staff members got to work closely with the production team and actors, teaching everything from the history of our property to how to hit a proper forehand.” RI Monthly reported that crews returned to the courts last summer to film Season 2 of the show, so it’s possible that Newport Casino will make another appearance.

Features as: The parlor, library, entryway, and staircase of the Morris house, located on Fifth Avenue in the show; Mr. and Mrs. Morris’s bedrooms were filmed in the Newport mansions

William Smith Slater hired General William Walker to build a home as a wedding gift for his daughter. The result was this historic home, which was completed in 1877. The Victorian house is filled with treasures—the fireplace surrounds, for example, were carved by Charles Dowler, who came to the United States to produce arms for the Civil War. Today, the house is open to visitors and is known as the Clouds Hill Museum.

The Clouds Hill Museum is the only Rhode Island site outside of Newport that was used in the series. The crew scheduled filming for Season 1 in late February of 2021, when a few hundred people were on site during two days of filming, museum director Wayne Cabral told Warwick Online, noting that the taping finished around midnight on the second day of filming (after five days of work to prep the set). Almost all the parlor’s furniture was removed, and the head set designer brought in items sourced from local antiques stores in East Greenwich and North Kingstown, museum president Anne Holst added. The producers were adamant about removing the existing curtains, which were disintegrating, Holst added, so she negotiated to leave the replacements (which cost $10,000) with the museum after filming.

Features as: Visit to the home of Aurora Fane scene

The Gothic Revival–style Lyndhurst Mansion was designed in 1838 by Alexander Jackson Davis. Lyndhurst’s third owner, Jay Gould, is the real-life inspiration for the “new money” character George Russell. “He was fantastically ruthless in business, to an extent that Mrs. Astor would never let him in, he was never allowed into society, and she didn’t let his children in until he was dead,” creator, writer, and producer Julian Fellowes said in a podcast. “But he was an incredibly affectionate father and a very caring and faithful husband…and his children all had these nostalgic memories of Lyndhurst, their house on the Hudson.”

In Season 1 of The Gilded Age, Lyndhurst’s interiors are the home of characters Charles and Aurora Fane (Ward Horton and Kelli O’Hara), who are related to the van Rhijns and part of the “old money” side of society. The Lyndhurst lawns and grounds also doubled as Central Park and the Sheep’s Meadow in the opening sequence. The home boasts a bowling alley that dates back to 1894, which was re-created to be the ferry terminal that Marian Brook (Louisa Jacobson) and Peggy Scott (Denée Benton) take to Manhattan for the first time in Episode 1. And finally, the house’s carriage house was transformed into The New York Globe newspaper offices.

The Belvedere Estate, located between Lyndhurst Mansion and writer Washington Irving’s Sunnyside home, is a century-old mansion on 25 acres in historic Tarrytown. The estate was originally part of Philipsburg Manor, a 90,000-acre property built for Florence and Casper Whitney. “While the mansion dates from the 1920s, it has a much older European feel that could represent something from decades earlier,” says Belvedere Estate sales director Linda Fiorentino, who recalls the massive legwork required to film at the mansion.

“I will never forget the background actors descending from a yellow school bus, fully dressed in period costumes and felt hats,” she says. The Season 1 scene was filmed at the pond at the back of Belvedere Estate, acting as a stand-in for Central Park in the scene when Marian meets Mr. Raikes at Bethesda Fountain in Episode 1. The pond is a man-made feature, and the water level sometimes sinks to a mere foot or two, Fiorentino explains. “Before filming, they filled the pond with roughly 600,000 gallons of water to fill to capacity, giving the illusion of a much larger body of water and to allow them to have pleasure boats filled with passengers on the water,” she says. They also re-created Central Park’s Shakespeare Bridge from rough-hewn logs and brought in trees, shrubs, and foliage to cover the existing link fence because it was too modern.

Features as: The drawing room of wealthy widow Sylvia Chamberlain

Toward the end of the 19th century, Colonel Elliott Fitch Shepard, a lawyer who founded the New York State Bar Association in 1876, purchased more than 500 acres on a hill high above the Hudson River north of Tarrytown. He engaged the renowned architecture firm McKim, Mead & White to design his family’s manor house here. The result was a 75-room Victorian structure that mimicked 18th-century Italian villa architecture. Think: hand-carved mahogany paneling, a grand stairway near the front entrance, high patterned ceilings, and elaborate cornice work. Unfortunately, Shepard died before it was completed in 1893, and it passed into the hands of William Rockefeller and Frank Vanderlip. These men were part of a group (including John Jacob Astor, who died on the Titanic in 1912) who went on to convert the building to the Sleepy Hollow Country Club, which remains a private members-only club today.

Scenes in the drawing room of wealthy widow Sylvia Chamberlain were shot on location here. “The entire room was redressed by our team in the Rococo style,” set decorator Regina Graves told 1st Dibs.

Features as: Part of Mrs. Astor’s residence

Glenview was built in 1876 by John Bond Trevor, a highly successful stockbroker, who engaged New York City architect Charles W. Clinton to build his estate. The mansion was a paragon of luxury and modern comfort, featuring indoor plumbing, gas illumination, and a coal-burning furnace to circulate heat throughout its 37 rooms. The exterior had elements of Victorian Gothic and French Second Empire design, complete with a mansard roof, a gray stone facade constructed of blocks hewn from a Hastings-on-Hudson quarry, and decorative sandstone elements brought from Indiana.

The mansion makes an appearance as Caroline Astor’s residence in Season 1. “They were all so complimentary about Glenview, and of course we did a lot of polishing and waxing,” Laura Vookles, chair of the museum’s curatorial department, told The Rivertown Enterprise. “They focused on our exquisite interiors and filmed in six rooms, including the dining, library, and sitting rooms, and used all but one painting that is normally on view.”

The John Paine Mansion, also known as the Castle, was built in 1896 and was deemed the grandest house in Troy, New York. It has since served as a private residence, a college administration building, a movie set (see: Martin Scorsese’s 1993 drama The Age of Innocence), and, currently, a fraternity house. In the show, one of the bedrooms in the Castle features as Tom Raikes’s office.

This residence, the home of Troy locals Bill and Sue Comiskey, stands in for the Brooklyn residence of the well-off Scott family. At one point early in the series, Arthur Scott (John Douglas Thompson) and his daughter, Peggy (Denée Benton), sit on carved-oak chairs around a damask-covered dining table. The home’s elaborate details really shine in this historic home, which dates back to the turn of the 19th century. Stained-glass windows and an elegant china cabinet are memorable architectural features that are original to the location and transport the viewers back in time.

While filming what would be the Scott family residence, Bill, the homeowner, told News10 that a few prized family possessions actually made the cut. “My desk was in it, front and center…you [also] saw the whole front and back parlor into the dining room where they were having a meal,” he explained. “[There were] great shots of this room catching the stained glass, the fireplace, [and] this bookcase my grandfather made.”

Features as: The interior is used as George Russell’s workspace

Hempstead House was built for Howard Gould by architects Hunt & Hunt in 1912 on the north shore of Long Island. The mansion was eventually sold to art mogul Daniel Guggenheim (yes, that Guggenheim). Hempstead House is one of four mansions on the grounds of the Guggenheim Estate—which includes Castle Gould, Falaise, and Mille Fleur. The Tudor-style castle was the embodiment of Gold Coast opulence, a place where the esteemed family hosted grand parties, performances, and exhibitions by gatherings of the elite of the time. To say it is massive would be an understatement: 50,000 square feet, with 40 rooms and a 60-foot-tall entry foyer. In The Gilded Age, the mansion’s interior was used as George Russell’s workspace.

Features as: The late General Henry Brook’s house

Rock Hall Museum was initially an 18th-century plantation. The two-and-a-half-story Georgian-style home was built in approximately 1767 and later restored to its original appearance in the 1950s. In Season 1 Episode 1, the house’s white facade is featured within the first 15 minutes as a backdrop for the late General Henry Brook’s house. Marian, his daughter, is seen walking out of the home on her way to the train station.

The Hart Cluett Museum is a work of Federal architecture designed by Martin E. Thompson in 1827. He was hired by William Howard. Thompson brought the design of the Hart Cluett House back to New York City, where many examples of the 1827 Federal-style townhouse were copied throughout Manhattan. This house, a museum open to the public today, was featured in The Gilded Age in Episode 2 as Anne Morris’s home.

#6818. Why Is Everyone Bragging About Their Ferritin Levels?

Losing hair, feeling sluggish, or having brain fog? Experts are turning to a blood-work statistic that may be the sneaky cause

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

“Maybe you’re not depressed and unmotivated … maybe you just have low ferritin,” says Elizabeth Orringo, a wellness influencer and host of The Wellness Process podcast, in an Instagram reel. The caption then prompts viewers to comment “Iron” to get a link to her Substack, which details how she raised her ferritin from 16 to 142, making her body “feel like a new person.” The video has 244,000 views and nearly 5,000 “Iron” comments. But what is ferritin, how does it relate to iron, and why do thousands of women online care?

Ferritin and iron aren’t synonymous, but they are closely linked. “Ferritin is a protein that stores iron in your body, and iron is essential for producing hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells responsible for carrying oxygen throughout the body,” says Pooja Gidwani, a Los Angeles–based internist and longevity expert. “Ferritin is one of the best markers we have to assess how much iron your body has stored, rather than just how much is circulating in your blood at a given time.”

Iron has had its moment in the wellness world, but ferritin is just getting started; it stores iron for later use, so the less you have, the less iron supply your body has in times of need, like during increased blood loss, growth stages, and life in general. “I like to think of serum iron as your checking account and ferritin as your savings account,” says Amanda Kahn, a New York–based internist and longevity specialist. “You can have enough money to cover today’s expenses while your savings are becoming depleted.” While iron gets most of the spotlight, Kahn says ferritin often gives a clearer picture of the body’s iron reserves and can more efficiently identify iron deficiency before it progresses to anemia and other problems.

Even without a blood test, people often notice iron deficiency through low energy, hair loss, and fatigue, which can also be side effects of low ferritin. But another marker of low ferritin that has taken social media by storm is “ferritin face.”

“While ‘ferritin face’ isn’t a recognized medical condition, the broader connection between iron status, energy, and overall well-being is worth understanding,” Kahn explains. “Social media has introduced terms like ‘ferritin face,’ bringing attention to the relationship between iron stores, energy, and appearance.”

According to Google Search, searches for “ferritin face” are up 450 percent in the last three months and 5,000 percent year over year. Ferritin face refers to the more visible hallmarks of low ferritin, like pale skin, dark, hollow under-eyes due to lack of color, and puffiness as a result of inflammation. In a beauty landscape where going under the knife is often the first line of defense, “ferritin face” offers another explanation that plastic surgery can’t fix. “When iron is in short supply, the body deprioritizes skin and hair and redirects it to support vital organs, which is why it shows up visibly first,” says Tiffany Lester, an integrative medicine physician and women’s health medical director at Function.

Just because you have dark circles or look pale doesn’t mean you have low ferritin—and vice versa; someone without “ferritin face” can still have low ferritin. The first step is a blood-work panel that covers both iron and ferritin levels, since iron levels can be normal while ferritin can be low. “If your iron levels read normal, but you have low ferritin, which means your body may still have enough circulating iron to meet its immediate needs, but its stored iron is depleted,” says Gidwani.

However, experts point out that laboratories often have different ideal ranges for ferritin levels, and a “healthy” ferritin level can be hard to pinpoint. “Reference ranges reflect a population average, not your optimal baseline,” Lester explains. This means that an adequate level for you may not be normal for someone else. “A lab may tell a woman that a ferritin of 16 nanograms per liter is ‘normal,’ while another woman has a ferritin of 100 nanograms per liter and is also considered normal. I often ask, ‘How could women possibly feel the same across such a wide range?’” says Kahn.

Doctors agree that ferritin below 15 nanograms per milliliter and iron below 30 nanograms per milliliter indicate a deficiency. However, Kahn points out that ferritin levels that are too high aren’t good either. “I also pay close attention to women with ferritin between 30 and 50 nanograms per liter, particularly when they’re experiencing fatigue, exercise intolerance, or hair shedding,” she says. This isn’t to say levels in the 100s are unhealthy. “Reference ranges reflect a population average, not your optimal baseline,” Lester adds.

There is no one-size-fits-all approach to improving your ferritin levels, but you can follow the same protocol you’d use to increase iron and ferritin, since more iron means more for ferritin to store. You can’t pinpoint the causes of the deficiency, but the best place to start is diet. “Diet is often assumed to be the cause, but menstrual blood loss, gastrointestinal blood loss, and impaired absorption are important considerations,” says Gidwani. Historically, the best food sources of iron have been animal sources like red meat, which contains heme iron, generally absorbed more efficiently than the nonheme iron found in plant foods like lentils, beans, and spinach, Gidwani adds. “Pairing plant-based iron sources with vitamin C, such as citrus fruits or bell peppers, can improve absorption.”

Habits are important too, Lester explains. Your daily coffee or tea with breakfast may be affecting your iron and ferritin levels. “Caffeine blocks gut absorption of the iron-rich foods we are consuming,” she adds. Consider having your morning caffeine an hour or two before or after you eat.

The same goes for supplements—experts say to avoid drinking caffeine when you take an iron supplement. “Oral iron is usually the first treatment, and alternate-day dosing can improve absorption and sometimes tolerability,” Gidwani says. “IV iron may be appropriate when oral iron isn’t tolerated, isn’t effective, or absorption is impaired.” Experts also recommend pairing an iron supplement with a vitamin C supplement, similar to the aforementioned food pairings, because vitamin C helps iron absorption.

Nature Made® Iron 18 mg Gummies with Vitamin C

If ferritin remains low despite consistent supplementation, it may be worth looking into why the iron isn’t being absorbed. Popular culprits are gut conditions like celiac disease, autoimmune gastritis, SIBO, and IBS, as they all interfere with iron absorption. Even poor stomach acid can affect absorption.

Bragging about your TikTok followers may not be the most socially appropriate thing, but bragging about your ferritin levels certainly is. However, more isn’t always better. “I always remind my patients that we need to look at the entire physiological picture, and there is also a meaningful difference between treating a genuine deficiency and simply trying to push a laboratory value higher,” Kahn emphasizes.

“My philosophy is that laboratory values should be interpreted in the context of the individual, not just whether a number falls inside a ‘normal’ reference range,” she adds. “The goal isn’t to chase a perfect ferritin number. It’s to identify deficiencies, understand why they’re occurring, and help women feel and function their best.”

#6817. Enterprise AI Spending Outpaces Adoption Growth, Report Finds

Enterprise AI spending is growing faster than the number of organizations paying for it, according to a new Menlo Ventures report that points to a shift from buying access for employees to financing work performed by agents.

The venture capital firm's 2026 State of Enterprise AI report estimates deployment spending reached a $176.8 billion annualized run rate by September, up from $33 billion in 2025. The share of enterprises paying for AI rose from 55% to 65%.

A larger bill can reflect broader use inside an organization, but it does not independently establish that the additional work is useful or profitable.

Menlo's methodology describes revenue figures as annualized run rates. The $176.8 billion estimate therefore should not be read as $176.8 billion already spent during the first nine months of 2026.

The report also distinguishes unusually heavy spenders from the typical respondent. Average reported spending reached 4.7 times the prior year's level, while the median reached 2.2 times. That gap suggests a smaller group of large spenders drove the average substantially.

The practical implication is that an industry growth figure may be a poor benchmark for an individual organization's budget. Buyers need to understand their own workload growth and the results it produces.

"Agents are changing the economics of software," Menlo principal Derek Xiao said in the firm's announcement.

Menlo reports that agents account for 80% of tokens on OpenRouter, a service providing access to multiple models. That measures activity on one platform, rather than all enterprise AI use. Token consumption also measures processing volume, rather than completed business outcomes.

An agent that makes repeated attempts can consume more resources without delivering proportionately more value. For procurement teams, the relevant comparison is consequently the cost of completing acceptable work, including the review it requires.

Menlo estimates that Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google capture 69% of enterprise AI deployment spending. That measure is distinct from their shares of enterprise language-model API spending, a narrower category. The figures should not be used interchangeably.

The report draws on a Morning Consult survey of nearly 400 U.S. enterprise decision-makers responsible for more than $4 billion in AI spending. Market totals are modeled estimates informed by surveys, public filings, and third-party reports. Menlo discloses investments in Anthropic and OpenRouter.

A separate announcement from Information Services Group describes buyers putting more emphasis on the economics and reliability of production deployments. ISG says ongoing security and observability work remains necessary as organizations scale.

That provides a useful distinction between market demand and business value. Suppliers can generate growing revenue while customers still determine which deployments justify the cost.

For enterprise leaders, the new spending estimate strengthens the case for examining usage beyond license counts. It leaves the harder purchasing question with the customer: How much worthwhile work did the increased spending actually buy?

Menlo's State of Enterprise AI report is available here.

John K. Waters is the editor in chief of a number of Converge360.com sites, with a focus on high-end development, AI and future tech. He also co-scripted the documentary film Silicon Valley: A 100 Year Renaissance, which aired on PBS.  He can be reached at [email protected].

Beth Gillette is the beauty editor at Cosmopolitan, where she specializes in covering skincare, makeup, and more. Although she’s had hormonal acne since her preteen years, she’s never let that lessen her love for glam, whether that’s testing the newest foundation before it launches or updating her entire makeup routine to get rid of pore-clogging ingredients.

Jasmine Hyman is the assistant beauty editor at Cosmopolitan where she writes about all things acne. She is constantly vetting and testing beauty products specifically for her sensitive and acne-prone skin, and she doesn’t play around when it comes to her skincare routine. She treasures her self-care nights and monthly facials more than anything else.

Julee Wilson is the beauty editor-at-large at Cosmopolitan. She’s known for her thoughtful storytelling, honest opinions, and Black girl–approved product recommendations. She’s tried it all—from the fanciest serums to the toughest acne spot treatments—and never gatekeeps.

Celia Shatzman, contributing beauty writer

Celia Shatzman is a contributing beauty writer at Cosmopolitan. She’s battled acne even longer than she’s been a beauty editor, which means she’s tried every spot treatment, cleanser, moisturizer, SPF, makeup, and gadget she can get her hands on during her quest for clear skin.

Connie Yang, MD, FAAD, board-certified dermatologist

Connie Yang, MD, FAAD, is a board-certified cosmetic dermatologist at PFRANKMD in New York City. She specializes in medical and cosmetic dermatology and has an expertise in acne, laser skin rejuvenation, and treating pigmentation and acne scarring across all skin types. Her practice focuses on achieving natural-looking aesthetic results through individualized treatment plans that incorporate injectables, skin tightening, and nonsurgical face and body contouring.

Amy Wechsler, MD, PC, board-certified dermatologist and psychiatrist

Amy Wechsler, MD, is one of only a few physicians in the country board-certified in both dermatology and psychiatry. In 2008, Dr. Wechsler published a book about her “stress aging” theory called The Mind-Beauty Connection. She joined Chanel as its dermatological advisor in 2011, developing products and creating educational content. Dr. Wechsler’s work has also earned her appointments as assistant clinical professor in dermatology at SUNY Downstate Medical Center and adjunct assistant clinical professor in psychiatry at Weill Cornell Medical College. She graduated from Columbia Business School in 2024 with an MBA, which provided the knowledge that led her to found Spotless, an acne clinic in NYC, with her daughter, Zoe, in 2025.

Rishi Chopra, MD, FAAD, board-certified dermatologist

Rishi Chopra, MD, is a board-certified dermatologist and Harvard fellowship–trained cosmetic and laser specialist practicing at Hudson Dermatology & Laser Surgery in New York City. He is recognized for his expertise in injectables, laser medicine, skin longevity, and the treatment of skin of color.

Karan Lal, DO, MS, FAAD, board-certified dermatologist

Karan Lal, DO, MS, FAAD, is a double board-certified adult, pediatric, and cosmetic dermatologist based in the Phoenix/Scottsdale area. He is the only dual fellowship–trained cosmetic and pediatric dermatologist in the United States, specializing in laser rejuvenation, melasma, hyperpigmentation, and complex skin conditions.

Jaimie Glick, MD, board-certified dermatologist

Jaimie Glick, MD, is a board-certified dermatologist in New York City specializing in medical, surgical, and cosmetic dermatology. She graduated magna cum laude from the University of Pennsylvania before earning her medical degree from SUNY Downstate College of Medicine. She has conducted research on laser treatments for acne scarring, authored numerous peer-reviewed publications, and has lectured nationally and internationally on acne, lasers, and other advances in dermatology.

Shari Marchbein, MD, board-certified dermatologist

Shari Marchbein, MD, is a board-certified dermatologist and founder of Niche Dermatology in NYC. She is also an assistant professor of clinical dermatology at Mount Sinai School of Medicine. Dr. Marchbein’s academic and clinical interests include the treatment of acne, in particular adult female acne, acne scarring, and rosacea. Dr. Marchbein has been sought out as a leader in her field for the treatment of acne and rosacea and has published multiple articles on acne pathogenesis and treatment. She has presented at renowned national conferences on the topics of acne and rosacea, including the annual American Academy of Dermatology and Advances in Dermatology meetings.

Soo-Young Kim Abrams, licensed aesthetician

Soo-Young Kim Abrams is a New York State licensed aesthetician and founder of SYK Skin, her boutique facial studio in SoHo. Before aesthetics, she spent a decade in fashion and media, working alongside top photographers, makeup artists, and models and touring with Rihanna for a cover story. Rooted in her Korean heritage, she built her career at some of New York City’s most respected skincare destinations before opening SYK Skin. She is known for her advanced facial massage, lymphatic drainage, and a whole-skin approach—calming even the most inflamed skin while focusing on lasting health, radiance, and aging gracefully.

Samantha Susca is a facialist in New York City and founder of boutique skincare studio Refinery4 in lower Manhattan. With over a decade of experience focused on thoughtful and personalized skincare, she combines clinical manual skill with intuition and technology to create treatments tailored to personalized needs. Known for her quiet influence and transformative results, Samantha serves on the Board of Advisors for ELLE magazine.

Celia Shatzman (she/her) is a Brooklyn-based writer and editor who has penned stories on topics ranging from beauty to fashion, travel, celebrities, health, entertainment, finance and more. A graduate of the Medill School of Journalism at Northwestern University, she is a beauty and style contributor at Forbes and her work has appeared in New York, Cosmopolitan, WWD, ELLE, Conde Nast Traveler, Afar, Travel + Leisure, Women’s Health, Marie Claire, Byrdie, Refinery29 and NYLON, among others.

#6813. Stylist Soki Mak on 10 Things That Inspired Kim Kardashian’s All’s Fair Season Two Wardrobe

From 1990s Helmut Newton shoots to classic Bond girls to unexpected Comme des Garçons finds

In fashion, anything from niche archival research to a favorite film to an outfit you saw on your morning commute can make for inspiration. In our new series 10 Things, we ask industry professionals and tastemakers to divulge the (you guessed it) 10 things that had the most impact on their aesthetic choices.

The second season of Ryan Murphy’s legal drama, All’s Fair, opened with reality star-turned-actor Kim Kardashian in a patchwork Alexander McQueen suit. The rare ensemble, composed of a peplum jacket and fluted skirt, came from Lee McQueen’s theatrical Spring 2004 collection, titled Deliverance, in which models danced down the runway in shimmering gowns, dramatic feathered skirts, and tulle galore. “There were comments about Kim’s clothing being inappropriate in the workplace, but that’s what it should be,” Soki Mak, the visionary behind Kardashian’s Allura Grant character, told Harper’s Bazaar. “If I’m going to watch a show, I want to be like, ‘What the hell is that?’”

When Mak first joined the All’s Fair team—handpicked by Kardashian, via Instagram, to dress her onscreen as a high-powered lawyer—she had never ventured into costume design. The stylist, who has worked with everyone from Rosalía to Pamela Anderson, spent the first season developing the visual identity of Allura, merging her client’s own flair for shock value and fantasy with the limited character descriptions she received. We saw hyper-cinched waists and archival Jean Paul Gaultier; Hermès Birkins and suits with exposed thongs. It was Kardashian, with a twist.

But for Season Two, Mak focused on separating Kardashian from her character, tracking Allura’s emotional journey through darker color palettes and less expected silhouettes. She dug deeper into designer archives, emerging with moody gems from some of the most beloved collections of the ’90s and early-aughts. Rare vintage pieces from Maison Margiela, Comme des Garçons, Yohji Yamamoto, and Alaïa each made their cameos.

Ahead, the stylist dives into 10 influences that shaped Allura’s costume design, from Kim Kardashian herself to classic Bond girls to a baker-boy cap she had to fight for.

[For Season One,] no one gave us any sort of visual references. I’d never been a costume designer before, but usually, when I’ve worked on character-based stuff—I used to work a lot with Nadia Lee Cohen—we would develop the character first, so when I go into styling, it’s quite easy to visualize that person. There was no time for that, and there was no visual reference for Allura. So, when I came in, I was just thinking, “Okay, what do I see her as?” I looked at Kim personally, and she’s this fantasy. There is no one like her. So I’m like, “Okay, if you have all of the money in the world and all of the access in the world, all the power in the world, what would you look like?”

I’ve always thought of Kim as someone that creates and shocks and is the first to do something, whether people like it or not. And that’s the energy I wanted to go into this with. She challenges the norm. I’ve also always been a big believer in trying to be a trendsetter rather than a follower. In some of these moments, I would find it difficult to make a mood board because the references weren’t there. That was where I would say to Kim, “Trust me.”

For Season One, we started reaching out to brands, and Jean Paul Gaultier was [the first to say], “Let’s do it.” The minute we had them, the whole narrative of the show changed. They went deep into the archives and started sending these looks that hadn’t been worn in 20 years. It was amazing. We were sourcing vintage and archival pieces on the side, but we really focused on Jean Paul Gaultier because everything else compared to that just looked sad.

When the images started circulating from the first season, a critic that I respect wrote that the fashion was “kind of obvious.” Although I disagreed, I understood where he was coming from. Maybe Kim wearing a Mugler suit that accentuated her body and her curves was something we had seen her wear before. This season, I wanted to do something really different. I wanted to go less out-there with the colors and a little less predictable with the shapes and the styling. I picked designers and pieces that weren’t obvious choices, and I think it showed growth from last season. We took it somewhere else completely.

For hair and makeup references, I would go on Pinterest and pull old Helmut Newton shoots because I wanted it to look very timeless. I think that was the key. Everything looked … not minimal, there was definitely no minimal… but very ’90s-based and gorgeous.

Kim loves Madonna. There were a lot of old Madonna images for her platinum hair and makeup, a lot of which was done by Pat McGrath.

I think I’d made a point this year that I wanted to take it down a dark route. I almost wanted Allura to be like, “I just had a shit experience in the first season My man’s left me. I’m pissed off. I’ve gone away, and I’ve come back, and I’m serious now.” So everything’s much more covered up. There are darker layers. She’s experimenting. When I was going through the [recent] runway shows, everything was very pink and quite eclectic, so we mainly went with archival pieces. I used a lot of really rare Yohji Yamamoto, Comme des Garçons, and Lee McQueen.

There was a Margiela skirt suit [from the Spring 1994 collection, Retrospective] and it was just very kitsch. It was a long skirt with a suit jacket and was paired with a black leather baker boy hat from Hermès. We were in a bidding war with a collector in Japan. When we were filming the scene, someone in production or maybe Ryan [Murphy] had mentioned they wanted to tone down the hats for this season. But I got that memo after styling the look, and I was adamant that the look needed the hat. I begged. And then she sat at the table wearing a hat and I could see everyone was like, “How is she getting to wear a hat?” I just felt like the look needed it. It took [Kardashian] out of her normal visual stance and how she usually portrays herself.

Comme des Garçons is very destructive and not really tailored to fit a woman’s body in the way [Kardashian] usually likes. And we got her in [a gray jacket and long lilac-gray column skirt] and worked it around her body. She never once made any comments. She would just look at herself for a second and be like, “Cool.” And then go on set.

I have to let Kris Jenner take credit for [Elizabeth Taylor’s 1969 Scorpio cape, worn by Kardashian in Episode 1], because that’s her cape. She would come to set all the time and once had a conversation with Ryan about the fact that she has this cape. He was like, “That’s it, we need it.” From there, we shipped in a $10 million diamond that was most similar to what Elizabeth Taylor was wearing [in original imagery]. It was flown into L.A. in someone’s pocket, and we had it on set for like five days with Kim’s security. It’s a piece of history. It’s really special. Each day, it would go to Kim and then back in her car home because no one wanted to take responsibility for it.

In general, a lot of my choices in clothing and costume referenced old Bond films where the women were super sexual and curvy and had Brigitte Bardot hair. There was glamour, sex, opulence, money. The outfits were completely inappropriate and not really wearable in everyday life. But if I’m going to watch a show, that’s what I want to see. I want to be like, “What the hell? What is that?” There were comments about Kim’s clothing being inappropriate in the workplace, but that’s what it should be. It’s fun.

#6812. Merlot Nails Are the Most Luxurious Way to Wear a Red Manicure This Fall

Cozy up with a glass of wine and start reading all about this expensive-looking trend.

I’ve never been a big fan of a classic red manicure on myself, but when it comes to deeper shades, I’m all in. Burgundy nails, black cherry nails, spiced cherry nails... these are all my speed. So, when a new expensive-looking crimson shade came along this fall, I was automatically on board. Meet merlot red nails, the rich, wine-inspired shade that’s giving my usual fall manicure colors some very chic competition. (I love a good glass of red wine almost as much as I love a good fall manicure, so this trend has been especially intriguing.)

These high-gloss, juicy nails combine red with subtle purple and berry undertones for a rich, full-bodied color (much like a full-bodied bottle of merlot). Ahead, I’ll break down everything you need to know about trending merlot nails, including inspo pics and how to tips from nail artist Vikki Swan.

As the name suggests, merlot nails take inspiration from the deep, reddish-purple color of a glass of merlot wine. These manicures use burgundy and dark cherry red polishes that have subtle berry or plum undertones for a rich, multi-dimensional finish. Unlike a bright cherry red manicure, merlot is deeper and more muted, making it particularly great for fall and winter, and also making it super versatile and easy to wear. “Merlot red is a classic in its own way, just like traditional red nails, but with a deeper, more seasonal feel,” says Swan. “The darker wine tone gives the manicure a fall mood and makes it look richer and more elegant. It’s expressive, but still very versatile and easy to incorporate into different fall looks.”

The easiest way to get merlot nails is to find a polish that resembles your favorite glass of vino tinto. Look for deep wine and red-burgundy shades, recommends Swan, rather than a traditional bright red or nearly-black oxblood.

Prep is key for any manicure, but “this is especially important with dark and red shades,” says Swan. “If the cuticle and nail plate are not prepared properly, the final result will not look as clean and polished.” Dark colors emphasize imperfections on the nail and cuticle line, meaning you want to ensure dead skin is removed from the cuticle area and the nail is totally clean. “The cuticle area needs to be cleaned thoroughly so the color can be applied neatly and evenly without flooding the skin,” says Swan.

Once your nails are prepped, apply two thin coats of your favorite merlot polish and finish with a top coat of your choice. A super glossy one works well, but “I also like a matte finish with small gold accents,” says Swan. She also advocates for a merlot French manicure or micro French if you wanna incorporate a little minimalist nail art. Now, top off that glass and check out these merlot red nail ideas that will make your fingertips look absolutely regal.

Catharine Malzahn is a contributing beauty writer at Cosmo. She’s covered and tested all things nails, from the coolest new polish colors to cuticle care and nail art trends.

Catharine Malzahn is a contributing beauty writer at Cosmopolitan and was previously the beauty assistant at Good Housekeeping, Woman's Day, and Prevention.

#6810. Phishing Threats Totaled 7.3 Billion in Q3 2026

E-mail phishing threats reached 7.3 billion in Q3 2026, with September activity increasing 41% from August, according to Microsoft Threat Intelligence.

According to a report from Microsoft Threat Intelligence and the Microsoft Defender Security Research Team, phishing detections reached nearly 3 billion in September alone.

The findings also highlighted changes in attacker techniques, including business-service impersonation, credential theft, and social engineering through Microsoft Teams.

The Redmond-based firm recognized approximately 129 million malicious messages spoofing the sender domains of tracked business services during Q3.

DocuSign was the most frequently spoofed brand in September, accounting for 29% of the month's tracked spoofing activity. Adobe, SurveyMonkey, and Barracuda also experienced increases toward the end of the quarter.

The research found that some malicious messages were delivered despite failing e-mail authentication checks and being identified as threats.

In September, tenant- or user-level security overrides applied to 63% of these messages with a recorded security outcome — most involved tenant-level exceptions.

Microsoft warned that overly broad exceptions intended to support legitimate business communications can weaken protection against impersonation attacks.

The company emphasized that these findings do not establish whether recipients opened the messages or whether accounts were compromised.

Microsoft also recorded approximately 141,000 malicious Teams call attempts during Q3.

Attackers increasingly used ordinary personal names instead of explicitly impersonating IT support personnel. Such display names accounted for 46% of an observed sample in July, rising to 88% in September.

Meanwhile, QR code phishing declined 67% compared to Q2, totaling roughly 12.1 million attacks.

CAPTCHA-gated phishing activity increased toward the end of the quarter, reaching 3.1 million detected attacks in September. SVG attachments played a significant role in the increase.

Credential theft remained the primary objective of malicious attachment campaigns, with approximately 94% to 96% of payload-based attacks directing users to phishing sites or fraudulent sign-in pages.

Microsoft recommended reviewing Exchange Online Protection and Defender for Office 365 configurations, enabling Safe Links and Safe Attachments, and strengthening authentication protections.

The company also advised organizations to review security exceptions and verify the identities of external Teams contacts before responding to suspicious requests.

For more information, go to the Microsoft blog post.

However, some confusion and misconceptions exist surrounding details of the program, including which programs may qualify, how parents can apply for scholarships, and how public school students can benefit.

#6808. In ‘Possible Love,’ Jeon Do-yeon Delivers the Year’s Most Shattering Performance. Can It Take Her to the Oscars?

In the nearly three decades since she made her big-screen debut in 1997’s The Contact, Jeon Do-yeon has earned a richly deserved reputation in South Korea—and far beyond it—as the kind of actor who inhabits her characters so fully that it ceases to feel like acting at all. (International audiences likely know her best for 2007’s Secret Sunshine, a wrenching portrait of a grieving mother that made her the first Korean performer to win an acting prize at the Cannes Film Festival.)

Critics often reach for the word “fearless” to describe her, but when we speak via Zoom at the tail end of a marathon press day in Seoul, Jeon waves that notion away.

“I’m always scared, and I’m full of fear, especially in front of the camera,” she says, with a laugh. “I’ve been working as an actor for quite some time, but it’s an ongoing process.” In fact, it’s important to her that she never gets too comfortable. “I actually enjoy having that fear and anxiety, and trying my best to work through it, because sometimes something completely new comes out of that struggle.”

That willingness to sit in discomfort is vividly, devastatingly evident in Possible Love, out now on Netflix after a theatrical run in October—and recently selected as South Korea’s official submission for the 2027 Academy Awards. The film marks the long-awaited return of legendary auteur Lee Chang-dong (arguably best known for the hypnotic 2018 masterpiece Burning, which became the first Korean movie ever shortlisted for the best international feature Oscar and topped critics’ year-end lists across the West) after an eight-year hiatus, and a reunion for Jeon and Lee nearly 20 years after Secret Sunshine.

Constructed with Lee’s signature novelistic sweep, Possible Love centers on the complicated dynamic between two married couples from starkly different strata of contemporary Korean society. Jeon stars as Mi-ok, a pragmatic mask-factory worker living quietly with her young son and her husband, Ho-seok (played by her frequent screen partner Sul Kyung-gu). Years after a mass factory layoff and a violently suppressed labor strike, Ho-seok remains haunted by the trauma. When the funeral of a former co-worker brings them into the orbit of Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong, best known as the rich mom in Parasite), an intellectual documentary filmmaker chronicling laid-off laborers, and her wealthy, enigmatic husband Sang-woo (Zo In-sung), Mi-ok agrees to let Ye-ji film their daily lives. Yet what begins as a study of liberal empathy—and a moving portrait of across-the-divide solidarity—gradually warps into something far more strange and ambiguous, exploring the fault lines of privilege, hidden desire, and voyeurism.

Oscar buzz has swirled around her performance—a stunning and powerfully subtle tightrope walk of stoicism and simmering longing—since the film premiered at the Venice Film Festival in September, but Jeon remains pragmatic about what all this fanfare actually means. “When I won the award at Cannes 20 years ago, I remember thinking, Is this going to change my life? Probably not. Am I going to change as an actor because I have a Cannes award?” she reflects. “I’m very happy that we’re competing at the Oscars, and it’s wonderful that people are talking about the film, but I don’t think it will change me or the way I perform in any way.”

Below, Jeon discusses her on-screen reunion with Sul Kyung-gu, the unlikely magic fostered by Lee Chang-dong’s aversion to having his actors rehearse, and how a story of trauma and class tension deeply rooted in Korean society found universal resonance.

Vogue: Now that Possible Love is streaming on Netflix and reaching a massive global audience, how are you feeling? Have you been hearing much feedback?

Jeon Do-yeon: I watched the movie once again as soon as it was on Netflix. I think Possible Love is a type of movie that leaves a different afterglow for different people, and people can analyze it differently and interpret it in endless ways. Now that it’s on Netflix, I feel like people are finding their own ways to think about the movie—it leaves a lot of food for thought. I’m very proud that people are talking a lot about it.

To go back to the beginning, you obviously have a deep history with director Lee Chang-dong. How did he first approach you about Possible Love? I believe this idea had been gestating for almost a decade.

I do know that Director Lee worked on this project for quite a long time—he had it in his mind for more than 10 years. Ten years ago, he wanted to talk about this worker and his wife, the couple who had been laid off. Sometimes that story diverged into different paths, and sometimes they were scrapped; I know there were a lot of different versions along the way. When I knew that he finally had a script, I really wanted to know what it was about. I was waiting for that script. [Laughs.]

Given how layered the story is, what struck you most when you finally read it? What drew you to Mi-ok?

When I first read the script, I could feel the 10 years’ worth of thought and effort that Director Lee put into it. I was very touched reading it, and I was like, “Of course this is a Chang-dong film. It is this good.” And then I thought about what I could relate to about my character, Mi-ok. Of all the traits that she has, I think she holds this anxiety, and that anxiety stems from her wish to protect certain things. Although Mi-ok may seem a little bit fragile or weak from the outside, I think she’s a very strong woman inside, so that is something that I took note of.

Zo In-sung as Sang-woo, Jeon Do-yeon as Mi-ok, and director Lee Chang-dong on the set of Possible Love.

One of the aspects of your performance I found most striking is the physicality—the way Mi-ok holds herself is such an important part of how her story is told. Did you develop that beforehand, or did you find it on set?

If I hadn’t worked with Director Lee before, then I would have spent a lot of time trying to learn more about this character and to deeply understand her. But I know how he works, and he always stresses emptying my mind as an actor. He wants me not to express, but to feel the character. The preparation process for me was mostly about making sure that I get very accustomed to the lines that my character speaks, so it really feels like it’s me speaking, but it’s actually Mi-ok speaking through me.

You’ve worked with Sul Kyung-gu more than any other actor in your career, I believe. So much of the film relies on the subtleties of that relationship—did your real-life friendship and trust help?

I think I really know him well in real life, and as an actor as well. But while we were working on this project, and as he transformed into the character of Ho-seok, I discovered new facets of him. There’s always a new side of him that would surprise me, so I’m still looking forward to working with him on another project so I can discover yet another new side of him. We have this friendship and trust that we’ve built over the years, and I’m pretty sure that they helped. When you’re trying to express the chemistry of a very long relationship of a married couple, sometimes you have to make efforts to show that aspect. But we didn’t have to try too hard because we already had that trust built between us. If we do look like a real married couple in the movie, I think it’s partly thanks to that.

Jeon Do-yeon as Mi-ok and Sul Kyung-gu as Ho-seok.

At the opposite end of the spectrum, this was your first time working with Cho Yeo-jeong. The dynamic between Mi-ok and Ye-ji walks a very delicate line between sisterhood and something more transactional. Did the two of you discuss that, or did you prefer to discover it in the room?

We actually didn’t talk about our characters before going into production. When you work with Director Lee, he’s sort of against the actors having too many biases or prejudices or information about characters before going into the shoot, because he believes something very novel and fresh can come out when it’s your first time being in that scene, when it’s your first time talking. I didn’t want to jinx that by speaking with her about our characters beforehand. In the beginning, my character, Mi-ok, believes that if Ye-ji films us, then that is a way of protecting my family—a way of finding hope. But as they get closer, she realizes that there is a gap between the two people, herself and Ye-ji, and the wall grows higher and higher as they get closer.

Director Lee is known for his naturalism. Did that mean doing dozens of takes until you lost the sense that you’re acting? Did scenes ever head in unexpected directions based on how you were all interacting?

Director Lee is not actually the type who shoots a lot of takes, because he doesn’t really tell us exactly what it is that he wants from a scene. What he tries to do instead is to look into the chemistry and the conversation between the actors and try to find something new from it. Instead of Director Lee saying, “Okay, let’s do the lines,” he would just say, “Why don’t we talk? Let’s talk.” He likes everything very lively and raw, so that’s how we did it, and he didn’t want us to have a lot of rehearsals. And regarding whether the direction of a scene actually changed after working—it didn’t happen, because there was no fixed direction in the beginning.

Jeon Do-yeon as Mi-ok and Cho Yeo-jeong as Ye-ji.

Korean cinema has obviously exploded in popularity globally over the past decade, and Possible Love is getting a huge amount of international attention. How do you view this global wave? Do you think much about reaching Western audiences?

I don’t have plans on “going global” or anything as an actor! But I do hope that Korean content and Korean cinema will be beloved around the globe going forward as well. It’s just such a joy to be able to share different stories and different emotions with people that speak different languages and have different cultures. It’s such a good opportunity for us to transcend borders, transcend language. I hope more of those opportunities will come.

Possible Love is rooted in a very specific Korean tragedy, yet the hollowing out of industrial working-class communities is something people recognize all over the world. Did you worry at all during filming about whether such a locally specific story would translate, especially on a global platform like Netflix?

When we were filming, we actually did think about how this is a very Korea-specific sort of incident. Would people around the world be able to resonate with this story? Particularly because there is no dramatic event that happens throughout the movie; it’s just about the four people and their emotions, and that’s what really brings a narrative towards the end. We were a little bit worried. But I actually realized after screening overseas that the issue of laid-off workers is not something that’s specific to Korea—it’s happening all around the world, and it is still happening in some parts of the world. I could feel that a lot of people who are not Korean, who don’t live in Korea, are resonating with the themes and the emotions that are captured in the movie. And the moon at the very end of the movie? Anybody in any part of the world can see the moon. That’s something that’s very universal.

This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

#6807. ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Fans Are Upset Over “Grammy Night” Dance-Off Pairings

It’s Grammy Night this week on Dancing With the Stars, and aside from the remaining couples dancing to Grammy-winning songs, we’ve entered dance-offs! And fans are...not thrilled about the pairings.

In case you’re new to dance-offs, “couples face off against one another on the ballroom floor as they dance head-to-head in the same style at the same time.” Judges then pick the winners, who get extra points added to their scores.

Sounds simple enough, but the pairings are causing some backlash:

Amber and Pasha vs. Ezra and DaniPerforming rumbas to “The Boy Is Mine,” performed live by Brandy and Monica.

Jenna and Val vs. Tatyana and JanPerforming cha-chas to “The Middle,” performed live by Maren Morris.

Connor and Rylee vs. Maura and MarkPerforming cha-chas to “All I Wanna Do,” performed live by Sheryl Crow.

Basically, fans feel like couples with similar scores and dance backgrounds should have been paired together. Example: Jenna should go up against Amber due to them both having previous experience with complex routines (Jenna was a professional dancer and Amber is an Olympic skater). Meanwhile, Tatyana should have gone up against Maura, and Ezra should have gone up against Connor, since they have similar overall scores.

Guess we’ll see what happens tonight (November 10), but expect some backlash. Reminder: Dancing With the Stars returns to its original schedule after airing on Monday night last week. Tune in live at 8 p.m. ET on Disney+ and ABC.
