#6801. The Kitchen Trends Designers Expect to See Everywhere in 2027

The National Kitchen & Bath Association’s 2027 forecast has arrived.

Above: the kitchen of an Athens home designed by Nashmita Rajiah.

Partial walls, hidden appliances, and pantries with room for prep are among the kitchen features expected to gain ground next year, according to the National Kitchen & Bath Association’s 2027 Kitchen Trends Report. Based on a survey of 830 kitchen-industry professionals—including designers, manufacturers, remodelers, and architects—the report looks at the layouts, materials, lighting, and technology they expect to be popular over the next three years. Here are the main takeaways.

NKBA reports growing interest in partial walls, movable partitions, and separate kitchen zones—a shift from last year’s forecast, when open layouts were still gaining ground. Dedicated prep spaces and back kitchens are also emerging features, cited by nearly half of designers.

Kitchens are still expected to get bigger, with 52 percent of designers anticipating growth. The kitchen’s surrounding rooms are growing, too. NKBA reports that mudrooms and laundry spaces are increasingly being integrated into kitchen plans. The vast majority of designers expect attached mudrooms to be popular over the next three years, with 45 percent anticipating mudrooms getting larger and 43 percent expecting laundry spaces to grow.

Appliances are increasingly being incorporated into cabinetry rather than left on display. Eighty-five percent of designers agree cabinets are being designed to hide appliances and other functional elements, and roughly two-thirds say open shelving is on its way out in favor of enclosed storage.

Pantries are taking on more work, too. Nearly 90 percent agree they are becoming multifunctional extensions of the kitchen, and three-quarters expect dedicated small-appliance stations to be popular. Separate beverage areas continue to gain support, with 90 percent anticipating their popularity, up from 85 percent in the 2026 report.

Neutrals remain the leading color of choice, followed by greens and blues. For cabinetry, light and medium tones draw equal interest, and white oak is the preferred wood for roughly half of designers. Islands don’t necessarily have to match: a little more than half expect them to feature a different color from the surrounding cabinets. Quartzite and quartz lead countertop preferences, with nearly half of designers favoring honed or matte finishes.

The lighting forecast includes under-cabinet lights, illuminated cabinet interiors, nighttime path lighting, sconces, and pendants. Eighty-four percent of designers agree kitchens will incorporate multiple layers of light, and 78 percent say lighting is increasingly being used as a design feature rather than just a functional necessity. Under-cabinet lighting leads the forecast at 87 percent, followed by interior-cabinet lighting at 76 percent.

NKBA identifies ventilation, water filtration, touchless faucets, and sound-absorbing materials among the report’s wellness features. Designers are also discussing ways to make kitchens more resilient: 65 percent cite leak-detection systems and automatic shut-off valves, 62 percent cite backup power, and a little over half point to ventilation and air filtration.

Julia Cancilla is the social media & news editor at ELLE Decor, where she oversees the brand's socials and covers design, pop culture, and emerging trends. She also authors the monthly ELLE Decoroscope column. Her work has appeared in Inked magazine, House Beautiful, Marie Claire, and more.

Love Is Blind Season 11 star Rob Feeley is breaking his silence after a truly messy season. Quick recap: Rob got engaged to Michaella Giorgio in the Pods, but things went south during a cast-wide bar hang, where Rob told everyone he didn’t care about their relationship. Obviously, Michaella ended things, and Rob has some things to say now that he’s watched the season.

“Now that the reunion has aired and this chapter comes to a close, I’ve been reflecting on everything this experience has taught me,” Rob wrote on Instagram. “I’m truly grateful for the people I’ve met, the memories made, and the personal growth that came with both the incredible moments and the challenges. Looking back, there are moments I wish I had handled differently. There were times when I felt overwhelmed and let my emotions get the best of me. While those moments don’t reflect the person I strive to be, I recognize that they happened, and I take responsibility for how I reacted and where I could have communicated better.”

Rob went on to “acknowledge the hurt I caused Michaella,” saying “she deserved to feel heard, respected, and understood. I’m genuinely sorry for the times I fell short and for how I reacted in certain situations. My intentions don’t change the fact that my actions affected her, and I take responsibility for that.”

Rob also confirmed that he and Michaella have been in touch since the show filmed two (two!) years ago, and that they have moved on with “mutual respect.” He then reminded fans that they only saw “a small part of a much bigger experience, and not every conversation or situation can be fully understood from what makes it onto the screen.”

The burgeoning reality star ended his musings by teasing some “projects and opportunities” he’s been working on, and noted that “There’s a lot to look forward to in the coming weeks, and I’m excited to share what’s next.”

Every year, the art, film, fashion, and entertainment industries head to the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA) for an evening of glamorous fundraising, celebration, and live music. The Art+Film Gala, as it’s called, has seen everyone from Kim Kardashian and Kendall Jenner to Charli XCX and Troye Sivan to Cindy Crawford and Kaia Gerber, welcoming models, actors, philanthropists, musicians, athletes, and more.

The familiar faces were joined by Anya Taylor-Joy, Alix Earle, Andrew Garfield, Benito Skinner, Candice Swanepoel, Chloe Kim, Emily Ratajkowski, Jordyn Woods-Towns, Julia Garner, Lindsey Vonn, Monica Lewinsky, Odessa A’zion, Rosie Huntington-Whiteley, Salma Hayek, Viola Davis, and more.

#6790. How Creative Director Hype Is Lifting Resale

Hype around new creative directors’ hit pieces — from Matthieu Blazy’s pony hair heels for Chanel to Michael Rider’s massive Celine Disc sunglasses — is having a halo effect on the resale market that’s rippling across eras and raising prices on key items.

That’s according to Ebay’s latest Watchlist report, which goes live today and takes stock of the rising resale trends for Fall/Winter 2026. The report sheds light on how creative debuts over the past year are impacting what and who people are searching for and selling, and how far the hype is extending beyond current collections.

Searches for Matthieu Blazy, for instance, jumped 291% when his first Chanel collection hit stores. At the same time, listings for Karl Lagerfeld-era Chanel rose 87% year-on-year. Searches for Demna rose 42% following his first Gucci runway show, while listings for Tom Ford-era Gucci increased 49% year-on-year, reflecting how users capitalize on current interest to sell past collections. It follows the trend of pieces from defining designer eras increasingly entering circulation on Ebay, from Demna’s Balenciaga (up 204% year-on-year) to Phoebe Philo’s Chloé (up 165%).

At Dior, meanwhile, searches for Jonathan Anderson rose 92% following his first couture show. Average sales prices for John Galliano-era Dior, meanwhile, increased 81% in the same period.

It’s a shift reflected across the resale market. Blazy’s appointment drove searches for the designer up 10,976% on The RealReal, according to The RealReal’s 2026 resale report, released in August, reflecting the impact current brand heat can have on its past collections circulating in the secondhand market. On Ebay, Chanel didn’t rank among the top-purchased luxury brands from 2022 to 2024. In 2025, it snagged fifth place, and in 2026, it jumped to third, trailing Louis Vuitton and Gucci (which have held the top two spots since 2022).

“When someone new takes the helm, they’re not necessarily reinventing the wheel but very often revisiting the codes, silhouettes and references that made the house interesting in the first place,” says stylist Brie Welch, who worked on the report as Ebay’s resident stylist. “Seeing a brand reinterpreted through a new creative lens naturally sparks curiosity about its past collections.”

It’s a sign of where consumers are at. Shoppers are following brands and their runway shows closely — evidenced by their inclination towards ultra-specific fashion search terms and the impact of a debut show on searches, listings, and sales. That consumers are turning to secondhand marketplaces like Ebay is indicative of shoppers’ desires to tap into current trends while finding better value. It’s reflective of trends in the primary marketplace: spending isn’t expected to dip, but consumers are placing greater emphasis on perceived value. If shoppers determine that this is better in the secondary marketplace than the primary, brands ought to pay attention.

Galliano’s Dior isn’t the only category seeing a price hike. Cultural heat has driven luxury secondhand prices up across the board, per Ebay’s findings. However, the fact that luxury prices continue to tick up has likely also played a role in the spike. Still, Kirsty Keoghan, Ebay’s general manager of EU fashion and luxury, credits many of the price increases (measured for this report from January to September 2026) to celebrity sightings.

The Row’s Margaux Bag, for instance, continues to climb in price, up 137% year-on-year. Celebs including Zoë Kravitz and Kendall Jenner sported the bag during this timeframe. Demand for Gucci’s Giglio tote, carried by Dakota Johnson and Suki Waterhouse, was up 103%.

“There is an intentionality about owning something with cultural relevance, longevity, and a sense of value,” Keoghan says, noting that shopping for secondhand designer fashion has become more culturally responsive.

This ties into the return of the It-bag, as shoppers look for styles they’re seeing blow up in culture. Global listings for Balenciaga’s Le City bag, which is having yet another resurgence, are up 936%. (Who could forget Sienna Miller getting papped in a denim mini skirt with her red city bag slung over her shoulder back in 2004? Now, the bag — which had its 25th anniversary on Monday — is on the arm of everyone from Harris Dickinson to Bella Hadid.) The Loewe Amazona 180 (up 440%), the Valentino Garavani VLogo Bag (up 358%), and the Bottega Veneta Veneta Bag (up 158%) are also seeing surges in listings, which Welch puts down to celeb style mainstays such as Kravitz and Jacob Elordi getting papped wearing and styling such bags.

Current runway trends are also feeding back into secondhand market purchases, as consumers seek to tap into what’s trending now via previous season pieces. At a moment when consumer anxiety is still high — which isn’t necessarily putting a dent on spending — opting for a pre-loved item when making a purchase as a style choice can feel like a safer bet versus a brand-new splurge, even as resale prices hike with demand, Keoghan says.

“We are seeing how quickly a new runway moment can evoke an interest for shoppers in a brand’s archive, sending them in search of special pieces with a story,” Keoghan says.

Prada skirts were a breakout trend not just in fashion discourse. Seemingly inspired by the show, shoppers turned to the secondhand market to source past collection skirts in the days following Prada’s SS27 show on September 22 in Milan. Global searches for “Prada skirt” spiked more than 360% compared to the beginning of September, reflecting a runway-inspired uptick.

“Suddenly, you’re looking at a sort of dated silhouette differently,” Welch says, noting that consumers are finding success looking at the secondhand marketplace for A-line skirts that exist in the market. “You can find an earlier version of the idea, sometimes at a more accessible price point, and make it your own.”

This season’s emphasis on shoes was also a search booster for resale. On Ebay, Chanel — which has had a heavy rotation of slingbacks on recent runways — seemed to have the biggest impact once again. Searches for slingbacks are up over 65% versus the start as fashion month, and searches for Chanel slingbacks are up 50%.

“People are shopping with a sharper point of view; they want to be part of the conversation, and they are shopping pre-loved to achieve that,” Keoghan says.

#6783. Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce Re-Created One of Their First Public Moments After the Chiefs’ Win

Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce made a rare move following the Kansas City Chiefs’ win over the New York Jets yesterday. The newlyweds left Arrowhead Stadium together, re-creating one of their first public moments as a couple by driving off in a vintage Cadillac Coupe DeVille. Onlookers filmed the happy couple waving to the crowd as they departed.

When Swift attended her first-ever Chiefs game in September 2023, the pair did the same thing, leaving in Kelce’s 1970 Chevrolet Chevelle 408 Stroker convertible. They seem to have a thing for the classic cars, and even raffled off a 1970 Chevelle at their wedding, an apparent homage to the 2023 moment.

The singer attended Kelce’s game against the Jets with her parents and her friend Karlie Kloss. It marked Swift’s first appearance in years with Kloss, who also attended the singer’s wedding in July.

Swift usually leaves Arrowhead Stadium undetected. Back in October 2025, she told BBC Radio 2’s Greg James that her greatest skill as a spy would be “entering and exiting the building without being seen. Just put me in a garbage can, roll me, I don’t care. Honestly, I can fit in like, a purse. Sometimes I just can’t deal with it [the paparazzi and attention] and in those times, I won’t deal with it. I’m just digging tunnels under every building I go into, airlifting in through the skylight.”

In January 2025, Parade spoke with Ty Richmond, president of event services at Allied Universal, who detailed how intricate plans can be to get VIPs in and out of football games. “When you have a very high-profile individual [coming to an event], the logistics of that person getting into the venue and getting into the specific location where they need to sit is a job and a process in itself,” he said, adding that for someone at Swift’s level of fame, thousands of security professionals could be involved in days of preparation.

“If, for instance, there are fans that are known to be targeting [a star] and/or have been a threat in the past because they’re fixated on a talent or a personality, those are all very specialized, very confidential issues that have to be understood and mitigated properly,” he added.

#6782. ‘Clashing Through the Snow’ First Photos Show Christopher Briney and Michelle Randolph on a Chaotic Cross-Country Road Trip (Exclusive)

These two rivals have to find their way to NYC and you won’t believe who they run into.

What’s this?! A special early gift from our friends at Amazon?! That’s right, we’re finally getting our first look at Clashing Through the Snow, the upcoming Prime Video rom-com that is ready to take you on the ultimate road trip with Christopher Briney and Michelle Randolph.

The film follows two rival book editors who get stranded on their way to New York from Los Angeles. Despite not getting along with each other, the two decide to drive cross country after hearing that budget cuts might leave one of them without a job. However, with each of them chasing a career-saving deal, they got to find their way to New York ASAP and every mile counts! One car, thousands of miles, and plenty of time to get to know one another. Sounds like the perfect recipe for some sparks to fly between them!

“Clashing has the warmth and sincerity that I look for in a holiday rom com,” director Carlson Young told Cosmopolitan. “I think you can expect to laugh and follow Chris and Michelle through their journeys wholeheartedly!”

Christopher Briney plays Ryan, “a Type A editor at a book publishing company. He’s very career driven and likes things his way.” He notes, “You can expect a lot of laughs throughout the film. It’s really fun.”

He clashes with none other than Michelle’s character Hannah, who she calls, “a fiercely passionate, slightly chaotic literary editor who has a very strong opinion about pretty much everything. She’s ambitious, impulsive, and maybe a little too invested in her work. When her career is suddenly on the line, she finds herself on a cross-country journey with her biggest professional rival, who also happens to be her complete opposite.”

“Naturally, everything that could go wrong does. It's a really fun adventure, and there's a lot of heart underneath all the chaos,” Michelle adds. “There is something very special about watching two people who are so convinced they have nothing in common slowly start to see each other differently.”

For Michelle, this was a way to try something completely new as she is mostly known for her dramatic and horror roles.

“There was something really refreshing about doing a movie that’s primary intention is to make people laugh and feel good. I grew up loving romantic comedies. They're nostalgic, comforting, and often become part of people's traditions,” she revealed. “There is such value in joy! Especially during the holidays.”

One thing that is undeniable: how much we’re excited to see them play off each other. According to Carlson, Christopher and Michelle were right for their roles in a variety of ways.

“Chris is such a charming human and we knew he’d crush this role. He’s just a great actor and so fun to watch,” she said. “And when we saw Michelle, she has this effortless, magnetic quality and encapsulated the earnest nature of Hannah so well. She’s really funny. I’m just generally in love with her and I can’t wait for audiences to experience her in this role.”

They’re not the only major names in the cast! Paris Hilton, Julia Fox, Tan France, Andrew Schulz, PJ Byrne, and Zarna Garg also appear in the film. And there’s one other actor whose character has been a total mystery…until now: Lukas Gage!

“Lukas said to me, ‘What about Chris Elliott in Scary Movie as a north star for Teddy?’ I said, ‘Hell yeah,’” Carlson said.

According to Michelle, “Lukas plays Teddy, the incredibly enthusiastic host of a rather unconventional bed-and-breakfast that Hannah and Ryan stumble upon during their trip,” she revealed. “He's wonderfully strange, slightly unsettling, and somehow completely oblivious to how bizarre everything around him is. Lukas is hilarious in the role. It's one of my favorite little detours in the movie.”

It’s definitely the perfect kind of vibes for a rom-com, which Carlson says was inspired by other great films.

“I thought about Four Christmases, Planes, Trains, and Automobiles, and While You Were Sleeping. I wanted to feel the nostalgia that gets me out of bed in the morning, and nod to the classics that are always a sort of cinematic comfort during the holidays.”

Will Ryan and Hannah make it home on time? You’re going to have to tune in to find out!

Clashing Through the Snow premieres on Prime Video on November 23, 2026.

#6780. How Lafayette 148 Became New York’s Newest Heritage Brand

What’s Lafayette 148’s secret to longevity? After 30 years in business, the company has claimed a seat as one of New York’s newest heritage labels. Co-founder and CEO Deirdre Quinn attributes that status to a combination of consistency and evolution, the balance of knowing what needs to change over time and what absolutely cannot.

The brand’s biggest turning point was during the pandemic, when abrupt shifts in customer demand collided with supply chain challenges that threatened to put the company out of business. Quinn and Emily Smith, Lafayette 148’s creative director who joined the brand in 2002 as an intern, made the decision to move the label further upmarket, recommitting to its vertically integrated business model to protect margins and avoid the trappings of order minimums that most brands have to meet. They invested in better quality materials and shifted the majority of sales from wholesale retail to its direct-to-consumer network of stores and e-commerce, with more full-price sellthrough even as prices have increased in step with quality improvements.

Lafayette 148 creative director Emily Smith.

Today, Quinn says she sees Lafayette 148’s competition being less fellow American brands and more as European luxury brands. The brand holds a two-hour slot for its presentations on the New York Fashion Week calendar (Quinn and Smith say they prefer the time to mingle with guests and clients that presentations allow), and this year, started hosting a showroom in Paris for the first time, and also started selling in Harrods last year. The brand projects sales for 2026 will be up 12% over 2025, to $150 million, growth that Quinn attributes to the luxury pivot.

Now, Lafayette 148 is eyeing a bigger US takeover. This fall, the brand opened its first store in Dallas, Texas — an investment more brands are making following the shuttering of the city’s Neiman Marcus — and has plans to open its first stores on the West Coast in 2027. Abroad, the Middle East and Japan are two regions the team is eyeing. That expansion is bolstered by the company’s first C-suite supporting Quinn, including a chief marketing officer, chief merchant and chief commercial officer.

In a joint interview, Quinn and Smith spoke about the recipe for succeeding as an independent label in New York through intentional reinvention.

Vogue: Lafayette 148 is celebrating 30 years in business this year. What are the steps you took to ensure you’re still standing today?

Deirdre Quinn: Luckily, as a privately owned company, we were able to evolve into what works for us. We want people who want our brand. I don’t need to force it. I’ve watched a lot of people come and go in my 30 years. Luxury has always been the goal for us. So we had to rebuild. Now, we live in the next six months because if that last several years have taught us anything, it’s that you can’t plan like you used to. It makes it exciting.

Emily Smith: For me, it comes down to the quality. We’ve always had really great quality, and I think that’s because we’re vertical. I’ve been working for Deirdre for many years. I grew up here and grew up within the factory, and so I just knew the potential and that we could push it even more. We’re more innovative today with our suppliers, with more of our point of view. That has been the defining difference between where we were and how we’ve evolved. And that part’s been really fun because each season you can stick to the DNA, but just move it a little bit further each season, and move our client along a little bit every season too, but not to a place where she doesn’t recognize it anymore. That’s really important.

Vogue: What advice would you give to a brand starting out today? What advice do you still find yourself seeking?

DQ: I deal with a lot of young brands that want advice and how to get into this industry and what do I think? I usually say to people, “You might not want to hear it from me because I’m a very straight shooter and I have to be honest. I’m not going to act like this is an easy industry. It’s a really tough industry and you should learn from others before you get too far down a road that you didn’t realize was so complicated.”

The advice that I would ask might be around the best way to finance a privately owned business. That’s quite interesting to me. Certainly the thoughts on being more of a global business and what experiences they’ve had in it, doing more non-sized business. We are such a sized business — we have 58 sizes — and it’s the hardest part because of the engineering that goes into making a garment look good.

The label, previously a mid-tier department store name, has transformed itself into a luxe favourite for high-end customers. How did it pull it off?

Vogue: Have you ever considered raising outside investment?

DQ: I thought about it at the worst possible times — the times where you needed help with your cash flow — and that would be a horrible time to sell the company because you wouldn’t get what you put into it. Today, I’m not looking at all. I don’t need the distraction. I have learned to never say never, but for now, I think it’s too exciting for us. I have a plan through 2030, and I’m optimistic about that.

It’s such a power and privilege to not have to answer to someone else. I know that I am a very hands-on owner, and I would be so afraid of somebody coming in here and the first thing they want to do is buy less expensive fabrics or something that just starts a race to the bottom. And it doesn’t mean that there might not someday be some amazing person or company that says, “Wow, you’ve built an American luxury brand. That’s not normal around here. Together, we could take it to another level.” But again, for now, I’m just really focused on rebuilding and continuing to grow what we have and both top and bottom line.

Vogue: You’ve described Lafayette’s customers as successful career women. How do you evolve who your customer base is? Are you thinking about how to capture younger generations?

ES: I want to take a step back to take a step forward on that one. When we were working on the 30th collection, I came across some old sketches that were by the first designer here. And there was sort of this sense of responsibility that you always have in this position to maintain the brand and maintain the clients and never change it too much. And it was really fun to go back and look at where we had started and to see the progression of how it’s evolved. The biggest takeaway was that when Lafayette started, it was addressing career women who needed boardroom suits for the office every day. And look how much our lifestyles have completely changed.

Those are things you almost don’t think about. You just subconsciously are evolving them because we are the clients. We know what those changes are. We are in touch with them. I think it’s more of a sensibility than really thinking about a demographic. We never talk about an age range. We know our customer is an accomplished woman. She’s busy at any age, at any stage in her career or whatever she has going on, and that idea of versatility and wardrobing and the product that she has in her closet is always relevant. I think the one thing I’ve heard consistently from all of our clients is usually she wants to be taken seriously. She never wants to walk in a room and feel silly or fussy or like the clothes are wearing for her. I think that can cross any age range and just making sure that we stay true to our brand DNA and all of that just will kind of translate to any demographic.

Behind the scenes of Lafayette 148’s 30th anniversary campaign shoot with costume designer-turned-model Sophie de Rakoff.

ES: Not really. Proportion and relevance are two important things for me, and technology, because I do think it affects fabric constructions and things like that. But we’re not interested, and our client’s not interested, in what’s the new hot thing right now. To me, it’s more the hemlines are up or down, little things that are more subconscious than specifically this is the statement for the season. I love when people are like, “What’s the color of the season?” I’m like, “I don’t know.” That feels like such an old-fashioned thing to ask, right? It’s sort of what works for you. You should dress for what works for your shape, your style. For us, tailoring is always more important.

As far as building and growing our base, to me, it’s more about getting our brand in more conversations and having more people wearing it, I think is the biggest growth opportunity. I think we’ve been a hidden secret, and there’s sort of a nice nuance to that. But I think just slowly getting it to other people at a healthy pace that feels manageable that we don’t ever sacrifice the integrity of what we’re doing. And potentially we do collaborations with other categories, but we’re so focused on ready to wear and that’s our expertise.

DQ: We’re open to that. I think building the brand and investing in the marketing is really a focus for now because I think that’s what helps set us apart on top of the product. It has to feel right.

Vogue: How do you plan to maintain this growth from here, what comes next?

DQ: We’ve planned it into the future. Luckily as a privately owned company, we’ve able to evolve into what works for us. We want people that want our brand. I don’t need to force it. [As we continue to expand into Europe], I think the best part will be, we’re a 30-year-old company. We’re not this new brand. We’ve got the stability and the infrastructure to support everything it takes to build a proper long-term partnership.

I am lucky that my partners don’t push me. I don’t have a board. I don’t have a boss, so I don’t focus on a metric like having to hit double-digit growth. Single digit is fine. It’s an extremely open-book type of operation that we’re running, and my team has been with me through the bad times, and I want them to be with me through the good times. We’ve had some really tough times in the last five years, and now I see a really bright future, so I'm excited. I’m more excited for them than for anything else.

#6779. Nicole Kidman Celebrates the Art of Ballet in a Voluminous Chanel Tutu

She made her LACMA Gala debut in a messy high ponytail

Every year, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art welcomes the art, film, fashion, and entertainment industries to its annual fundraising event. Since its inception back in 2011, the Art+Film Gala, as it is known, has become a staple fixture on the fall calendar, seeing everyone from models to actors to philanthropists to musicians to athletes return time and time again. But this year, the starry festivities also saw a new face or two—including the one and only Nicole Kidman.

Making her LACMA debut, Kidman showed up to the event wearing a voluminous Chanel dress from Matthieu Blazy’s Spring/Summer 2027 collection. On top, the taupe-and-cream piece featured a long-sleeve corset bodice, with a raw-edge neckline that contrasted the structured boning below. From the hips, layers and layers of semi-sheer tulle cut at different lengths created a high-low tutu skirt that, even when still, gave the illusion of movement.

Before heading inside, the Babygirl actor—with a messy high ponytail and open-toe heels—stopped for photos by Chris Burden’s Urban Light art installation, which doubled as a red carpet for the evening. She was joined by the likes of Alex Consani, Kim Kardashian, and Paris Hilton.

LACMA’s annual gala was founded to support the museum’s efforts to expand its programming, making film more central to its exhibitions and education. It has placed a focus on the intersection of art and film, and takes a moment each year to celebrate individuals for their contributions to the visual and cinematic arts. Tonight, it honored the work of painter Vija Celmins, known for her photo-realistic explorations of nature, as well as Dune filmmaker Denis Villeneuve. Blackpink’s Rosé was tapped for a musical performance, and, for the 15th year, Leonardo DiCaprio and LACMA trustee Eva Chow served as co-chairs.

#6769. Balmain Resort 2027 Menswear

“For me, the men’s and the women’s, they are kind of like one entity. I really want the men and women to be able to talk to each other.” Antonin Tron was riffing as we riffled the rails of his first pre-spring collections for Balmain, including this first-ever menswear collection for the house. “I don’t necessarily think of them as a couple,” he qualified: “but I think at Balmain the women are quite sexy and out there. And if I was to do something very different for men, it would be weird.”

Looking at his rails simultaneously, that relationship was manifest in substance as well as spirit: “We have a lot of overcrossing material,” Tron confirmed. Yet there was one fundamental difference in his approach to the two wardrobes: while his Balmain woman is an imagined character, his man is more internalized. “I’m also making things that I can’t find myself,” he said. The tailoring block, for instance, arose from his frustration with suits that were either too narrow or too oversized. Here the shoulders were strong, the waist defined and the fit flattering without constriction: very much surfer’s suiting. “Clothes have to help you, no?”

This approach was also apparent in a bodacious pair of heavy cotton canvas trousers, artfully distressed and cut with articulated knees, whose engineered construction looked more thoughtful than luxury utilitarianism tends to. Alongside them was a boxy, leather-collared canvas jacket whose pockets were edged with metal rivets: work-kink.

Reference-wise Tron’s masculine pantheon ranges from the impishness of 1990s Brad Pitt to the gothic wasted glamour of Lou Reed and Andrew Eldritch, the Sisters of Mercy frontman whose band Tron has seen 25 times. Most significant is David Nuuhiwa, the Hawaiian surfer who disrupted and drove forward that pursuit in California during the 1960s and ’70s. What appeals to Tron, he said, is less the beach aesthetic than Nuuhiwa’s impulse to experiment and push forward.

These influences washed through a wardrobe that veered between faded denim and utilitarian outerwear, leather tailoring, laced trousers, leopard-print silks, and richly embroidered evening pieces (many of whose kaleidoscopically immersive fabrics were, like the denim, shared with the womenswear). The double-breasted suiting was especially powerful, its confidently controlled proportions offering a co-ordinated counterpoint to the more flamboyant material treatments.

Tron sees this sensuality as a rejection of bourgeois convention in luxury: the class-generated current his personal temperament crashes against. His instinct is that luxury should enable freedom rather than impose rules. Entwined within spirit and material, the central filament that connects this new Balmain man and the new Balmain woman is Tron himself. “I think slowly, I’m finding that line: I’m finding the woman and the man, basically.”

#6765. The Best Dressed Celebrities at the LACMA Art + Film Gala

From Nicole Kidman in Chanel to Anya Taylor-Joy in vintage Pierre Cardin

Last night, a glamorous cross section of the art, film, fashion, and entertainment industries gathered at Los Angeles County Museum of Art for its annual Art + Film gala, which fundraises for the museum’s film initiatives, exhibitions, acquisitions, and educational programs.

This year’s guests decided to embrace a bit of play with their looks. The event is sponsored by Gucci; so fittingly we saw a lot of the brand on the red carpet. Rosie Huntington-Whiteley, who walked in the Spring 2027 show, embraced drama in a slinky, backless black gown with a slit not at the front, but up the back to reveal just a bit of bum cheek. When Demna spoke about this collection this past fashion month, he said he was most proud of the structural feats of his jersey dresses, light as air but engineered to hang just so. Whiteley walked the show alongside additional LACMA guests including Alex Consani, in a dramatically twisted full-skirted gown, Elsa Hosk, who wore a gray wool gown with a thigh-high slit, and Candice Swanepoel in a dress with full-length silver fringe and slits up to her hips.

Anya Taylor-Joy, styled by Law Roach, pulled from the Pierre Cardin archives, selecting a embroidered silvery-white slip with a ruffled organza evening coat. Kylie Jenner wore a look from couturier of the moment, Ashi Studios, that featured a halter neck gown with an allover deer-like animal print and an oversize tassel at the back. And Julia Garner wore a sculptural black taffeta gown from Loewe, which she paired with oversized earrings from Lisa Eisner.

Perhaps the most fitting look of the evening, Nicole Kidman pulled a much-talked-about dress from Chanel’s Spring 2027 collection by Matthieu Blazy. She and Prince William attended the Festival of Remembrance event in London

Every year, the Festival of Remembrance welcomes people from all over the country to Royal Albert Hall for an evening of celebration, honoring active members of the military, veterans, and all the families who have lost loved ones in the armed forces. With musical performances and personal testimonies, the Saturday evening event kicks off Remembrance Sunday, the official day of remembrance in the United Kingdom.

As always, members of the royal family made an appearance at the annual festival. But this year saw a particularly strong turnout, with King Charles III and Queen Camilla in attendance, as well as Prince William and Princess Kate.

For the occasion, Kate, always intentional with her style choices, put together a look full of meaningful pieces fitting for such a meaningful event. Her black-and-white polka-dot dress, for starters, was the same piece worn to Prince Philip’s memorial service back in 2022. Courtesy of Alessandra Rich, it featured a high mock neckline and long sleeves, with a drop-waist pleated midi skirt and a black belt accent. The princess updated the piece by adding a red poppy—the symbol of remembrance—and her silver Irish Guards regimental brooch, which represented her role as Colonel of the Irish Guards.

For jewelry, the future queen brought a piece of her late grandmother-in-law with her, wearing a sparkling pair of diamond earrings that once belonged to Queen Elizabeth II. The statement jewels featured a cluster of diamonds that created a floral-shaped stud, from which an additional strand of diamonds hung, framed by an outer oval frame of... yes, more diamonds.

#6758. Balmain Resort 2027

“For me, the men’s and the women’s, they are kind of like one entity. I really want the men and women to be able to talk to each other.” Antonin Tron was riffing as we riffled the rails of his first pre-spring collections for Balmain, including his first-ever menswear collection for the house. “I don’t necessarily think of them as a couple,” he qualified: “but I think at Balmain the women are quite sexy and out there. And if I was to do something very different for men, it would be weird.”

Looking at his rails simultaneously, that relationship was manifest in substance as well as spirit: “We have a lot of overcrossing material,” Tron confirmed. The same embroidered surfaces, treated denim, and snakeskin jacquards traveled between the two wardrobes, but in womenswear their expression was differently calibrated. This was a more relaxed continuation of the luxuriously louche and wanton glamour of his last runway collection, which itself had been informed by the Californian desert. “With pre-collection I can explore a bit more the casual side of Balmain,” he said.

That meant injecting a dose of dishevelment into Balmain’s appetite for decoration. Sensuously draped dresses in snakeskin and beautiful, borderline-hallucinogenic florals came with cropped flight jackets, while satin tailoring, sheer lurex blouses, and embellished animalier were countered by washed denim and biker leathers. There were micro cardigans over exposed bras, skirts that succumbed into flowerings of asymmetric ruffle, and lavishly embellished pieces whose surfaces seemed weathered by weeks of sun exposure. What blurred in the haze of Tron’s gaze was much distinction between dressing up and down.

This dissolved tension was more than a styling proposition. Tron has little patience for the idea that luxury dressing must conform either to bourgeois standards of propriety, or fashion’s customary cringe of faux-intellectual snobbishness. “For me, this thing with sexiness is also a class thing,” he said of the physical ideals through which notions of elegance are policed. Balmain, in his view, offers a space to articulate sexuality rather than apologize for it.

He recalled meeting a client in Los Angeles while shooting the collection in Joshua Tree. When he mentioned his last show’s desert-and-hallucinogenics theme, she cheerfully volunteered that she had a house there and used to do exactly that. She was accompanied by her muscular husband. “They both wanted to be hot, and that’s it,” Tron observed. This seemed a pretty good expression of the collection’s carefully direct hedonism. Super-long leather boots and Lucite-heeled wedges provided the strut, while the tasseled Zabriskie bag offered easygoing swing.

His instinct is that luxury should enable freedom rather than impose rules. The filament that connects this new Balmain woman and the new Balmain man, in spirit as much as substance, is Tron himself. “I think slowly, I’m finding that line: I’m finding the woman and the man, basically.”

#6749. How To Crack Resale’s AI Algorithms

The next time someone asks ChatGPT to find them a designer handbag, the answer could be a previously owned version, even if they weren’t originally looking to shop secondhand.

Rémi Bouchez, who was appointed as Vestiaire Collective’s new CTO in March, says the resale platform is working to make its product listing available to OpenAI’s broader agentic shopping systems, which would allow secondhand pieces to appear alongside new products in AI-generated recommendations. The proposed plan follows Vestiaire Collective quietly launching a dedicated app plugin within ChatGPT last month, allowing shoppers to search its pre-owned luxury inventory and compare products using conversational prompts within the chatbot. A shopper searching for a new Prada bag could now conceivably be shown a pre-owned version at a fraction of the price, or an archival design that is no longer available firsthand.

At a time when luxury consumers are questioning rising prices, this could significantly impact the shopping journey. And this is just one part of a wider transformation in how secondhand fashion is discovered. Resale platforms are simultaneously rebuilding their own search and recommendation algorithms, using AI to understand product images, interpret shoppers’ tastes and determine which listings get seen. As a result, the rules of discovery are changing on two fronts: within resale marketplaces themselves, and through the AI assistants that could increasingly direct shoppers towards them.

Bouchez believes that if AI agents like Muse, Instinct and Duet reach mainstream adoption, it could fundamentally change how luxury shoppers weigh up their options.

“These agents are capable of ingesting a ton of information — way more than human shoppers can. They remember user preferences over time, and they can catch things like discreet terms and conditions or shady seller behaviors and put them in front of a user who would have otherwise missed them,” says Bouchez. He explains how an AI agent could compare a Prada bag across several platforms, assessing its condition, authentication details and seller reliability before recommending the best value option, raising the stakes for resellers.

It’s an opportunity resale platforms have long been waiting for. Finding a particular product secondhand has traditionally meant scrolling through multiple marketplace apps, deciphering inconsistent descriptions and comparing endless individual listings. AI now promises to take much of the legwork out of that hunt.

Across the resale industry, rival platforms are investing in both forms of discovery. Depop has enabled shoppers to search its marketplace through Apple’s Visual Intelligence on supported iPhones. Last month, The RealReal introduced its own AI shopping assistant, Ask TRR, built on Google Gemini AI that enables shoppers to search in natural language — or by uploading images of products they’ve seen for visual search — while learning shoppers’ preferences. Speaking on the company’s third-quarter earnings call last week, CEO Rati Levesque said Ask TRR’s early adopters spend 20% more per transaction than non-users. The RealReal is also preparing for shopping journeys that begin outside its own platform. A spokesperson tells Vogue Business the company is restructuring data on its 1.5 million listed items to make them easier for external AI agents to find and recommend.

Together, this represents an AI-driven sea change for resale. While AI may struggle to replicate the subjective judgement involved in fashion discovery, resale presents a more straightforward opportunity. A shopper searching for a particular archival bag doesn’t need their algorithm to have good taste, just to identify the right model and compare available listings by price, condition and authenticity.

Resale discovery is increasingly moving beyond keyword search. At Vestiaire Collective, visual search can now recognise multiple objects in an image and identify similar listings, while its search systems increasingly interpret natural language requests. AI can also extract information from photographs — including aspects of fit and visible defects — that previously depended on sellers filling in descriptions.

Poshmark is also using AI to bridge the gap between what sellers photograph and what shoppers can find. Its “Smart List AI” tool automatically generates searchable titles, descriptions and product categories from uploaded photographs. Chief product officer Heather Friedland says it makes listing creation less of a “heavy lift” once the photos are up, and that listing on Poshmark is now five times faster than before. Poshmark’s AI tool also automates offers, letting Poshmark negotiate with buyers on behalf of the seller, which she says makes selling 50% faster. “We want sellers to focus most on what they do best: source great items and have Poshmark take care of the rest,” she says.

At Depop, shoppers are increasingly browsing the personalized Suggested For You feed rather than starting with a search, says chief product officer Sonia Biddle. Its algorithm responds to individual preferences and emerging cultural trends, while AI identifies listings by category, color and style, making products discoverable even when sellers haven’t used precisely the right keywords.

“Fashion often starts with an idea: an era, an occasion or someone whose style you love, and that’s not always something you can put into words,” Biddle says. “AI helps us understand what you’re after, not just the words you type.” For sellers, that means some longstanding tactics like keyword hashtags may become less important, while product photography, pricing and reliability are becoming harder to ignore.

Depop’s visual search also allows shoppers to upload a photograph or screenshot — including of something spotted in a first-hand retailer — to find similar secondhand pieces. A new-season jacket might inspire a purchase, but not necessarily from the brand selling it.

Resale execs recommend sellers photograph items in natural light, capturing multiple angles and clearly showing any signs of wear. Photo: Courtesy of Depop

As images become more central to discovery, platforms are also investing in how listings look. Last month, Vestiaire announced a partnership with AI photography company Photoroom to standardise the main photograph of every new listing — around 40,000 items a day — bringing the often inconsistent images uploaded by individual sellers closer to the polished aesthetic of first-hand luxury retail.

The technology removes backgrounds, adjusts lighting, centres products and adds realistic shadows. According to results from a randomized A/B test conducted by Vestiaire Collective and Photoroom, listings processed using the new technology had a 5% higher sell-through rate than those using Vestiaire’s previous in-house photo-editing tool, while unique product page views increased by between 3% and 7%.

Next, Vestiaire is experimenting with much more ambitious AI image enhancements that can make the items themselves look more PDP shoot ready, Bouchez says, like digital ironing.

It’s a delicate balance: AI can make a pre-owned handbag look like something fit for a luxury DTC site, but an algorithm that makes a scuff disappear could also undermine the trust on which resale depends. Yet Bouchez says Vestiaire has seen an approximately 6% improvement in the proportion of enhanced listings selling within seven days since these AI image updates, without a corresponding increase in returns.

For sellers, getting discovered still depends heavily on the algorithms operating within resale marketplaces themselves. So what determines which listings appear first, and can sellers influence their ranking?

At Vestiaire, the answer isn’t simply the lowest price or the newest upload. Bouchez describes a three-stage ranking system that identifies relevant products, reorders them according to marketplace factors and then adjusts results to individual preferences. Those factors include condition, pricing, location and seller reliability. Because Vestiaire operates globally, proximity can matter: a nearby item may mean faster shipping, fewer customs complications and easier returns, which may mean it gets surfaced first.

Vestiaire assesses what constitutes a fair price according to factors including condition, location and whether the seller is a professional offering returns. An implausibly cheap luxury item may raise questions about authenticity, rather than look like an irresistible bargain. Bouchez says that analysing these factors is still a combination of humans and AI.

“Trust is a big pillar for Vestiaire — we invest a lot in that trust, on manual verification, on assessing a listing before it’s published,” he says. “Obviously, we want to keep the same level of trust but lower the investment with AI, but the more we can keep this USP high and even increase the trust, the better our position as a platform.”

Depop’s search algorithm prioritises how closely a listing matches a shopper’s query, including brand, category, size and color. Popularity signals — views, likes and additions to shopping bags — also matter, alongside seller history, location and personal shopping preferences. If a listing is underperforming, she recommends new photographs, a more detailed description and a pricing review.

Shoppers, meanwhile, are becoming more deliberate about influencing what appears in their feeds.

“It’s been really interesting hearing our community talk about ‘training their algorithm,’” Biddle says. “People know that what they like, view and save shapes what they see, and they’re becoming really deliberate about it.” But there’s a downside to this hyper-personalization: the more accurately a feed reflects established tastes, the less likely shoppers may be to encounter something unexpected.

Good product photography is increasingly important for visibility on resale platforms. Photo: Courtesy of The RealReal.

To counter AI’s tendency to reinforce existing preferences, Poshmark introduced a new “Tastemaker” programme in September, enlisting fashion figures including Courtney Grow, Colleen Allen and Jalil Johnson to curate shoppable edits from across its resale inventory. The platform has also established a dedicated human merchandising team to work alongside its AI and machine learning specialists, identifying emerging trends and bringing a more editorial approach to product recommendations.

“On trends, a purely algorithmic system tends to amplify what’s already popular,” Friedland says. “Human curation is our counterweight. Our tastemakers bring in new styles and AI then figures out which shoppers those styles will resonate with.”

For shoppers looking to escape their own personalized recommendations, Biddle suggests sorting search results by price or newest first, too. Visual search can also help uncover pieces that shoppers cannot easily describe. On Poshmark, Friedland recommends saving searches for specific archival pieces and liking items to help refine future recommendations.

And as AI agents take on more of the shopping process, the question of what consumers don’t see becomes even more significant. Vestiaire’s ChatGPT integration allows shoppers to compare up to three selected listings, asking the AI agent to explain differences in price, condition and seller information. But it also introduces another gatekeeper: instead of scrolling through hundreds of listings themselves, shoppers may increasingly rely on an AI assistant to decide which options are worth considering — and which never make it onto their shortlist.

For first-hand luxury brands, the implications go beyond losing the occasional sale to a cheaper pre-owned alternative. Resale platforms are accumulating information about which designs consumers continue to desire, years after they disappear from stores. Depop’s Biddle argues that these signals can be valuable for brands developing future collections.

“Resale tells brands something their own sales data can’t: what people still love years after it left the shop floor,” she says. “When we see searches spike for a particular era or label, it’s often an early sign that something’s coming back.”

Poshmark is similarly using AI to identify patterns across searches, listings, likes and transactions, tracking demand for particular designers, eras, silhouettes and price points. Friedland says combining these signals with scarcity and actual resale prices can help distinguish fleeting trends from enduring desirability — offering brands a measure of a product’s success beyond its initial sellthrough.

For luxury brands, the stakes are particularly high. If AI assistants can connect consumers with archival products as readily as current collections, brands may find themselves competing with their own past successes, without controlling how those products are presented or compared.

As sellers learn to level up their listings, shoppers train their feeds and luxury brands compete for attention, the question is how much influence any of them will retain over what an AI agent ultimately recommends.

Just as our wardrobes shift with the seasons, so do our makeup routines. Foundations get lighter, blushes get brighter, and lips get redder. But while the holiday season typically brings bright red lips into the spotlight, winter 2026 is shaping up to be a little less cherry red and a little more raspberry. Allow us to explain.

The current beauty trends are all about looking lived-in, casual, and effortlessly polished. Berry shades are the easiest way to create a festive, more dimensional lip color without going full-on red. Plus, “I think people are ready for a little more color after seasons of nude lips and clear gloss,” says celebrity makeup artist Shyanna Lundi. “Berry is an easy way back into color because you can tap it on with a fingertip for a soft stain or build it up for a full evening look.” Versatility is the true beauty of the trend: “The same shade can feel completely different depending on how you apply it,” as Lundi puts it.

Berry isn’t just one shade, either. The family runs from bright raspberry to soft cranberry to deep blackberry. Some variations lean more red, while others lean more violet, and many strike a wine-like balance between the two; range is part of what makes the trend so wearable. Whether you want a barely-there wash of color or something with more impact, there’s a berry hue for nearly every makeup mood.

Lundi points to Pamela Anderson’s recent soft cranberry lip at the CFDA Fashion Awards as a prime example. “The sheer wash of color and fresh skin made her old Hollywood curls feel modern.” In fact, that’s been one of Lundi’s favorite ways to style the trend. “I love a satin berry with a softly blurred edge, dewy skin, and a little blush in the same color family,” she says. “I press the lipstick into the center and blend outward with my fingertip, keeping the corners clean, so it still feels polished.”

That softly blurred finish is key to making the look feel current rather than too sophisticated or overly done. Especially with more matte formulas, a diffused edge lets the color look more like a natural flush instead of a sharply defined, high-contrast lip. Pair it with fresh skin and blush in a similar tone, as Lundi suggests, and the result feels effortless, yet richer and more intentional.

Hailey Bieber wore the same blurred berry lip during her September 30 appearance on Quotidien, the French talk show known for its flattering lighting. Her French-girl-inspired soft glam went completely viral, with her raspberry-tinted lips as a highlight.

If you’re more of a gloss girl, you’re in luck. Berry doesn’t have to mean a satin or matte finish; a sheer, glossy version can make the shade feel even fresher. According to Lundi, it’s just as easy to create an extra-juicy effect. “For a glossier lip, I like to blend a deeper pencil inward and put the shine right in the center,” she says. “That’s where it catches the light.”

Whether you prefer a blurred stain, satin finish, or glossy wash, the takeaway is that there’s no single way to wear a berry lip. The key is finding the shade and formula that work for your desired look and level of intensity—and, luckily, there are plenty to choose from. #6746. Jimmy Carter’s Family Farm Just Sold for $8.5 Million

The Georgia property will become part of a nearly 7,000-acre wildlife management area, with public access possible as early as 2027.

President Jimmy Carter’s family farmland near Plains, Georgia, was just sold to the Conservation Fund as part of an approximately $8.5 million acquisition that will protect nearly 2,500 acres of fields and woodland. Announced November 9, the deal sets the stage for the land’s eventual transfer to the state of Georgia, with public access potentially beginning as early as 2027.

The purchase encompasses approximately 1,600 acres owned by the Carter family, along with an adjoining tract. It does not include Carter’s boyhood home and farm, which are already preserved by the National Park Service as part of Jimmy Carter National Historical Park.

Instead, the newly acquired property is slated to join the nearby Lanahassee Creek Wildlife Management Area, expanding it to nearly 7,000 acres. The land provides habitat for gopher tortoises and other wildlife, while neighboring creeks support rare freshwater mussels. Plans call for the Georgia Department of Natural Resources to take ownership in 2028.

The acquisition also continues restoration work Carter initiated himself. At his request, the family preserved a stand of mature longleaf pine and replanted much of the surrounding acreage with the same native species. Once used to grow crops, including peanuts, the property became a retreat where he and Rosalynn spent time away from public life. The family acquired the land around the turn of the 20th century, according to the Conservation Fund.

“They liked to go and walk the land,” Blake Sullivan, who managed Carter’s farm and timberland for more than four decades, told The Washington Post. “For both of them, it was a place of rest and renewal.”

Carter continued visiting into his final years, arranging to be driven through the property when walking became difficult. Amy Carter, the president’s daughter, told The Post, “I think his very favorite place was to be in the town and on the land where he grew up, and where he had those very deep roots.”

She also brought a little of the late Princess Diana with her for the special day by accessorizing with Lady Di’s famous Collingwood pearl drop earrings. #6737. Go Inside Miu Miu’s Handbag Atelier In Tuscany

Twenty years in, the brand’s matelassé leather remains a luxury calling card.

March 4, 2006, was perhaps like any other day in the mid-aughts. Myspace was the top website in the U.S., while Beyoncé’s “Check On It” was No. 1 on the Billboard charts. Cult-classic teen mermaid drama Aquamarine had just premiered the night before. And in Paris, during the fall/winter fashion shows, the date would prove to be the unexpected start of a new era—not just for one brand, but for fashion as a whole.

At the 18th-century Left Bank restaurant Lapérouse, Miu Miu presented its first-ever show in the French capital—now its permanent runway home—signaling a crucial differentiation from its sister brand Prada in Milan. Paper-thin knits, ultra-mini dresses, peplum jackets, chunky platform wedges, and mismatched-lace oxfords walked the intimate runway, on models adorned with white eyelashes and poppy-red lips. On the handbag front, an experimental leather-making technique was introduced, one that would become Miu Miu’s signature and a staple of aughts aesthetics: matelassé.

Originating in early 18th-century Marseille, the quilting technique was traditionally used in bedding or upholstery. In Miu Miu’s collection, it was developed in the form of a leather handbag—the Coffer—a slouchy shoulder tote in chocolate brown with a twisted handle and a bold metal clasp. A counterpoint to the youthfully eccentric clothes, the bag itself was a subtle debut, with only three shown on the runway and in only one colorway. Nonetheless, it was an immediate hit, carried by Anne Hathaway, Lindsay Lohan, and Isla Fisher in its early years. For the relatively young but increasingly iconic brand, a calling card was born.

Twenty years since that collection, Miu Miu has transformed its matelassé technique into a rainbow of colorways and style offerings. The seemingly seamless Wander and boxy Arcadie styles boast prime spots in the brand’s portfolio of leather goods, especially when it comes to the matelassé iterations—just take a look at the brand’s 2026 campaign starring Gigi Hadid.

The handbags come to life in Miu Miu’s leather goods workshop in Tuscany, the architecturally award-winning headquarters called The Garden Factory, built in the Valvigna region near where Miuccia Prada’s husband Patrizio Bertelli grew up, and designed by Guido Canali in the mid-1990s. Completed in 2015, the building itself is a physical manifestation of the Prada Group’s minimalist aesthetic.

The Garden Factory’s nickname derives from the property’s one-to-one ratio of building to greenery, a complete balance of cool steel and native vines, and plenty of glass windows to bridge the two. Inside is row upon row of accessories—66,000 leather goods and 77,000 pairs of shoes—carefully filed from the collections over the years to serve as both record and inspiration. Instead of season or collection, the cabinets are organized by product category, and matelassé has its own section.

Despite its creation 20 years ago—or perhaps in part because of it—the very tactility that makes Miu Miu’s matelassé leather so appealing is hitting a peak in current luxury collections across the board. To a consumer, the in-person experience was always a factor, but in the Instagram age, brands are turning to hyper-visual signifiers of craftsmanship to keep up with the market. Be it ASMR-inducing sequins, fluffy feathers, slick latex, or impossibly buttery leather, touch and feel appeal, even through an iPhone screen, is increasingly important. To see a matelassé handbag is to wonder how it feels, and to feel one is to experience its pillowy, permanent spring, an effect somewhere between plissé and origami. That effect is intentional, yet the product itself is softer in practice. That, too, is intentional.

The quilted technique is achieved by layering elastic Lycra with thin padding and nappa lambskin leather, sourced from Miu Miu’s tannery in France. Strategic patterns are stitched onto the layers and then the Lycra is removed, allowing the leather and padding to fold back into itself without losing the valleys created by the stitches. Thus, the matelassé effect comes to life. The smaller the product—like a card holder—the harder it is to craft. 3-D modeling is never used. Leather products are always assembled by hand, an important standard for the brand, and inspected manually by experts who know every detail of the bag’s design.

How does one become an expert in Miu Miu bags, you may ask (besides simply being a loyal fan)? Prada Group has its own leather goods academy where craftspeople spend six months learning about the brands’ luxury practices and standards. Even after those six months, it takes five to 10 years for a craftsperson to know how to make an entire bag themselves, start to finish.

From anywhere in the building, you have a view of the gardens outside, along with 45-degree-angled ceilings that let light in without creating too much heat. Stations are bustling with artisans, most of them women, in teams of two. They wear white lab coats emblazoned with the Prada Group logo.

The building’s minimalism, it seems, isn’t a lack, but an open space for creation to take place. And like the windows bridging steel to vine, or the archives linking past and present, or even the stitched valleys of a matelassé handbag, Miu Miu has mastered the spaces in between.

#6734. Alix Earle Quietly Supports Sofia Franklyn’s ‘Call Her Daddy’ Tell-All Book Amid Rumored Rift With Alex Cooper

Sofia Franklyn and Alex Cooper’s public falling out over Call Her Daddy may have gone down six years ago, but the drama seems to be alive and well, since the Sofia With an F host dropped a LOT more details in her new tell-all memoir, Daddy Issues.

She first announced Daddy Issues back in February, exclusively telling Rolling Stone, “The decision [to write the book] was one I came to on my own. Six years ago, I was reeling from an experience I didn’t understand. I needed to grow up and be free of ego as much as humanly possible.”

Alix Earle, who’s had her own beef with Alex ever since the Unwell Network dropped her Hot Mess podcast in February 2025, made sure to not-so-subtly support Sofia’s book on social media, posting a TikTok of herself reading Daddy Issues. Oh, and she also poked fun at that Interview magazine Q&A where she claimed she’s “never read a book,” adding text over her video that reads, “There’s a first time for everything!!!”

In case you aren’t aware of the layers this simple move has—and are still asking yourself, Wait, Alex Cooper and Alix Earle aren’t the same person?—allow us to catch you up to speed.

Sofia—who hosted Call Her Daddy with her bestie and college roommate Alex Cooper under Dave Portnoy’s company, Barstool—had a public falling-out in 2020 after they disagreed on negotiations with Barstool over the future of the show. While Sofia’s boyfriend at the time, Peter Nelson (aka “Suitman”), advised the girls not to renew their Barstool contract and take the show elsewhere, Alex wanted to sign on for one more year under the condition that she and Sofia owned the intellectual property of the pod.

In 2021, Alex continued Call Her Daddy without Sofia, eventually signing a $60 million deal with Spotify and another $125 million deal with SiriusXM in 2024. The latter includes exclusive advertising and distribution rights for Call Her Daddy, as well as the Unwell Network, her company.

Which brings us to Alex’s rumored rift with Alix Earle. When developing the Unwell Network, Alex signed the TikTok creator as one of the first podcasters under the company with Alix’s show, Hot Mess, in August 2023.

Things seemed to be going well until this time last year, when Variety reported that the Hot Mess podcast was dropped by the Unwell Network amid feud rumors between the social media personalities.

Sources gave a bit more context to the Alix vs. Alex situation with Us Weekly, saying, “They’ve had a lot of drama between them [since] they decided to collaborate on Unwell. They clashed over business, and their friendship is over because of it.”

While Alix has seemingly taken a hiatus from podcasting, Alex specified that “Alix not being able to podcast has nothing to do with Unwell” in a March 2025 TikTok post. She added that “Unwell gave her everything back” and that Alix owns her intellectual property.

As for Daddy Issues, Sofia also told Rolling Stone, “A book is reflective, vulnerable; it can’t be performative. The writing practice has been intense—sitting down, laying everything bare—but probably the most enriching thing I’ve ever done.”
