#6710. Bob Dylan Just Dropped a 39-Disc Box Set. I Listened to Every Single One

It showed up in my inbox on a Tuesday afternoon without any particular fanfare, just an email from Legacy Recordings with a link to a stream. Artist: Bob Dylan. Title: Rolling Thunder Revue — The 1976 Live Recordings. Total Tracks: 381.

The link brought me to a bare-bones Sony Music web page, a couple light grey boxes arranged against a dark grey background. A small window in the middle of the page occupied maybe 10% of the available space. Inside the window were lines of text with lengthy, baroque file names, one on top of another. You could see about five at a time, starting with the first:

Bob Dylan_The Rolling Thunder Revue The 1976 Live Recordings_G0100060414779_01_01_Visions of Johanna_USSM12603067_CT122.

Bob Dylan_The Rolling Thunder Revue The 1976 Live Recordings_G0100060414779_01_02_If You See Her, Say Hello_USSM12603068_CT122.

This, it hardly needs to be said, is not the ideal way to familiarize yourself with the 31 hours and 18 minutes of new music included in the latest box set from Bob Dylan Industries. Like previous installments of the Live Recordings series, 1976 is an exhaustive accounting of (nearly) every second of (nearly) every show and concert given by Bob Dylan on a legendary tour. If a document of a performance from this tour exists, it is here, whether you want it or not.

There’s a certain thrill to a release like this, especially for the Dylan mujahideen, those of us willing to engage in the struggle. The 1976 Live Recordings is best thought of as a choose-your-own-adventure set, allowing you the opportunity to ramble along with the Rolling Thunder Revue at whatever pace you find comfortable. You can dip in on St. Petersburg (4/23/76) for the first recorded edition of “Idiot Wind,” then mosey on to Gainesville (4/25/76) for the only-ever performance of “Dink’s Song,” then settle in for a long date with Oklahoma City (5/18/76), one of the strongest complete shows. And if you want to summit the whole mountain—well, hit “play” on Lakeland (4/18/76) and let it rip. Just remember to stay hydrated.

As exciting as the sheer volume of new Bob Dylan music is, these ultra-complete tour retrospectives can be an intimidating listening experience. This is especially true in the case of The 1976 Live Recordings, which captures not the crackerjack bonhomie of the inaugural Rolling Thunder Revue, but the second, flabbier incarnation—halitosis and head scarves rather than whiteface and roses.

Dylan caught lightning in a bottle with the first Rolling Thunder, trucking around northeastern college towns with his ramshackle rock carnival while simultaneously 1) shooting an autofictional art film, and 2) trying to piece his broken marriage back together (partially by forcing his wife to act in said art film). The looks were immaculate, the vibes heady, the performances electric. Just peep a few minutes of a 1975 “Isis”—talk about the ghost of electricity howling in the bones of a face. The music press tailed the show from town to town throughout, breathlessly reporting on the latest feats of derring-do from Bob and co-conspirators. Rolling Thunder became a viral sensation, a meme, an object of FOMO decades before the term was invented.

For Dylan, it was the culmination of a thrilling 24-month period in which he’d returned to touring, recorded three brilliant albums, and reclaimed his reputation as the most vital force in rock songs. Taken together, Planet Waves, Blood On The Tracks, and Desire, along with the Before The Flood tour in ‘74 and Rolling Thunder in ‘75, seemed a clear statement of intent. You can’t repeat the past? Whaddya mean you can’t, of course you can.

Riding high on good will and good press, Bob got the band back together the following year. It was only natural. The first Rolling Thunder had been an experiment of sorts, a burst of creativity fueled in large part by spontaneity and esprit de corps. There was a real “let’s put on a show!” energy to the proceedings. Tour dates were announced only a few days in advance, the itinerary unfolding according to the whims of the man in the wide-brimmed hat, and concerts were given not in theaters, but in New England’s stuffiest gymnasia and rotary halls.

The mercurial, DIY approach was a big part of the magic, but it also limited the tour’s reach. The sequel would be a professional operation: fully produced, well-rehearsed, hosted in cavernous coliseums across the American South. Better, boozier, browner.

Those latter two descriptors certainly applied to Rolling Thunder ‘76. As for the former, it depends on who you ask. The energy of the ‘75 shows was dialed back considerably, the wiry charge dissipating somewhere between the action on stage and the tens of thousands in the stands. It would have been impossible to reproduce the energy of a room like Plymouth’s War Memorial Auditorium (capacity 1,500) in a place like Fort Collins’ Hughes Stadium (capacity 30,000), and Bob didn’t even try. Instead, he and the band dialed up the cream quotient, turning the sound into something thicker, a little less wild. If Rolling Thunder ‘75 was a bantamweight, dodging and dancing around the ring, ‘76 was a heavyweight—slower, steadier, with a brutal left hook.

Some of the best Desire cuts (“Hurricane,” “Sara”) were stripped from the ‘76 setlists, replaced with Blood On The Tracks material that neatly mapped the emotional geography of Dylan’s crumbling marriage. Most shows included some, if not all, of the following: “Tangled Up In Blue,” a tale of missed connections and cruel fate; “You’re A Big Girl Now,” a bitter, disillusioned sequel to “Positively 4th Street;” “Idiot Wind,” the breakup song to end all breakup songs, a kiss-off to both a former lover and a former self; and “You’re Gonna Make Me Lonesome When You Go,” a sweet little number written, not coincidentally, about the young A&R rep Bob had been seeing on the side. To the surprise of no one, Sara Dylan would file for divorce early the following year.

Listening now, it’s clear that the live Blood material is the lifeblood of Rolling Thunder ‘76. Bob is invested in these songs like they’re written in his soul: performances of “Idiot Wind” and “Shelter From The Storm” highlight every show in which they appear, and “Tangled” is always interesting, even if it’s occasionally more tuneless than it ought to be. The other stuff is more hit-and-miss.

Take the 4/22/76 taping for the Midnight Special television program, which notably lacks any Tracks tracks. Instead, Bob and company meander through an abbreviated selection of greatest hits in a vain attempt at pleasing the crowd (and, presumably, network execs hoping to sell ad spots against the programming). It’s the Dylan pupu platter: a few “protest” songs, a few mid-Sixties rockers, and a couple contemporary cuts as a sop to the actual fans present. Several Rolling Thunder cast members make appearances—Joan Baez, Bobby Neuwirth, Roger McGuinn—but no one’s heart seems to be in it. Dylan was dissatisfied with the results at the time, and he refused to allow the performance to air. Now here it is a half-century later, available for all of us to judge ourselves. Turns out Bob made the right call.

I can’t help but compare The 1976 Live Recordings to last year’s salvo from BD Industries, Through The Open Window: The Bootleg Series Vol. 18 1956-1963. That volume covered plenty of well-trod ground, tracing Bob’s earliest days in the Greenwich Village folk scene. Still, producers Sean Wilentz and Steve Berkowitz managed to string the collection’s hundred-odd tracks into something coherent and compelling. The result is a release that is intentional, engaging, and, despite its marathon length, essential.

The same cannot be said about this latest set. On a personal level, I find 1976 Bob much more compelling than I do 1962 Bob—I like my Dylan aged, like a fine Cabernet. But the experience of listening to The 1976 Live Recordings is somewhat less satisfying than that of Through The Open Window. Any time I return to Sony Music’s cursed promo portal, I feel like I’m pulling the lever of a slot machine. Sometimes I hit a jackpot like “Going Going Gone,” with its revised lyrics about “diamonds and rust,” a nod—or a shot?—at Baez. Other times I get bupkis—yet another by-the-numbers edition of “Oh Sister.”

It’s worth noting that The 1976 Live Recordings, like previous releases of the 1966, 1974, and 1975 tours, isn’t being marketed as part of the Bootleg Series. The first Bootleg volume—released all the way back in 1991, now closer to the beginning of Bob’s career than it is to the present—set a high standard for classic rock box sets. Deep, voluminous, and impeccably sequenced, the inaugural release presented an extraordinary alternate history of The Great American Artist, one nearly as strong as the actual history. Even if selections were weighted toward Dylan’s first decade, a number of brilliant recordings from Bob’s wilderness years were also included. See “Lord Protect My Child,” a powerfully vulnerable ballad from the Infidels sessions. See also the alternate take of “When The Night Comes Falling From The Sky,” featuring the hot-rod stylings of Roy Bittan and Little Steven Van Zandt. “Blind Willie McTell,” “Foot of Pride,” “Series of Dreams”—the list goes on and on. My favorite Bob record shifts with the seasons; there are simply too many colors in the man’s mind to settle on one. Sometimes, however, the answer to that question is the last disc of the first volume of the Bootleg Series. It is that good.

Whatever its merits, I won’t ever say the same about The 1976 Live Recordings. Rather than present a considered set of highlights from the ‘76 run, Bob Dylan Industries has simply thrown open the gates of the vault. The words of William Mulholland upon the opening of the Los Angeles Aqueduct come to mind: “There it is, take it.” Those of us familiar with the Expecting Rain message boards have had it for years—most of it, anyway. I had my fingers crossed that someone would have rustled up a tape of Salt Lake City (5/25/76), which featured the only-ever performance of “Lily, Rosemary, and the Jack of Hearts,” but no such luck. If a tape of that show does exist, it’s still sitting in a tomb somewhere, waiting for someone to ride through the devilish cold and find it.

That, more than anything, is the central disappointment of The 1976 Live Recordings: there’s very little here that hasn’t already been in circulation for some time. Of course, bringing new and heretofore unknown delights to light was never the primary purpose. Neither was telling a story in the manner of Open Window. A release like this will surely boost the cultural footprint of Rolling Thunder ‘76, particularly amongst lower echelons of Dylan fans—those who do most of their listening through YouTube and have no idea what a FLAC is—but that’s more a happy byproduct than a raison d’etre.

The real aim here is purely legal: the maintenance and extension of copyright. EU law dictates that recordings published within 50 years of their creation are protected for 70 years following their publication. Miss that deadline and the recording enters public domain, allowing any interested parties to do with it what they will. This simple fact explains the last decade-plus of releases from Bob’s archives: The 1966 Live Recordings in 2016, The 1974 Live Recordings in 2024, and now The 1976 Live Recordings in 2026. There’s a lot of juice left to squeeze in these lemons, and Sony Music is intent on squeezing them.

The general attitude of Bob Dylan Industries seems to be that any scrap of music ever made by Dylan is worth preserving and exercising ownership over. There is a cold, calculating logic behind these box sets, one which prioritizes financial motives over the music itself. The 1976 material would benefit greatly from the deft hand of a curator, someone who had dedicated the time to separate the wheat from the chaff (releasing the complete Fort Worth show on streaming services is a poor substitute). This careful editorial approach is what makes the inaugural Bootleg Series release or Through The Open Window such powerful collections. In this case, however, it would yield an incomplete copyright arrangement. So here we are instead.

Fine by me. Even if The 1976 Live Recordings ends up being too much of a good thing—seriously, if I ever hear another “Vincent Van Gogh,” it’ll be too soon—I can’t say I’m dissatisfied with the finished product. If anything, it makes me excited for the years to come, as later Dylan tours approach their semicentennial.

I’ve long been obsessed with the 1978 shows, for instance. That year’s incarnation of Dylan featured radically glitzy rearrangements, powerhouse Street-Legal cuts, and a plethora of ruffled shirts. The At Budokan live album documented a specimen from the early days of the tour, but the best performances came at the end, as Bob refined the schmaltzy big band sound into something soulful and desperate. I’ll be first in line for a hypothetical 50-disc The 1978 Live Recordings set. Then there’s the gospel tours of ‘79 and ‘80, and the “Bob Is Back” run from ‘81, and the butt rock and eyeliner era from ‘84… It goes on and on.

The important thing is that this music was made, and now it is being made available. Copyright holders and Dylan obsessives can agree on that much, even if we’re getting different things out of a release like The 1976 Live Recordings. We always did feel the same, we just saw it from a different point of view.

#6709. Rosalind Eleazar Got the Role of a Lifetime

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

In the new film Misty Green, the Slow Horses actress shows just what she’s capable of.

As soon as the credits rolled on the Toronto International Film Festival premiere of Misty Green, the word was out: The film’s star, Rosalind Eleazar, had delivered a career-defining performance. Her portrait of a struggling Hollywood actress in the heartbreaking drama, written and directed by Chris Rock, was a showstopper, critics wrote. Overnight, it seemed like a foregone conclusion that she would be in contention for an Oscar. Misty fights, does drugs, and lies, but also sings beautifully, looks out for her mentally ill brother, and loves her best friend unreservedly. She’s damaged by her upbringing and the cruelty and racism of her industry, which has made her strong and funny, but also vulnerable and fragile, which she masks with a tough exterior. The performer playing her needed to be able to embody all the sides of a very complicated character; it would be an incredible challenge for even the most seasoned actress. For Eleazar, it was her first leading role in a feature film.

Prior to starring in Misty Green, Eleazar, who has had an accomplished career in theater in her native U.K., was little known internationally outside of her role on Slow Horses. She gives a beautiful performance on the acclaimed Apple TV series, but it’s the kind of ensemble part unlikely to springboard a British actress into a starring role in a Hollywood film. When her agent sent her the script for Misty Green, Eleazar recognized immediately that it was unlike anything she’d read before. “Chris really wrote her fearlessly, and he wasn’t frightened to show the uglier side,” she says. “He and I were keen not to sanitize her and make her soft and palatable. I was pretty bowled over with what he wrote and how unapologetically he wrote it.” Misty speaks her mind to a pathological degree and has a hard time turning down cocaine. The film follows a crazed seven days in which the actress, facing eviction, gets a chance at her dream role. On the other side is an offer to make the money she needs in an unthinkable way, which hangs over her head unsettlingly. “The character just came off the page to me,” Eleazar adds.

She auditioned for the part via a string of Zoom auditions from London. After one was plagued by an iffy Wi-Fi connection and booming heavy metal music nearby, she was certain she’d lost her chance. Rock disagreed. When she was later asked to do a chemistry read, she bought her own ticket to Los Angeles, sure that reading for the part in person was her best bet. She waited weeks before getting the call from Rock that the part was hers, and she was on a plane back to California within a week.

Rock has said he was dazzled by Eleazar’s understanding of the role, casting her over bigger-name stars. She says he trusted her and gave her leeway to shape the part. “He has this expression, ‘My movie, your character,’” Eleazar says. “He allowed me to really explore Misty, because she’s unique and wild and untethered. In order for me to do that, I needed to also feel untethered and without boundaries.”

Misty’s wildness is in contrast to the more restrained character she plays on Slow Horses. As Louisa, an intelligence officer deeply impacted by the loss of her colleague and love interest, Eleazar paints a vivid picture of prolonged grief. Slow Horses, which premiered in 2022, has steadily gained popularity over its six seasons, offering Eleazar consistency at a pivotal time in her career. “Going off doing other jobs and coming back is interesting, because you see your development of a character over six years,” she says. “It feels like family, like your home.”

The rapturous response to Eleazar’s performance in Misty Green will undoubtedly transform her career, but she doesn’t yet know what impact it will have on the roles she is offered. “I do hope that it will give me more choice,” she says. “But our job is not like a lawyer, where you start as a junior associate, and you can see your trajectory to partner. It’s just not like that. It depends on what’s around. It depends on where you are in your career. It depends on your age.”

Whatever comes next, this year has brought incredible joy to Eleazar’s life. The day after Misty Green premiered, she was given a TIFF Tribute Performer Award alongside A-list stars. “I can’t even put into words how special a moment it was,” she says of the premiere. “Then, the next day, to be recognized for my work in Misty, with Helen Mirren and Penélope Cruz, was the icing on the cake. Seeing my mom’s face when I was making the speech was a reminder of the things that are important to you.”

Beauty Tip: For a warm and juicy scent, try Lancôme La Vie Est Belle Very Cherry Eau de Parfum.

Early on, your CV is mainly the plays you’ve done in drama school. At one of my first TV auditions, they said something like, “You seem to have done a lot of theater, and you haven’t done loads of TV.” I was like, “Well, if you give me this part, it’ll be a start.” And I actually got it.

Tilda Swinton has been really sweet to me. I was really nervous doing The Personal History of David Copperfield, and she just sensed it. She subtly squeezed my hand. She knew that’s all she needed to do, rather than making a big deal. That was enough to be like, “It’s okay.”

I would really like to hang out with Misty and analyze her. But she doesn’t seem to eat much.

If I gave myself advice when I was 15, I wouldn’t have listened to it. I needed to mess up on this, this, this, and this in order for me to understand stuff. Just be a sponge and let it unfold.

I would love to see more female lead roles. You often look on IMDb and see the synopsis of potential projects coming up, and 80 percent of them will go, “A man who is…” It’s still baffling to me how many male-led films are being made in comparison to those with women.

#6708. The Best Drugstore Foundations for Women Over 40

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

If you can remember what a modem sounds like, these under-$20 picks are for you

We all have different expectations for our foundation: Some prefer sheer coverage, others full; some want a dewy finish, and others a natural finish. But when you’re 50+, perhaps the most important quality is finding a hydrating formula that won't exacerbate wrinkles, spots, and texture. Although there are excellent foundations for mature skin for all budgets, don't sleep on what's right at the drugstore.

“You can absolutely find a high-quality foundation that caters to the unique needs of mature skin, such as hydration, anti-aging benefits, and a smooth, even finish that isn’t cakey—even at the drugstore,” professional makeup artist Allie Renee tells Harper’s Bazaar. “Many foundations are formulated specifically with mature skin in mind and can provide a beautiful result without breaking the bank.”

To prove it, we've gathered the best drugstore foundations for mature skin, with expert picks from Renee and top-reviewed products. Find your new go-to below.

Makeup artist Allie Renee is a fan of this formula, saying it is “hydrating and has a luminous, radiant finish.” The artist likes using L’Oréal Paris’s formula on her clients as it reflects light in a flattering way, enhancing natural glow while blurring the appearance of fine lines.

It’s hard to beat a flexible foundation formula at under $10 a bottle. Renee says Maybelline’s hydrating, medium-coverage Fit Me Dewy + Smooth foundation is “a great option for a natural, dewy finish that won’t settle into fine lines or create a cakey appearance.”

A lit-from-within glow is ageless, and this foundation helps you get it in just a minute or two. It covers and conceals while adding just the right amount of radiance (in other words, you won't look glittery).

This prestige-inspired foundation features tiny pigment droplets suspended in a clear skincare essence; when blended on your skin, you get sheer, even coverage that also plumps fine lines and hydrates. There’s a small shade range, but we’ve found that the shades are fairly flexible and blend in well because they’re so sheer.

E.l.f. Cosmetics delivers a medium-coverage, buildable foundation that still refreshes skin thanks to a one percent Hydrating Hibiscus Complex. And with a whopping 36 shades—available with warm, cool, and neutral undertones—it’s easy to find a natural-looking match.

A serum foundation is generally a great choice for mature skin, as it offers a more moisturizing formula and additional skincare benefits. This one from No7 does just that and offers a bit more coverage than some other serum foundation options.

Powder generally settles into wrinkles, but some are better than others in this regard. Mineral Fusion's is triple-milled, so it's extra smooth on the skin. It also includes skincare ingredients similar to those in the liquid formulas on this list. Use it as your base or for touch-ups when shine takes over.

This instantly blurring foundation applies ultra-smoothly thanks to a built-in sponge (you simply twist it up until the product appears, then sweep it directly onto your skin). The targeted delivery system also makes it great for use as a concealer.

For a medium- to full-coverage option, try this foundation from Milani that also has a matte—but not drying—finish. The shade range is impressive, and so is the coverage.

For light-to-medium coverage, go for this skin tint from NYX. With shea butter, mango butter, niacinamide, and SPF 30, your face will be hydrated and protected from the sun throughout the day. It’s perfect for those who want a glowy finish.

What Should I Look for in a Foundation for Mature Skin?

Renee recommends keeping an eye out for “a balanced foundation that allows the skin to feel comfortable without emphasizing texture or fine lines on the complexion, as this will ultimately achieve a smooth, natural-looking finish.” The key to striking that balance, she says, is finding one that satisfies both personal preferences while addressing the specific needs of mature skin. “Remember, the goal is to enhance, not cover, your unique features,” she adds.

Are Matte Formulas a Dealbreaker for Mature Skin?

Matte foundations can make mature skin appear drier and exacerbate the look of fine lines. Instead, “Look for a dewy, radiant, or satin finish,” recommends Renee. “These types of finishes will give your skin a youthful glow without emphasizing texture or dryness.” That being said, if you have mature skin that still leans oily, you may be able to wear a matte-finish foundation.

#6706. Andrew Scott On the Real-Life Story Behind His Heartbreaking Performance in Elsinore

In the fourth scene of the fourth act of Hamlet, our melancholy hero stands on a desolate Danish plain watching a Norwegian army march into Poland on a trivial errand. Turning to the audience, in the last of his soliloquies, he imagines “the imminent death of twenty thousand men that for a fantasy and trick of fame go to their graves like beds.”

How must it have felt for Ian Charleson, the sandy-​haired Scottish actor who rose to international stardom in Chariots of Fire but was dying of AIDS by the time he played his own legendary Hamlet at London’s National Theatre in 1989, to utter those lines? A silent, unjust war raged around him, as young men all over London were dying in isolation, their sheets burned as soon as their bodies were carted out, or, if they were lucky, driven home to take their final breaths in their childhood beds, eliciting whispers from the neighbors.

There is no way to know whether Hamlet, a role steeped in questions about life and death, was ever before played by a man who understood that his own death was so close. Those extraordinary circumstances are what animate Elsinore, the new film directed by Simon Stone that revisits and rejoices in Charleson’s final months. Many great actors have described their art as a means of escape—from the humdrum of reality, from the cage of the self. Andrew Scott, the Irish actor who is playing Charleson in Elsinore to a degree of fanfare approaching Oscar preordainment, does not share this view. Nor, he suspects, did Ian Charleson.

“The more I act,” Scott tells me from the quietest recess of a West Hollywood hotel restaurant on a 100-degree October day, “the more I see it not as pretending to be someone else but as exploring different parts of myself. Who would I be if I was born in this era or in this body or in this set of circumstances? A great actor once said that acting is an escape from acting. I think there’s a lot of sense in that.”

Scott, who turned 50 last month, grew up in Dublin in the shadow of the AIDS crisis and, like so many gay men of his age, has often thought how lucky he is to have been born just a few years later than the generation that died en masse. With better education and better treatment, men of his era survived, but for them sex and death could never be wholly disentangled.

“The fact that the current generation of young gay people feels a freedom from that is wonderful,” Scott says. He began his professional stage career at the Abbey Theatre in Dublin, in 1996, and he remembers what he calls “a conspiracy of silence around sexuality” at the time, a carryover from the beginning of the crisis when governments refused to speak or act. Elsinore revives not only the National Theatre of the 1980s but also the gay bars and cruising grounds of Hampstead Heath, where the Sisters of Perpetual Indulgence, a group of activists who dressed as Catholic nuns, educated gay men on safe practices at a time of governmental neglect. “People would ask them, ‘What do we do? How do we protect ourselves?’ ” says Scott, who learned more about Charleson and his era from his friend Stephen Beresford’s rigorously researched script. “Because there was no information, no help, all this silence. The terror of that silence is the thing that offends. That should be where the shame lies.”

Though Scott found mainstream success on British TV shows such as Sherlock and Phoebe Waller-Bridge’s Fleabag—as the so-called Hot Priest—he has remained dedicated to the theater and just completed a two-week run of Simon Stephens’s 50-minute monologue Sea Wall in New York. (In fact the play’s 19 performances were filmed as part of an upcoming motion picture about the process of creating theater.) In recent years Scott has taken on a pair of haunted gay roles, in Netflix’s stylish retelling of the Ripley story and, opposite Paul Mescal, in 2023’s All of Us Strangers. And yet he is still the rare openly gay actor whose sexuality has been greeted with a collective shrug.

“Well, it isn’t very interesting,” he says, shaking his head. “What was so insidious was that Ian and his predecessors had something to contribute to the film and television industry but weren’t given the opportunities in the same way, or else they were given the opportunities but they were also given a sort of silent choice: You can have that, but you have to conceal a huge part of your identity in return, while their straight counterparts didn’t have to make that sacrifice. In fact that part of their identity was celebrated rather than concealed or derided. I do feel that the playing field is starting to level out. There’s that great expression that prejudice doesn’t survive proximity. If you see people, you become less frightened of them.”

FACE FORWARD “He has no shield,” says costar Olivia Colman of Scott. “An instant and direct route to any emotion. He is the most beautiful empath.” Dior jacket and collar.

In the film Charleson bemoans the fact that all anyone remembers of Chariots of Fire, which won best picture at 1982’s Academy Awards, is the theme music. For those who came up in London’s theater scene when he did, the telling of his story feels overdue. Charleson was, by all accounts, a beloved figure in his artistic circle: clever and churlish, an excellent dancer and singer, abundantly generous to young actors. Hilton McRae, a Scottish actor who first met Charleson as a fellow student at the University of Edinburgh and was a close friend throughout his life, has seen Elsinore three times. “Andrew is Ian Charleson,” he says. “There’s that same sense of mischief. That same wicked wit. And I think off-screen he’s got the same kind of Celtic integrity about how to run his life.”

McRae missed his old friend’s Hamlet because he was busy playing Macbeth in his hometown of Dundee. So for him the film has been an almost uncanny invitation to enter into Charleson’s mind at a crucial moment. “When he had to say the lines ‘we defy augury. There’s a special providence in the fall of a sparrow. If it be now, ’tis not to come; if it be not to come, it will be now; if it be not now, yet it will come. The readiness is all.’ How do you say these things knowing what’s coming? How much was he hoping, how much was he in a kind of denial? I saw him when he’d finished. I went round to look after him one day, and he had Much Ado About Nothing and King Lear by his bedside. He was looking at Benedick, and he was looking at Lear. He wanted to do them. The marvelous thing about this film is that it’s basically about how important art is.”

For Juliet Stevenson, who plays Gertrude, Hamlet’s mother, in Elsinore, making the film offered an almost mystic mix of art and memory. Stevenson starred in Hedda Gabler at the National Theatre at the very moment when Charleson played his Hamlet; the two plays were in repertory on the National’s main stage, the Olivier. Years later, in 2017, she played Gertrude when Andrew Scott took on the role of Hamlet in an acclaimed run in London’s West End. She first met Ian Charleson when she was 20 and newly out of the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art. An actor had broken her leg in a production of The Tempest at the Royal Shakespeare Company in Stratford-upon-Avon, and Stevenson joined the cast while they were in dress rehearsals. Charleson was Ariel, and she remembers seeing him suspended over the stage by wires singing “Full fathom five.”

Scott as Charleson in a still from Elsinore.

“He was very beautiful, very camp, very kind of golden,” she recalls. “It’s easy to sentimentalize people who die young, who have a story like Ian’s, but he really was adored. He was supremely witty, funny, naughty, and acerbic, but kind, generous. Men or women—we were all a little bit in love with him.” Stevenson will never forget the moment she greeted Charleson at the National in 1989, not having seen him since Stratford. “Backstage the National is a great big community. Every show shares the green room, the canteen, the corridors. I was in a crowded elevator, waiting before the doors shut, and I looked across this landing and saw Ian walking towards the bar. I said, ‘Hey, Ian! Hi!’ He turned and said, ‘Hi, Juliet!’ I said, ‘Welcome to the National. How are you doing?’ He said, ‘Well, they say I’m dying! Isn’t that crazy?’ I just kind of stared at him. And then the elevator doors shut. The young man who’d been trying to keep it secret saw me and launched that message across that landing with a kind of strange gaiety. But—he was playing Hamlet! He turned his suffering into art. I hope that doesn’t sound pretentious, but I do believe that’s what he did.”

The director Richard Eyre’s much-ballyhooed staging of Hamlet arrived at the National with Daniel Day-Lewis in the title role; the actor was making a sort of homecoming to the stage as a newly minted movie star. (He would go on to win an Oscar for his performance in My Left Foot the next year.) Day-Lewis’s Hamlet was perhaps doomed by unreasonably high expectations; he did not receive the expected raves, and in September 1989, in the middle of a scene in which the prince confronts his father’s ghost, he walked off the stage and out of the production. Day-Lewis has not performed onstage since that night.

If there’s something Eyre disputes in Elsinore, where he is played by the actor Johnny Flynn, it is the suggestion that he offered Charleson the opportunity to take over Hamlet with a kind of benevolent calm. Charleson had been a huge success as Sky Masterson in Eyre’s production of Guys and Dolls at the National in 1982, and Eyre regarded him as a hugely capable classical actor too. But casting him this time was fraught with danger. “It was unimaginably painful,” Eyre remembers. “Daniel was a very close friend, and it was a terrible shock when he dropped out. I made the decision to cast Ian with the knowledge that he was ill and in defiance of a lot of my colleagues, who thought I was making a big mistake. My character appears absolutely stoical and generous, but in reality I was a total mess.”

The film acknowledges Charleson’s reluctance to come out publicly and even, at first, to his Hamlet castmates. Ian McKellen had come out a year earlier, on a live BBC broadcast, in part to protest Section 28, a Thatcher-era law that banned schools from “intentionally promoting homosexuality.” Charleson, always out to his friends, felt that the circumstances of his career made public disclosure impossible. “McKellen went on to become this astonishing global movie star, but at the time he didn’t have a movie career to worry about,” Eyre explains. “Ian Charleson had starred in Chariots and had a significant presence in Gandhi. He was lined up to be the next Robert Redford. I think he would have matured into a real international film star. But interestingly, he wanted more to do theater. He thought being a movie star was slightly ridiculous, as of course it is.”

At a moment when many queer people in the United States feel less safe, and when American investment in combating HIV globally has evaporated with the dismantling of USAID, Elsinore has a sense of political urgency that its creators may not have envisioned for it. While Scott knows that the film does not depart wholly from the somber tenor of his recent screen roles, he plays Charleson for laughs because humor was his essential mode, and he regards his unlikely Hamlet—with its four thousand lines over four hours—as a herculean effort against all odds.

“In some ways my fear was that we would fetishize Ian’s death rather than celebrate his life,” Scott says. “And actually his decision to play Hamlet at the very end of his life, to nail his colors to the mast in that way, when time was running out, is so life-loving.” Margaret Johnson, the doctor who cared for Charleson in his final months and who spoke extensively with Stephen Beresford as he was researching the screenplay, remembered occasions when he would come to her office the morning after a performance looking especially beleaguered. “Not tonight,” she would tell him. He would acquiesce, but then Johnson would watch him out her office window hailing a cab to the National. “As he says, I’d rather die of Hamlet than of AIDS,” Scott adds, quoting his character. “That’s somebody who wants to live. That’s important for me to say.”

Olivia Colman, who plays Johnson in Elsinore, was drawn to the tension between her character’s responsibility for the preservation of life and Charleson’s wish to focus on joy, even if it cost him time. “Art and joy make life worth living. He really proved that,” she says. Colman, like Eyre, thinks Charleson would be proud of Scott’s portrayal. “Oh, Andrew! He has no shield. An instant and direct route to any emotion. He is the most beautiful empath, and because it’s real, he’s not acting. He’s being.”

Scott and his two siblings lost their mother in 2024, and he says that work has had a grounding effect in the aftermath. Hollywood actors often speak of the necessity to strike while the iron is hot, and if he has the glorious awards season that has been augured for him (Scott would be the first openly gay man to win an acting Oscar), he will have his pick of roles in 2027. But instead he would like to do less. “I think it’s time to get my work-life balance back a bit, to sort of smell the roses,” he says. He wouldn’t mind a romantic comedy, or even a musical. If Charleson had King Lear at his bedside, perhaps it was because he knew that dying young would prevent him from doing the thing great Shakespearean actors, such as John Gielgud and Laurence Olivier, do: play Hamlet in their relative youth and play Lear as they age. But for Scott, such ambitions are far from the mind.

#6704. The Real-Life Wardrobe of Jamie Campbell Bower, Who Only Wears Suits If They’re McQueen

“I don’t know, I suppose I’m an artist,” Jamie Campbell Bower says with a laugh, after I ask him to describe himself. He’s correct, in more ways than one. If you’ve been consuming pop culture for the last decade and change, it’s less a matter of if you’ve seen the 37-year-old Londoner before, but where. He’s acted in some of the biggest franchises in Hollywood—including Twilight, Harry Potter, The Mortal Instruments, and Stranger Things—while also nurturing a multifaceted music career. As of this month, he’ll be heading to Middle-earth as Celeborn in the third season of Amazon Prime’s epic Lord of the Rings series, The Rings of Power.

During a hectic week of Rings of Power in New York City, Bower and I spent a quiet early morning talking about the bands that helped him find his style as a teenager, the difference between performing as an actor and a musician, and why he loves playing the bad guy.

All clothing and accessories, subject’s own. Coat by MM6 Maison Margiela. Sweater by John Lawrence Sullivan. Vintage skirt. Shoes by John Lawrence Sullivan. Sunglasses by Persol (throughout). Necklace (bottom) by Kinraden. Other jewelry by Pianegonda.

Jamie Campbell Bower: It’s complexity. With any character, there has to be a level of complexity. Playing in the shadow self is really illuminating, to be Jungian. You have to know it in order for it to not take over. I found it particularly interesting to rationale and reason, even though this character was doing terrible things. I have always found it really interesting to dig away and find the why. So much of that character was really about isolation and pain and not feeling like they had a sense of belonging in the space for them. Obviously, they find this power that gives them this sense of safety. It becomes the wall, and it gives them purpose, and it hides them from the world and from being hurt. What draws me to any character is complexity and understanding the balance. It’s almost anthropological in a way.

It was amazing. I was so terrified on day one. I’m always nervous about joining any show, doing any gig. But I remember day one of actually shooting with other cast members, turning around to Nick Müller, our A-camera operator, and I just went, “Look, Nick, you’ve been here way longer than I have. If I’m in your way, just tell me to fucking move.”

I’d been a part of Twilight as well—joined that on the second movie after watching a cultural moment explode—and I was in that position again with Stranger Things. It was so big. I was joining this new world, but everyone was wicked and super kind. I made some amazing friends. I love Millie [Bobby Brown]. She’s just the best. She’s like my little sister, and also like my big sister at times as well. She’s got so much sage advice and is so brilliant at what she does and so driven. I am in awe of her, and I was from the moment I met her.

I’ve got the hand of Vecna. I took it out on Fallon [the other] night. I told this story, but I got my bag searched in Mexico City on the way in over the weekend. We pulled up and one of the people there looked at me—her eyes got big. She said, “Vecna.” I’ve got three massive fuck-off suitcases. They’re going through them and I’m like, “Look, I’ve got the hand of Vecna in here. Do you want to see it?” And then it ended up being the quickest bag search ever. I got some elf ears with me as well, both made by the same guy, Barrie Gower.

It was the summer when I was 15. I spent it wearing a visor with spiky hair, because I used to skate growing up in super baggy jeans. I remember turning up being like, “That’s not you.” Skating is a part of who I am, but I was looking to represent myself in some way, shape, or form.

Then we started this indie band when I was 16, 17. Devonté Hynes had this band called Test Icicles. I always used to look at those guys with their skinny jeans and their big hair, and I was just like, “That’s a bit of me, that.” How skinny can my jeans get? How drain pipe-y am I? That’s where I really started to find my own identity.

I’ve been fortunate enough throughout my career to meet and work with such beautiful creative people in fashion and find myself more within that, too. I was talking about it to somebody yesterday: When you try a fit on that is not you, it’s like having a bad haircut. You don’t want to do that. I’m even the same if I’m doing a photoshoot. I always go through the rail and I’ll say, “That’s not my vibe. I can’t say that I’m going to wear that.” Of course, I’m always willing to try, I’m always willing to push. But you know yourself better as you get older.

It was from Alexander McQueen. I loved the identity of that brand, but I couldn’t afford a jacket, or a suit, or even a scarf. But the smaller pieces, the rings and the wallets, were like 100 bucks. Those were the things that I would gravitate towards and buy.

More recently, within the last 10 years, I remember coming here to New York for a show that I did called Will, going to Bergdorf, and buying a couple of pairs of Comme des Garçons trousers. As they were being rung up, I was like, “All right.” It wasn’t loads—we’re not talking thousands—but it was still a lot of money. That was probably the first big clothing purchase that I ever made. And I’ve still got the trousers. I used to wear them on stage in the band as well, which is foolish.

Got a bunch of stuff from H. Lorenzo the other day—some great shirts, some great jackets. I really like how they curate the store. My most recent purchase is a lot of stuff from the new Ann Demeulemeester collection. I actually just bought a sick leather trench from it—brown leather, which is fire.

Jacket by Thom Browne. Shirt, jeans, shoes by Ann Demeulemeester.

Going back to when we were kids: Test Icicles, the Libertines, the Rakes, Franz Ferdinand, Editors. Got to meet a few of those guys throughout my travels, which was always pretty sick. Nick Cave. Warren Ellis. Nick has got such a sharp style, as does Warren. Warren’s a bit more unbuttoned. I met Warren in Venice five years ago. He was stood at the end of the pier and I was so excited to meet him, I just bounded up. I was like, “Hi, Mr. Ellis. My name’s Jamie.” And I just blurted out to him for ages, and then I was like, “Thank you so much.” He said, "Good to meet you, mate. Bye.”

I think fluidity and being myself is always the main thing. I’ve never felt wholly comfortable in a regular suit. I remember we were invited to do a show in Venice, and the band that we were in was pretty heavy. We wore suits in an environment that for us felt almost quite subversive. The music that we played didn’t really fit that. I quite enjoyed that.

But on the whole, I don’t love suits too much. I like to keep it more interesting and fluid. I’m not saying that they can’t be interesting for other people, but I’ve never been interested [in them myself]. Apart from McQueen, but that’s because something like the McQueen shoulder is so identifiable and creates such an incredible silhouette. That’s probably the only time I’ve ever really been like, “I can wear this suit for a long time.” But yeah, I avoid anything that doesn’t feel right for me.

It’s hard to say. I do feel like so often they can blend. I’ve been so fortunate in my career, being drawn to things that feel like me and getting to explore different parts of myself on film. That does have an effect on the music that I’m making at the time.

With a film or a television series, you’re saying someone else’s words and building a character, but also at times injecting your own personal experience into that. In music, they are your words. You can make a choice to be like, “I’m going to build a world in this song to express something.” Or I can just be like, “This is me.” So, they can scratch different itches, but I think that they work in symbiosis sometimes.

The original movies came out when I was 12, so they were pretty seminal. I remember being in Hong Kong on a trip when The Hobbit was coming out. I was on my own, and I went to a cinema in a place called Pacific Place to watch it. That made a really big impact on me—it felt like a fantastical world that I could see myself in.

I started auditioning for it in 2024. Walking into it, of course, I was elated. I felt so lucky and so happy, like I was a little kid again. Like, I was 11 or 12 on stage in some provincial town outside of London, and now I get to fuckin’ walk into this Lord of the Rings world and be an elf? Dude, that’s sick.

Three non-negotiable albums that everyone… Oh, bloody Nora!

I discovered Dylan when I was like 16, when we were reading [J. D.] Salinger and Allen Ginsberg and books like On the Road. Let’s go with a classic. Freewheelin’ is old-school enough. It’s cool, pre-him going electric, which I adore as well. Highway 61 Revisited is a great record too. Take your pick between those two. Chopin’s Nocturnes are amazing. That’s a beautiful, beautiful piece to get into. Then there’s Nick Cave. I did an interview before and I chose Murder Ballads, which is a great record. But I also love some of the more recent work, like Ghosteen or Skeleton Tree. Ghosteen is amazing.

Oh, Ghosteen’s wicked. Let’s go with that. I referenced the artwork for Ghosteen on my last release. My album cover was by an artist called Thomas Cole, who did a collection of paintings about the journey from birth to death. He also did paintings of the Garden of Eden. From what I have now seen, those paintings heavily inspired the artist that did the paintings for Ghosteen as well, which is kind of insane.

So, he’s from the East. It’s the swearing.

#6701. Sabrina Carpenter Would Love to Star in a 9 to 5 Movie Musical

The star talks Dolly Parton, the French New Wave, and her Johnnie Walker short with Damien Chazelle.

For Sabrina Carpenter, a song and a role each offer a different way into a story. “Acting and music have always gone hand in hand for me,” she tells ELLE exclusively. “With music, I get to tell stories through my own perspective, and with acting I get to step into someone else’s world and bring their story to life, and that is always an exhilarating feeling for me.”

Carpenter gets to move between those perspectives in a new Johnnie Walker film directed by Damien Chazelle, the Oscar-winning visionary behind Whiplash and La La Land. With the Short n’ Sweet star at its center, the clip nods to French New Wave cinema through the director’s signature motion-driven style.

The short begins with Carpenter, in a mod embellished minidress, stepping into an unusually quiet party. As someone pours her a Go Go Highball, her signature Johnnie Walker cocktail, the scene comes to life: the guests spring into motion, and Carpenter gets swept up in the revelry while a meta quartet of directors looks on. Here, she opens up to ELLE about working with Chazelle, her favorite New Wave films, and the movie musical she’d most want to star in (hint: it’s a certain blonde’s workplace comedy).

This past year has been pretty surreal. Coachella will always be a standout for me, probably for the rest of my life. I had so much fun creating that show. Also getting to perform onstage this year with Madonna and Stevie Nicks. [I’m] still processing that.

Sometimes the best moments are just spending time with the people you love, and this summer spending some downtime with my close friends and my sister, we loved our Go Go Highballs for sure.

Getting ready for my Met Gala after-party comes to mind. But I can’t always reveal all the details to you guys; there’s no fun in that.

Working with Damien was a dream! I’ve admired his work for so long, and he has a brilliant way of making even the smallest moments feel larger than life. I love how he was able to capture the humor and playfulness that come with life’s unexpected moments.

I love La La Land! I think there’s something really special about creating a short moment or scene that feels almost like a whole movie, so I’m always trying to approach these projects from a cinematic viewpoint.

Two of my favorites are The Umbrellas of Cherbourg and Cleo from 5 to 7.

Well, I just rewatched 9 to 5 and you know I’m the biggest Dolly [Parton] fan. So that would be a fun one.

#6700. 11 Best Cowboy Boots in 2026, According to GQ Editors

You might think that cowboy boots are a privilege reserved for ranch hands and folks who can actually ride a horse. But with a little chutzpah, the best cowboy boots are just as adept on a saddle as they are on the subway. Is that so surprising? Before they blossomed into their fashionable forms, much of menswear’s most riffed on garments were rooted in function: cargo pants, work jackets, even suits. With enough time, they were adopted by civilians and adapted to their second lives as symbols of self-expression and creativity, not just job uniforms. Cowboy boots are no different.

In terms of styling, the classic move for western boots is to lean into their rougher side. Toss them on with some well-fitting jeans (preferably vintage boot cuts) and with a snap shirt. And that's still a great approach. But if you open up your mind and step outside of the saloon, the possibilities are practically endless. A slick pair of exotic leather cowboy boots matched with a ‘70s-inspired suit screams filthy rich oil tycoon if not Alessandro Michele-era Gucci. Or, why not mix up a preppy pair of chinos with a grungy graphic tee and some roughed-up suede ropers? The point is, you don’t have to pretend to be a cowboy to wear their boots. So treat them like any other pair of shoes in your closet and wear them however you want. Hell, we’d go so far as to call them an essential pair of boots for every wardrobe.

And if you’re having trouble, well, that’s why you’re here. We’ve wrangled together the best cowboy boots west—and east—of the Mississippi, from the budget-friendly to the ostentatious and every vibe in-between.

The good folks at Tecovas are living, breathing proof that direct-to-consumer brands aren’t all operated by algorithms tasked with solving imaginary problems. The DTC upstart might be the youngest of the bootmakers on this list, but it's quickly endeared itself to budget-strapped swashbucklers with a hankering for democratically-priced kicks.

Take, for example, the Cartwright, a handsome riff on a classic western silhouette made in Leon, Mexico, a bona fide cobbling capital of the world with over a century of expertise to draw on. It boasts hand-laid cording at the shaft, a resoleable Goodyear-welt construction, and a slew of colors and leathers to choose from, including genuine cowhide and goat leather. They’re not the cheapest boots on this list, but the relatively approachable price belies the craftsmanship involved. For $375, they’re one small step up from our favorite budget cowboy boots—but one giant leap in overall quality.

You can think of roper boots as the chilled-out version of the average western boot. Originally designed for calf roping, roper boots feature a shorter shaft and a shorter, squared off heel. These details made it easier for cowboys to dismount their horse and run after the calves they roped. Coincidentally, they also make roper boots easier to walk in which is why some people prefer them over other cowboy boots for everyday wear.

Our pick for the best roper boots currently goes to Red Wing. (Perhaps no surprise, given the brand also makes our favorite trend-proof boots.) Part of Red Wing's Heritage line, they're crafted with premium S.B. Foot Tanning Company leather, and feature Goodyear welt construction so you can have them resoled and keep ‘em going for a long time. Plus, if you’re just dipping your toes into the cowboy boot world, the minimalist uppers forgo the decorative western stitching which makes them easier to style.

If you’re after that western look but need a pair of boots that can handle the demands of a jobsite, a lot of guys will tell you to look to Ariat. That’s because they manage to blend classic cowboy style with modern-day features, and a palatable price point in perfect proportion. While they do offer a range of work boots in lace-up styles, their Groundbreaker boots are a standout with classic cowboy boot looks.

They’re made of full-grain leather, include a supportive and comfortable insole, and meet ASTM standards for slip resistance and electrical safety. Because it’s among Ariat’s most popular styles, it’s also available in a wide range of colorways, toe shapes, and even steel toe versions. Some more traditional cowboys will poo-poo the fact that these aren’t made stateside, but if you’re on a budget, you’ll get more than what you pay for.

Cowboy boots aren’t all rough-and-tumble affairs. In fact, the right pair can easily strut the red carpet or waltz into a fancy restaurant with panache. You’ll want a pair with leather that shines up well and in a darker colorway. For date nights and more formal affairs, these Tony Lamas will impress thanks to the exotic lizard skin uppers and low-key embroidery. They’re the kind of boots that can play well for the in-laws with a tailored suit or play a rock-’n’-roll star with some vintage jeans and a tight white tee.

These days, most boot brands walk in the shadows of one brand: Lucchese. They’ve been outfitting American presidents, high-profile celebs, and the Dallas Cowboy Cheerleaders for decades and it’s all thanks to their commitment to high-quality craftsmanship. Though any pair of Lucchese’s would earn you more than a few approving head nods, the most coveted are the boots that they make in their Texas workshop.

Using a range of full-grain leathers and exotic leathers like caiman alligator and pirarucu fish skin, each pair is crafted by master bootmakers using time-honored techniques. The Gavin, in their iconic Black Cherry, is a picture-perfect style featuring smooth Santini goat leather uppers with intricate embellishments, welted construction, and lemonwood pegs—made the old-fashioned way, basically. They’ll cost you a pretty penny, of course, but they'll last pretty much forever, and the drip you’ll get in return is priceless.

From Ralph Lauren’s western-inspired sub-label, these RRL boots meld high-end materials with old-world craftsmanship and feature American-tanned leather uppers, Goodyear-welted construction, and vintage-style rubber soles—all crafted in a multi-generational Texas bootmaking factory.

Frye is another American brand with proven boot quality chops. (In fact, it claims to be America's oldest continually-operating boot company.) Its Roper boot has all the same strengths as Red Wing's, and comes in a non-roughout leather.

We don't typically include the same designers twice on one list, but Tecovas are that good. The Johnny is for anyone who wants a softer, slightly more charming boot than the eternal Cartwright up top.

For fellas whose style skews a little more regular-guy than rodeo, these lower-profile, lower-priced Ropers have a Goodyear welt and Vibram outsole. Bang for your, ahem, buck.

Wythe's playing-card-inspired boots feature all the bells and whistles, including premium leather inside and out, hand-applied details, lemonwood pegs, and second-to-none construction all-around. While some brands tap the expert bootmakers in Léon, Mexico to pump out high-quality mass-appeal boots, Wythe tapped these artisans to really let them cook.

All of Yuketen's shoes are perfect, which is a big part of the reason Drake's now carries them. And while they're best known for their moccasin styles, the brand makes an exceptionally handsome cowboy boot too. Really, they're just showing off now.

The classic move for western boots is to lean into their rougher side. Toss them on with well-fitting jeans (preferably vintage bootcuts) and a snap-button shirt. But open up your mind and step outside of the saloon and the possibilities are practically endless. A slick pair of exotic leather cowboy boots matched with a '70s-inspired suit screams filthy-rich oil tycoon—if not Alessandro Michele-era Gucci. Or why not mix up a preppy pair of chinos with a grungy graphic tee and some roughed-up suede ropers? The point is, you don’t have to pretend to be a cowboy to wear their boots (though you certainly can). So treat them like any other pair of shoes in your closet and wear them however you want. Hell, we’d go so far as to call them an essential pair of boots for every wardrobe.

Peter Middleton knows a thing or two about the lifestyle having cut his teeth at Ralph Lauren and used it as a springboard for his own western-inspired brand, Wythe. “To me the beauty and shape of the Cowboy Boot (and a lot of the original design intent) lies in its curves and that’s what makes a great boot SEXY. There isn't a lot of men's footwear that has these dramatic curves, leather, and a high heel but the right cowboy boot has them all.”

He says that good cowboy boots should be made with natural leathers that age well with wear, mould to the wearer’s feet, and can be recrafted repeatedly. His non-negotiables include full leather construction from the insole to the outsole, linings, uppers, and heels. Look for Goodyear welted construction which will allow you to have the boots resoled and extend their life. The toe bug (the fancy stitching at the toe), should sit right where your foot flexes to help cover up the crease that comes with each step. Preferably, this would be corded by hand, of course.

Price points will vary, and you can get some well-made boots for around $300. The really great stuff will often be twice that much. Middleton says, “the best thing to do is wait and save up until you can buy the version you actually want because its impossible to cut corners and still deliver the product you want.” So if you can be patient, save up. If you can’t, try buying secondhand. But if you simply can’t wait, you’ll do well enough with plenty of the mid-tier brands until you’re ready to upgrade.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you.

#6698. This Couple Rented Out a 17th-Century Stone Village for Their Misty Cliffside Wedding in the Azores

Kathryn Mawhinney and Grayson Judge’s first date was technically a phone call. A seven-hour phone call, to be precise. “We both grew up in the Bay Area but didn’t meet until 2024,” says Kate, who at the time was still finishing college in Atlanta. Rather than waiting until they were in the same place, the two spent six weeks talking on the phone every day. “After that first call, I knew I needed to have her in my life,” recalls Grayson. “She was unbelievably charming, funny, and warm, and I knew there would be a line of guys waiting for her when she got home.”

When they eventually had their first in-person date, it was in San Francisco, halfway between their two hometowns. Grayson planned a night out at a tequila bar (margaritas are Kate’s favorite), followed by tapas for dinner, and finally a lookout point in the Russian Hill neighborhood. “I texted one of my buddies on my way home and told him I would marry her one day,” he says.

Fifteen months later, Grayson proposed at that same lookout point. “I got her there by convincing her we were on our way to brunch with my cousin, and instead brought her back to the place where it had all started,” he says. Despite the couple having previously talked about a general timeline for getting engaged, the actual proposal caught her off guard. “The second I realized what was happening, I immediately started sobbing uncontrollably,” she says.

When the couple was deciding where to get married, they landed on an intimate gathering of family and friends in Fajãzinha on Flores Island in the Azores. (They also plan to have a larger wedding next summer in a town the bride’s family grew up visiting.) The island is among the most remote in the Azores, and is where Grayson’s maternal ancestors are from. “My Azorean heritage has always been a source of pride for my family and me,” he says. “Returning to my ancestral homeland to marry the love of my life was truly an indescribable feeling.”

They rented out the entirety of Aldeia da Cuada, a 17th-century stone village turned hotel that was able to accommodate everyone in town for the week’s festivities. “The little houses were originally built higher on the island to escape pirates, and the whole place felt like a fairy tale,” Kate says.

Kate took the lead with conceptualizing and planning, while Grayson spearheaded logistics. “My man of honor jokes that it was really just me and my 100-page Canva board against the world,” she says. Kate sourced vendors from all over the world, including Etsy stationery artists and commercial wholesalers for embroidered towels and aprons.

Among their standout vendors was their florist, Alice of Jungle Utopia, who purchased special headphones that translated French to Portuguese so she could figure out how to import the flowers they wanted. “And on top of everything else, she even foraged in the mountains for garnishes for our Palomas. She is truly such an angel,” Kate says.

Carlota, the owner of Aldeia da Cuada, was also instrumental in the planning process. “She and her team went above and beyond, building cocktail tables by hand, learning to make passion-fruit margaritas on the fly, and working with civil and parish authorities to help pull off the first wedding our church had hosted in more than 20 years,” Grayson says. “I joke that Carlota is the second love of my life,” Kate adds. “We truly could not have pulled this off without her.” A month before the wedding, they also brought on a team of two from Mason Market (Sam and Tyler) to bring everything over the finish line.

For their welcome party, Kate chose a Ralph Lauren gown circa 2001 (her birth year) and paired it with Jimmy Choo heels and her mother-in-law’s diamond studs. “The earrings were especially meaningful: They had belonged to her mother and were originally given to her by Grayson’s late grandfather, whose ashes were scattered on Flores,” Kate says. Grayson opted for a dark brown suit and tonal shirt from Todd Snyder.

The morning of the wedding, Kate slipped into a robe and slip she had thrifted in France to get ready. “We didn’t have elaborate dressing teams or glam squads for everyone,” she says. “My best friends [got] ready on the floor using their iPhones as mirrors. They joked that they experienced the purest form of girlhood.”

The ceremony took place in the Church of Nossa Senhora dos Remédios, a Catholic church constructed in 1776. Kate walked down the aisle in a long-sleeved, open-back gown that she had found while shopping with her grandmother and mother. “We customized the Sareh Nouri gown extensively, removing the bow and extra train in the back, changing the short sleeves to long sleeves, extending the train, and adding tiny buttons along the sleeves,” she says. She paired the gown with Amina Muaddi heels, vintage earrings, and a veil with a removable blusher.

“I will never forget the first glimpse I caught of her through a small crack in the wooden church doors,” Grayson says of Kate’s dress. For his own look, he wore a Saint Laurent tuxedo with a Giorgio Armani tuxedo shirt, which had been gifted to him by his mother-in-law a few years earlier.

A local priest named Júlio presided over the ceremony, which was half in English and half in Portuguese. A few of the townspeople sat in the back pews to witness the ceremony. “There was something so moving about having them there,” Kate says. “It made me feel like we were becoming part of something much bigger than just our own marriage.

After the ceremony, the two were waiting to sign the marriage certificate when Kate felt a light tap on her arm. “I looked down, and a little girl handed me a drawing and said, ‘This is for you,’” she recalls. It was a picture she had drawn of the couple. “It was the pianist’s daughter, and we were told later that it was her first wedding and she thought that Kate was a princess,” Grayson says.

The group proceeded down to the town square of Fajãzinha, where a wine bar had been set up. “Each guest had a wine glass with a Portuguese scarf tied around it, which Kate had embroidered with their names,” Grayson says. The priest, local townspeople, taxi drivers, and shepherds all joined the celebration.

When guests arrived at the reception, a handwritten letter from Kate awaited each of them at their respective place settings. “Kate is the only person I know who would handwrite four-plus-page, personal, heartfelt letters to 29 people expressing her gratitude for their role in helping her become the woman she is today,” Grayson says.

Once speeches kicked off, the couple were both brought to tears when Grayson’s mother took the microphone. “She hired a genealogist and began the speech by reading the names of Grayson’s ancestors who had lived on Flores, including multiple couples who had been married in the very same church where we had said our vows just hours earlier,” Kate says. “We had no idea, and it made the entire day feel even more special.”

The group eventually migrated to the circular stone roof of an old atafona (traditional mill) and danced under string lights, drank wine straight from the bottles, and partied into the night on the makeshift dance floor (“with a constant fight for who was on aux”). The after-party moved to the pool, where everyone swam and danced until 6:30 in the morning. “As proof that I was having the best night of my life, I managed to roll my ankle and just kept dancing,” Kate says.

Looking back, it was these moments of friendship and family they say they’ll remember most. “I think an underrated part of a wedding is that while you’re marrying the love of your life, you’re surrounded by the people who were your entire life first,” Kate says. “One of my relatives, who hadn’t flown in decades because he was afraid of flying, got on a plane because I was getting married. My mom pressed three of the groomsmen’s suits when they wandered into her little stone house looking for help… They say your wedding sets the tone for your marriage, but I hope that week sets the tone for the rest of our lives.”

Flores Island. In the foreground is the historic stone village of Aldeia da Cuada, where we held our reception, and in the distance, Fajãzinha village and the Church of Nossa Senhora dos Remédios. The last time a member of my family was married in that church was 150 years ago. —Grayson
