#6695. Florence Pugh Won’t Let Fear Hold Her Back

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

The daring East of Eden star on her banner year, speaking out, and not standing for bullshit.

Florence Pugh says she “tries to be brave at least once a day.” Whether she’s raising her voice, taking on complex roles, wearing a sheer dress and an I-don’t-give-a-fuck attitude on the red carpet, or even—gasp!—showing cellulite onscreen, she is consistent in her courageousness. When we meet in late September, it has been two days since she made a powerful statement on Instagram about the lawsuit alleging gang rape at Cornell University, and then posted again when she learned her original post had been blocked by Meta. “No one fucking censors me,” she tells me. “Don’t even try. That’s just going to add fuel to the fire.”

It’s not so much that Pugh is fearless (she is still going through life as a woman, after all), it’s that she was raised with steel in her spine. “My dad has always hated bullies, and he’s always told me that if you ever see anything, you have to do the right thing. Otherwise you are just the same as them,” she says. “And I think that’s where that instinct of ‘I must speak out on this injustice’ comes from. It’s always important to stand up for people who don’t have the voice that I have. I have the ability, and I have to use it. I don’t know who I would be if I didn’t.”

Pugh is in New York City in the days ahead of the premiere of East of Eden, her latest project in perhaps the biggest year of her career to date, between the Netflix limited series and roles in three blockbusters: Spider-Man: Brand New Day, Dune: Part Three, and Avengers: Doomsday.

When she arrives for our lunch at the Greenwich Hotel, her aura precedes her. Before she’s in sight, I hear her thanking waiters, busboys, and a random guy who had the fortune of holding the door for her, purring “darling” and “love” at them as she floats by, her charming, deep British drawl on full display. When she steps into the courtyard, she waves at me from the other side as if we’re old friends.

As we tuck into some bigeye tuna and a green Caesar (she is happy to share), the conversation turns serious quickly. Pugh is arguably the highest-profile celebrity to post about the heinous accusations at Cornell, and I ask her why she felt compelled to do so. “Because I’m a woman who cares about women. I care about women I know, and I care about women I don’t know. And if we allow for stories like that to become in any way normal, then we are allowing ourselves to continue toward that destiny of abuse and rape being accepted as a norm,” she says. “Rape can never ever be a conversation that we move on from. It has to be something that we look at, face-on, and we demand justice, accountability, and for the rapist to see what they have done to someone’s life. Because if we don’t, we’re accepting it. And I don’t ever, ever, ever want to live in a world where we move on from it easily.”

I tell her I know it might seem odd to talk about Cornell in an interview that’s meant to be about her acting career, but she breaks into a smile and says, “It’s actually perfect.” You see, to her it’s all related, because she tries to be just as brave onscreen as she is off it. “I’m terrified of every single role that I’ve played. Like, ‘How am I going to do that? I don’t know if I can.’ But that’s also the thing that really thrills me, because it means that I get to come face-to-face with that feeling of fear again and override it. And the same can be said of things in life that are intimidating or are scary or require me to be brave. It’s like, ‘If I stay in this, I’m going to live in this fear. And if I punch through it, then I can overcome it.’”

Her characters demand a lot of her. They are complicated, nuanced, and often find themselves clawing out of their circumstances by tooth, nail, and, more than once, poison. At just 19 years old, and without any formal acting training, Pugh’s award-winning breakout role in Lady Macbeth (not that one) required her to embody a bride in 1865, so miserable in her cruel marriage that she murdered her way to freedom. In 2019, she played both a grieving twentysomething-turned-cult “May Queen” in Midsommar and the youngest sister in Greta Gerwig’s Little Women, managing to imbue the latter character with such humanity that she had audiences feeling empathy for Amy March (of all people), and also received her first Oscar nomination. And since her debut as Yelena Belova in 2021’s Black Widow, she has done many of her own stunts in the Marvel films, once jumping off a 2,227-foot-tall building nine times to get the shot.

Beauty Tip: For a warm vanilla scent that wraps you like a coat, try Max Mara Le Parfum Eau de Parfum.

Her range and repertoire are why Zoe Kazan, writer, executive producer, and co-showrunner of this year’s buzzy East of Eden adaptation, has said Pugh was the “only person” she envisioned for the role of the notorious Cathy Ames. “I thought it was the most gripping, sensational script, and I immediately started saying the lines out loud, so I was like, ‘Oh fuck, well, I’m Cathy,’” Pugh tells me. “I loved how she was a full human who does awful things, and has awful things done to her, and makes mistakes. I loved the question marks and the complexities to her, because that’s real to me.”

In John Steinbeck’s telling, Cathy is pure evil, and it’s unclear what made her that way (he himself seems not to know). Leave it to a woman to add depth to a female character. Kazan’s Cathy is just as ruthless, but she has a backstory that is used to add context, but never to justify her heinous acts. She’s fully formed, messy—okay, yes, likely sociopathic—and exactly the type of woman Pugh loves to take on. “I don’t know how to describe it other than I play characters that ask a lot of audience members,” Pugh says. “I think there’s something that excites, and also troubles, people about the way that I find humanity in even some of the most evil characters. I think it fascinates people.” As we take our final bites, I say people should just let women be, both in real life and onscreen. “And let us be big and beautiful,” Pugh adds. “I know that’s intimidating, but please let us, because it only makes great things.”

There’s so much scrutiny of how we look, how we dress, and how we age. And then when we do those things, they’re like, “Oh my God, she looks like this, or she’s done too much of that, or she’s gained weight, or she’s lost too much weight.” You can never get any footing right. I feel like the best work that I’ve ever done is when I truly feel ugly. When I’ve got shit makeup on and I’m either sick or ugly or having a hangover or a breakdown. I love that type of makeup because it allows me to be free.

What I love about acting is, I don’t have the typical self-consciousness of just being a woman. When I’m acting, I get to be comfortable in the body that I’m in. If the camera picks up that I have a stomach roll when I’m sitting down, then I have a stomach roll when I’m sitting down. And if the camera picks up that I’ve got cellulite on my thighs, then yeah, I’ve got cellulite on my thighs. I just give it over to the art. So performing is very freeing for me, and it always has been.

It is so crucial to be okay with how you are and who you are, because people are going to attack you regardless. They’re going to say really shitty things, no matter if you’re too small, too big, too wrinkly, too spotty, too loud, too quiet, too opinionated. They’re going to find issue with you, because that’s just the nature of the internet and people and opinions. So it’s really important to find peace with what you want to represent and who you want to be. Because then you can just be like, “Ugh, those dickheads.”

The moment I got that nomination, it’s like the pressure just vanished—there was nothing breathing down my neck anymore. I felt the energy of how people wanted to work with me change. It was not only just a pat on the back that I could feel, but it was a pat on the back that I felt like everybody could see. But it also made me even harder on myself to get another one. It’s like, I know that I’ve achieved this before. I can achieve this again.

I learned how to drive on the Warner Brothers lot when I was 19, for this pilot that I was doing called Studio City. And so I learned with the transpo captain, going around the Warner Brothers lot in a car, and I remember at the time thinking, This is so hysterical, this is so movie world. I just thought it was hysterical that I was constantly learning how to drive all of these amazing cars for so many projects, but I never had my license. [She has one now.]

The thing that I’m getting better and better at is protecting myself. Every time I work on a movie, I get more confident in the way that I can protect myself and the way that I can lead a film set, and just not stand for bullshit anymore. I’m not doing it. I’m not standing for bullshit behavior. I’m not standing for bullshit attitude. I’m not allowing for people to be rude to the crew. You just get bolder and bigger and more confident with time, and you want to be around and work with the right people. And the moment someone is making that vibe feel off, everybody feels it. I don’t want to deal with messy. It’s just about surrounding yourself with professionals who have the same way of working in mind: Show up on time, don’t be rude, don’t be a misogynist.

There’s something so magical about doing those big, stonkingly large movies with budgets and costumes and sets, because those are the films that I remember watching when I was a kid. But I’m not one thing. I also love doing really small things. I love how they both feed my soul.

I would like to have lunch with Cathy. No, actually I’d like to have lunch with Kate [what Cathy calls herself in later episodes]. But I wouldn’t be trying to fuss on her. I’d love to have dinner with Kate just because I’d be really interested to see how she talks to people outside of me. And then I’d love to have dinner with Amy March, because she’d take me to some fabulous place in Paris and I know she’d be wearing fantastic clothing. And then there’s poor Dani [in Midsommar]. I’d need to have a whole weekend with her. She’s so broken. I’d need to feed her soul food. I’d need to cook for her. I’d need to put her in front of the fire and wrap a blanket around her and just have hugs.

#6694. The New South of France

The French Riviera is always a good idea. Visit in the off-season to soak in its buzzy contemporary-art scene sans tourists.

The South of France became a see-and-be-seen summer destination a century ago, when the free-spirited American couple Gerald and Sara Murphy began hosting epic beach parties in Cap d’Antibes. At any one of them, you might find Jean Cocteau and Igor Stravinsky unpacking a picnic basket, Pablo Picasso or Ernest Hemingway flirting with Sara (who famously wore pearls with her bathing suit), or F. Scott Fitzgerald taking mental notes for Tender Is the Night.

The legacies of the Lost Generation are still a thrill to follow, though booking a room at the Hotel du Cap-Eden-Roc, where the Murphys liked to stow their guests, is now a trickier prospect. The French Riviera remains a wildly popular summer destination and will serve as the next setting for HBO’s The White Lotus. Instead, visit in fall or even winter, when you’ll have space to wander through the Picasso museum in Antibes’s Grimaldi Castle or take in Cocteau’s murals and frescoes in the Chapelle Saint-Pierre in Villefranche-sur-Mer or in the Villa Santo Sospir in Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat (which was recently renovated and is available to rent).

But what makes the South of France even more compelling now is the thriving contemporary-art scene, ignited, in part, by the collector Maja Hoffmann, who opened the dynamic museum complex LUMA Arles, with its Frank Gehry tower, in 2021. She has also helped create some of the city’s most fashionable hotels: L’Arlatan, with its tiled interiors by artist Jorge Pardo; the Grand Hôtel Nord-Pinus, reenvisioned by designer Duro Olowu; and Le Cloître, designed by India Mahdavi. (The latter closes for the winter after November 29.) “The energy around LUMA has drawn such an interesting mix of people that I sometimes prefer Arles to Paris,” says Mahdavi, who has a home there.

The winery estate Château La Coste, near Aix-en-Provence, boasts one of the most ambitious art-focused hospitality projects in the region, featuring site-specific works from Tadao Ando, Oscar Niemeyer, and Matisse’s grandson Paul.

This past spring, everyone was talking about the opening of the Zannier Ile de Bendor, a new resort located on the private island Ile de Bendor, a 10-minute boat ride from the coastal village of Bandol. Reopening after the winter season this May, it features 93 rooms, a 13,000-square-foot wellness center, an art gallery, and three ateliers that will host a rotating cast of artisans.

In Marseille, the seaside Tuba Club is a favorite of the creative set. There’s also Hôtel Amista, a new 24-room property near the Old Port reimagined by Dorothée Delaye. The can’t-miss shopping destination here is unquestionably Maison Empereur, a hardware store dating back to 1827 with a trove of one-of-a-kind home goods.

Lastly, in rural Provence, Cosima Ungaro, daughter of couturier Emanuel Ungaro, has reinvented two of the buildings on her late father’s medieval estate, La Cavalerie, into spaces for artists and travelers. “The light, the stars, the wind—these elements have exerted a magnetic pull on artists for centuries,” she says.

#6692. 18 Best Raincoats for Men 2026, According to GQ Editors

Decades ago, your only options for rainy weather coverage were some kind of trench coat, a coarse wool overcoat, or, if you really needed to be out in it, a thick rubber sack that kept you dry but didn’t breathe. Thankfully, material science has advanced.

There are, of course, umbrellas? And we won’t stop you looking into those. But ask anyone from the Pacific Northwest, and they’ll tell you their rain jacket does all that work with ease. That’s because raincoats aren’t an accessory to your outfit: they’re the main focus. A good raincoat can turn your sad ensemble into head-turning Paparazzi fodder, or at the very least, keep you dry and stylish when it’s wet out.

Still not convinced? We figured—so we tested the best rain jackets and coats for men on the market right now, from the tried-and-true natural-fabric mainstays to the buzzy, newfangled riffs, and everything in between. Here they are.

Arc'teryx's Beta LT jacket is the pinnacle of no-BS rain defense, beloved by wannabe Everest climbers, GQ Recommends editors, and meme-savvy TikTokers alike. Its custom Gore-Tex fabrication will keep you from getting soaked during the harshest of downpours, while its breathable pores work overtime to let water vapor (a.k.a. sweat) escape. That sleek, streamlined silhouette also lends itself naturally to a range of pairings, from straight-fit jeans and sneakers to a full-on “Scaling Kilimanjaro” kit—cargos, backpack, hiking boots—perfect for all of your wildcard outdoor activities.

It’s an investment, but hundreds of guys were showering in theirs for a reason: If you need top-tier weather protection and long-term durability—and are willing to invest—this is still the best rain jacket for serious outdoor use. That said, most dudes chasing the clout that Arc’teryx affords won’t need to max out its capabilities. Still, it’s good to know that if you’re ever caught in a downpour that won’t let up, the Beta’s the one waterproof jacket that won’t leave you high and, uh, wet.

When it comes to outdoor gear that keeps up with Mother Nature, Patagonia’s among the first to come to mind. The OG gorpcore label has more than its fair share of bangers for every climate from the iconic Baggies shorts to its range of plush fleece jackets, and when it comes to rainy weather, there’s the Torrentshell jacket. It’s a canonical piece of kit for Patagonia and has kept customers dry and fly for years.

The latest version features a three-layer shell system that maximizes water-repellency and breathability with a 100% recycled nylon face fabric. It features toasty microfleece-lined handwarmer pockets, welted zippers for water protection (plus pit zips for ventilation), and the entire thing can pack down into itself. So pack it up, throw it in your bag, and bust it out whenever the weather turns out to be worse than what the weatherman says. With a feature set like that, you’d expect to pay through the nose, but we’re thrilled to say that it doesn’t even break $200.

The advancements in rain-wicking technology tickles our lizard brains as much as watching a rock-crushing machine turn a boulder into pebbles. But as much as we appreciate multi-layered DWR-coated materials and heat-sealed seams give us joy, we also have a great reverence and appreciation for rain coats of yore. Enter the waxed jacket, a time-tested fabric used by sailors off the British coast since the 1800s.

If you’re gonna get a waxed jacket, you’d best get a Barbour, the reigning champ of waxed jackets. Barbour has more options and collaborations than ever, so it can be tricky to get your head around what’s what but for our money, the classic Beaufort is the Goldilocks of wax jackets. Where the Bedale is shorter and styles like the Border run down to the mid-thigh, the Beaufort is just right but still long enough to layer over your sport coats. Whichever you choose, don’t forget to re-wax at home after a few seasons. Guys seem to be nervous to do it, but it’s easy, and everytime I’ve re-waxed mine, people compliment me on how great it looks. The reward for your grunt work is a jacket you'll keep for decades to come.

This season, J.Press has unearthed a Rare Barbour: the Burghley. It hasn’t been in the brand’s regular rotation for a number of years, earning it a following among collectors in places like Japan. But now it’s back in all its sweeping, full-length glory.

Originally designed to extend past the knees (and over the saddle and tops of riding boots) the Burghley protects the rider from rain and thorns. It’s a dramatic silhouette that will set you apart from all the cropped Transport and Bedales out there. Sure, it has equestrian heritage, but you needn’t be keeping a stable to wear one. It’s a great alternative to a trench, at home in the city as well as the country. And yes, it’s still made in England.

The perfect trench coat does exist, and Burberry, inventor of the style's signature gabardine fabric in 1879, cracked the code on it long ago. In the nearly 150 years since, surprisingly little has changed about the silhouette, and for good reason. The classic fit means it's roomy enough to layer over your slouchiest Armani-inspired suiting, while the belted design gives it instant sophistication. Plus, the lining and under-collar check pattern is unmistakably Burberry—an investment-worthy flex since the coat was invented.

Its WWI heritage is well-documented—British officers wore it in the trenches, using details like the shoulder flap for rifle recoil and belt rings for canteens and grenades serving real military functions. Today, it’s less about battlefield utility and more about how that water-resistant cotton gabardine will keep you dry in light city rain. I like the black, but the classic tan is always an option for you too.

Another entry from Vancouver—what can we say, they know a few things about rain up there. Indie label James Coward sources fabric from mills known for their quality and considered production practices, then makes its garments locally in its workshop. This coat is cut from the brand’s durable, waterproof ‘Mastershield cloth, a dense weave that offers protection from the elements. A generous silhouette and roomy raglan sleeves give it natural gravitas in gloomy weather, all while keeping the look relaxed and easy to layer.

Whereas the Arc’teryx Beta is the brand’s versatile all-mountain shell, the Alpha SV is built for technical climbing and severe weather. A helmet-compatible hood, harness-ready chest pockets and pit zips make it the top dog of storm shells.

HAVEN puts a GORPcore spin on the refined, city-ready trench made from three-layer GORE-TEX PRO, a more rugged fabric typically found in shells for climbing and backcountry skiing. It’s serious storm gear with a city sensibility, ready to make you feel invincible during a rainy commute.

The wrap coat is Lemaire’s runaway hit. But this Ventile-cotton style is a rainy-day flex: densely woven, breathable cotton that swells when wet to help keep wind and rain out, without synthetic fibres or coatings. Chic.

Menswear can get a little obsessive about fabric specs and provenance. But when a jacket is this cool, you get why. 100 percent Giza cotton, woven at maximum density in Saitama, Japan and originally developed for the British Air Force and later recommissioned by Japan’s Coast Guard. Yeah, that’s the good stuff.

Prep never left, but J.Press is certainly on its way back. The label’s updated take on a classic hooded parka keeps the familiar military shape sans PFAS with natural Ventile cotton. Choose classic army green, or eye-popping orange.

Haider Ackermann's take on Canada Goose is coming into focus. The brand’s Snow Goose sub-label is more Milan than Manitoba, trading logo-heavy designs for cool colours and modern silhouettes that go well beyond down parkas.

Making a good rain jacket might not take a degree in nuclear science, but Outdoor Research’s founder was actually a nuclear physicist turned avid mountaineer. This stripped-back shell sheds weight and packs small without skimping on protection. Stash it and forget it.

Marmot, meanwhile didn’t pull back on features to shave weight. This soft, quiet waterproof shell is built for movement, with an “Angel-Wing” design that lets you reach overhead without the hem riding up and putting your backside on display.

Reigning Champ has also gone well beyond sweats and tees. This workhorse of a rain jacket is more downtown than summit in style but still meets the moment with GORE-TEX construction and a very digestible price.

Italian fabric. Fifth-generation Portuguese construction. New York City design. That’s the mix behind Knickerbocker’s full-length trench. Its tightly woven, water-repellent fabric helps keep rain out all with the kind of easy, downtown cool Knickerbocker does so well.

Uniqlo’s even more affordable sister brand, GU, delivers a lot of jacket for the money The throwback piping and punchy colours nod to the ’90s, while the water- and wind-resistant fabric makes it practical, too.

A waxed Harrington probably isn’t for a downpour unless your trousers are waxed, too, but it’s ideal for breezy, drizzly, and sunny fall days alike. And, aye, the waxed fabric comes straight from Scotland. No messing about.

Who wants to drag a sopping wet umbrella around only to forget it at the restaurant or in the back of a cab? When you’ve got a trench coat with your cell and headphones in the pockets, it’s almost impossible to lose. Through light mists, heavy rain, and even torrential downpours, the best rain coats are, ironically, the drippiest too. They’ll prevent you from showing up to the function like a poor wet dog and instead make your arrival a warm, dry welcome.

Trench coats that aren’t the only coats vying to shield you from the rain, though. Gorpcore’s popularity has given us waves of tech-y jackets, parkas, and anoraks all wrought from futuristic multi-layered materials that balance breathability with waterproof ability. The result is a cementing of this 21st century sportswear into must-have menswear. And let’s not forget the workwear-adjacent waxed jackets born from sailing the Scottish seas in 15th-century Scotland. With their rugged good looks and a lust for patina, they’ve become stylish staples when the weather’s all doom and gloom.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6691. Behold: Your Official ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Season 35 Cast Elimination Tracker

Get your dancing shoes ready, because season 35 of Dancing With the Stars is finally here! The reality dancing competition returned for a new season of live shows on September 15, and the show locked in some pretty major stars for the competition, from Olympian Amber Glenn to reality star Ciara Miller.

As always, this season of DWTS is pitting pop stars, reality show alums, actors, and professional athletes against one another in a heated classic ballroom competition. Each celeb is, of course, paired with a dance pro to guide them through their journey and help them get the biggest honor of all: the Mirrorball Trophy.

The entire season 35 cast was announced on Good Morning America on September 2, along with their professional partners, and here’s everything you need to know about the cast...including who has already been eliminated. (Side note: We’ll be keeping this updated each week, so check back to see who’s still in the competition.)

ABC always loves to throw an Olympian in the mix, and this season, it’s Blade Angel Amber, who revealed during an episode of House of Maher that “it’s been a dream of mine” to do DWTS “since I saw Meryl [Davis] do it in 2014.”

Dance experience: If you’ve seen Amber on the ice, then you know she’s a dancer at heart.

Last season, it was Alix Earle—but this season, the internet personality competing for the Mirrorball Trophy is Connor Wood, aka Fibula (who, btw, is good friends with DWTS alum Dylan Efron).

Known for: Brooke and Connor Make a Podcast and Fibs & Friends

Dance experience: If he has any, it’s news to me!

It wouldn’t be a season of DWTS without a few athletes, and in season 35, you can look forward to seeing two-time Paralympian Ezra Frech.

Known for: Tokyo 2020 Paralympics and Paris 2024 Paralympics (where he won two gold medals!)

Dance experience: He competes in track and field, but as far as I know, he’s new to the world of dance.

You know him for a million TV shows and movies, but did you know Harry was a professional dancer at the beginning of his career? Something tells us he’s still got it...

Known for: Glee, Shadowhunters, Grey’s Anatomy, and Crazy Rich Asians, among others

Dance experience: He served as a backup dancer for Beyoncé, Jennifer Lopez, Mariah Carey, and Madonna before transitioning to acting.

Maura was also rumored for months before her casting was announced. Back in March, she even told The Hollywood Reporter that DWTS would “be a huge challenge,” but one she was willing to take on. “I know I’d throw myself into it and all the looks and glitter,” she added.

Known for: Love Island UK, The Traitors, and Love Island USA: Aftersun

Dance experience: Maura told THR that she did “a bit of Irish dancing” when she was younger.

Big news for Fresh Prince fans, because Tatyana will be joining her onscreen big brother, DWTS host Alfonso Ribeiro, in the ballroom.

Known for: The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air and The Young and the Restless

Dance experience: While she’s better known for her singing skills, let’s not forget that we have her to thank for the TikTok dance trend set to Doechii’s “Anxiety.”

Jenna is stepping back into her dancing shoes! She started her career as a professional backup dancer before becoming an actor. But dancing has always been in her DNA, so we’re thrilled she’s back at it.

Known for: Step Up, Witches of East End, and The Rookie, among others

Dance experience: Where to begin! Jenna is an extremely experienced dancer and rose to fame thanks to Step Up. She was also a backup dancer for Janet Jackson.

She’s been in several iconic aughts movies, including Save the Last Dance. In fact, if she doesn’t recreate her dance from that movie, I will personally write a letter of complaint.

Dance experience: Once again: Save the Last Dance.

Along with an Olympian, most seasons of DWTS include a member of Bachelor Nation...and this season, it’s Tyler, who’s ready to compete six years after his ex, Hannah Brown, took first place in season 28.

Known for: The Bachelorette, Special Forces, and Going Home with Tyler Cameron

Dance experience: He competed on The Real Dirty Dancing back in 2022 (and finished as a runner-up!).

Back in December 2025, Jackson replied to a fan who asked whether he would “go on Dancing With the Stars next season” with a video compilation of dance clips, which he captioned, “Long story short... yes, yes I would.” Dreams do come true!

Known for: The Savannah Bananas baseball team and TikTok

Dance experience: Though he’s done plenty of choreography since joining the Savannah Bananas in 2022, Jackson surprisingly has no formal dance background.

As Jimmy Kimmel joked when his onscreen sidekick was announced: “Guillermo will become the first-ever parking lot security guard to dance with the stars.”

Known for: Jimmy Kimmel Live! (though he first rose to fame while working as a parking lot security guard at the Hollywood Boulevard Masonic Temple studio)

Dance experience: None that I know of, but I’m excited to see him bust out some moves!

Ciara was rumored to be joining the cast for season 34, but this year, it’s finally happening! As she told Us Weekly when the rumors first began, “I want [a pro] who is hard on me. Like, ‘You got to get this down.’”

Known for: Summer House, The Traitors, and Love Island USA: Aftersun

Dance experience: Ciara actually grew up dancing, and revealed to Us Weekly that she took ballet for 10 years.

Fans have been side-eyeing the middle Hanson brother ever since he showed up in the audience during season 34’s “Wicked Night” episode—and it seems that he is, indeed, hitting the stage this season.

Dance experience: Seeing as he spends most of his time behind the keyboard while performing, this is a little unclear.

Any Food Network fans here? Then you’re well aware of Giada, who’s been a household name for decades.

Known for: Giada at Home (among many other Food Network shows)

Dance experience: Unclear, but I’m excited to see what moves she might have!

Brooks Nader’s sister is following in her footsteps and we can’t wait!

Dance experience: TBD, but we’ll find out!

After cheering on his wife Whitney Leavitt during season 34, The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives fan fave is now stepping into the ballroom himself (though let’s not forget that he already took the stage last year during Whitney’s Dedication Night dance).

Known for: The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives

Dance experience: Aside from doing TikTok dances, Conner appeared in the Off-Broadway dance show 11 to Midnight.

#6689. Louise Kennedy on Her Sweeping Second Novel, ‘Stations’

At 59, the Irish novelist Louise Kennedy is the literary world’s latest great find. She’s also her own self-discovery project: After working as a chef for nearly 30 years, Kennedy was in her late 40s when she first tried to write fiction.

She’s since set raw-hearted and tragically romantic tales in the shadow of the Troubles, the decades-long political conflict in Northern Ireland. Sexual and political awakenings exist side by side in Kennedy country. Trespasses (2023), her debut novel about a Catholic-Protestant love affair in 1970s Belfast, was translated into more than 20 languages and made into a miniseries starring Gillian Anderson Anderson. Her follow-up novel, Stations, published this month, is a punkier and even more electric work. It opens with Róisín, a bolshy and unpopular teenager, striking up a friendship with Red, a troubled local boy from a wealthy family. The story then jumps-cuts into the future, where Róisín finds Red living in a London squat, and arcs all the way into midlife.

Kennedy spoke to Vogue over Zoom from her home in Sligo about being a late bloomer, Irish-granny maximalism, and why the Troubles have been taking off.

Vogue: According to the lore, you didn’t write a word of fiction until you were 47.

Louise Kennedy: It’s true, I wasn’t scribbling away in secret. I didn’t write a thing until I joined a writing group, and even that was under duress. A friend who was involved when it was being set up kept messaging me all day, and I kept saying, “No, I’m not going.” I was busy, I was tired, and it was a ridiculous notion. I’m a cook. Why would I go to a writing group? Then she turned up at my house and told me to get in the car, so I went along. I’ve no idea why she did it.

I don’t think it was a bad thing to be older and trying to write. I couldn’t have done this in my 20s. I’d have been way too self-conscious, and I wouldn’t have had the discipline. And if, in the very unlikely event, I had managed to publish something and anybody liked it, I wouldn’t have been able to handle the attention. Not in any shape or form.

You talk about writing in a way that isn’t tortured. You can write thousands of words a day. Is that the chef in you?

I think maybe it is. I was a chef for nearly 30 years. We worked what were called split shifts but were really double shifts: in at 10 in the morning, still there at 11 at night, then out for a few drinks. The only break you’d get was sticking your head out the back door for a cigarette. So I tend not to feel sorry for myself about deadlines.

Writing from the point of view of a teenage girl seems to come easily to you. What were you like at that age?

I was awful. I was probably a bit like Róisín, fighting with everybody, really self-centered, really dramatic, deeply unpleasant a lot of the time. And I think, like her, I imagined there was some better, bigger life outside the place I’d ended up.

You don’t shy from portraying the horrors of alcoholism.

I was practically brought up in a bar. My family had a pub, and if there’s a lot of drinking, some people will become alcoholics. Three out of four of my grandparents were alcoholics, and I had uncles and aunts and neighbors who were, too. I went to London in the ’80s and lived in that precarious way; we were all out drinking cider and smoking and doing whatever else. A lot of us stopped and some of us didn’t. Even when we were 18, 19, 20, there were signs that some people were going at it harder than everybody else. Several of them are dead.

Nobody asks a child what they want to be and hears, “An alcoholic wrecking my home.” Nobody wants to end up like that. In the early days of surgery, before proper anesthesia, they poured whiskey down people’s necks before they amputated an arm or a leg. For a lot of people it’s still the acceptable form of painkilling.

In Trespasses, it was gutting to read about Cushla’s constant vigilance and anxiety where taking care of her mother, Gina, is concerned. How did Gillian Anderson end up playing Gina?

On publication day for Trespasses in the UK, in April 2022, there was a dinner, and I knew Gillian was going to be there. I was nervous so I drank too much. I was sitting beside her and she told me how much she loved the book, and how much she loved the character of Gina, the mother. Because I was a bit drunk, I thought it would be entirely reasonable to ask whether she’d play Gina in the adaptation. And Gillian said yes! I thought: This is fantastic. Then I woke up in the morning going, “Oh my God, what have you done?”

Róisín grows up to write about interior design for a living. How would you describe your own aesthetic?

Irish-granny maximalist. My house is full of stuff. I’m obsessed with old hot water bottles.

Why do you think American readers are so drawn to books about the Troubles right now?

I think a lot of it is about time. There were books published about the conflict in the ’70s and ’80s, and then it seemed to dry up. It had gone on for so long and became such a dirty conflict that maybe editors didn’t want to publish it, and maybe people didn’t want to read about it. More than 25 years have passed since the Good Friday Agreement, and I think it took that long before people were ready. I do think it was about trauma, and it needed to be put to bed for a while.

#6688. ¡Vamos, España!

With Spain fresh off a World Cup win, there’s no better time to visit Madrid and the cooler northern regions of Asturias and Galicia

I lived in Spain in the early aughts, when the country was experiencing a mic-drop moment. The shiny, futuristic Frank Gehry–designed Guggenheim Museum had gone up in Bilbao a few years earlier, setting off what is now known as the Bilbao effect: a phenomenon that describes how investing in a visionary architecture project can transform a place. Food-obsessed travelers were flocking to a small beach town in a remote corner of northern Spain just to experience a meal at El Bulli, the legendary, now closed, three-Michelin-star restaurant headed up by Ferran Adrià.

Spain is now in the midst of another glow-up, thanks in part to its World Cup win, and Madrid is front and center. A recent influx of expats from South and North America has locals calling the city the “Miami of Europe.” But don’t let that dissuade you. Mallorquín designer Rosa Esteva, who designs the elegant, made-in-Spain fashion brand Cortana, emphasizes “the charm of those glorious old places that have survived through time.” That means staying at hotels like the intimate Hotel Orfila, booking a table at La Parra, wandering through El Rastro, Madrid’s legendary flea market, and checking out a late-night flamenco show at Tablao de la Villa. At the same time, contemporary places like Esteva’s new shop in the Salamanca neighborhood, the modern tapas bar Sala de Despiece, and the contemporary-art gallery Albarrán Bourdais are worth checking out.

The typical Spanish itinerary often includes a few days in Barcelona to take in the Gaudí before heading south to the beaches of Andalusia. But Vella González, the founder of fashion brand Boxcalf, which has a flagship in Madrid’s Malasaña neighborhood, extols northern Spain’s charms and cooler climate. “For non-Spaniards, it’s an undiscovered paradise,” she says. Start in San Sebastián, one of the world’s most celebrated gastronomic capitals, and eat your way through its pintxos bars, finishing with a steak at the Basque grill house Portuetxe.

In Bilbao, discover the next generation of art spaces, such as the light-filled expansion of the Bilbao Fine Arts Museum, designed by Norman Foster and Luis María Uriarte. The Bilbao effect can be felt in nearby Santander, thanks to the new Faro Santander museum and cultural space, a historic building reimagined by David Chipperfield and currently showcasing the works of surrealist painter Leonora Carrington. Move on to the pristine beaches, green hills, and exceptional dining scene of the Asturias and Galicia regions. In Asturias, splurge on a stay at the remote wabi-sabi styled Solo Palacio and explore the old-growth forests and prehistoric rock shelters of Las Ubiñas-La Mesa Natural Park. Cozy up in the Casa Beatnik Country House hotel in Galicia, and walk the last 10 miles of the famed Camino de Santiago trail to Santiago de Compostela and its Old Town, a UNESCO World Heritage site. It’s an idyllic ending to a new kind of Spanish pilgrimage.

#6687. Everyone Is Obsessed With Inde Navarrette

The 25-year-old breakout star of this year’s top-grossing horror film is only getting started.

It’s the face that launched a thousand memes. You know the one: sad puppy-dog eyes, furrowed brow, pronounced frown, the corners of the mouth curving dramatically downward. In Obsession, the surprise hit horror film directed by the then 26-year-old YouTuber Curry Barker, Inde Navarrette’s Nikki delivers the now-viral expression with aplomb. Her utter dismay is so convincing, she’s downright terrifying. And overnight, she became a star, her countenance now cemented in horror history alongside Jason Voorhees’s mask from Friday the 13th and Ghostface in the Scream franchise. “When I go outside now, people yell ‘Nikki,’” she says. “It’s almost like they’re yelling ‘Inde.’ It doesn’t help that both names end in a similar sound.”

The recent attention is new to Navarrette. Before her breakout this year, she had played supporting characters in a string of projects: the teen Netflix series 13 Reasons Why, the CW superhero drama Superman & Lois, and the action thriller Trap House. But she had never landed a lead role. At 24, she paused to reevaluate the trajectory of her career. “I started looking at life differently, because I wasn’t where I wanted to be,” Navarrette explains. “I wanted to make a piece of work that people could look back at and say, ‘Oh, she’s capable of more than we’ve seen her do.’” With Obsession, she did just that, and then some.

Her ambition started young. Born Danielle Fabiola Navarrette in Tucson, Arizona, to a family of mixed Mexican and Australian ancestry, she was surrounded by strong women like her mother, who gave her the nickname “Inde” for her independent spirit. It suits her: Navarrette is determined and sensitive, works hard, knows exactly what she wants, and isn’t afraid to feel things deeply. Ironically, as a child, she was “super scared” of horror movies. She and her siblings loved watching them, but Navarrette describes herself as an empathetic kid who internalized everything happening on the screen as if it were happening to her. To this day, she says, if someone puts a scary movie on, “I freak the fuck out.”

In Obsession, Nikki is a music store clerk’s secret, debilitating crush. Bear (Michael Johnston) is incapable of telling her how he really feels, so he makes a wish: that she love him “more than anyone in the fucking world.” Much to the audience’s surprise, it comes true—but not as he imagined. Not even close. Their relationship turns, well, obsessive.

Despite the violence and gore, the first time Navarrette read the script, she didn’t see it as horror. To her, the narrative was sadder and more psychologically twisted than she expected films in the genre to be—this was a story about a woman being robbed of her existence, her agency, and ultimately her sense of self. “It’s devastating that Nikki completely loses her entire life,” she says. “It’s not a new idea. Women couldn’t have bank accounts until 1974.” Navarrette nails the role because she understands Nikki’s vulnerability. She sees the person underneath and what it means to watch that person disappear.

Seen by some as an incel fantasy-turned-nightmare, Obsession explores Bear’s desire for control but leaves its interpretation up for debate, something Navarrette appreciates about Barker’s approach. The film does raise the eternal When Harry Met Sally question: Can a man and a woman truly be friends? “I think they can,” she says, adding that it comes down to having a healthy amount of “self-respect and morals and values and boundaries.” She trails off, then adds, “But of course, when you spend a lot of time with somebody, you’re going to potentially see them differently.”

For Navarrette, the real win is being part of something people can’t stop talking about. The buzz has led her from hosting Saturday Night Live, to Nikki-inspired Halloween costumes, to awards chatter, and ultimately to landing a huge new role: as Rogue in the upcoming X-Men reboot from Marvel Studios. “Her mind must be fascinating, because she is starved of human touch,” she says of her character. “I would personally die if I couldn’t hug my friends and family.” But amid all the noise, what matters most is that Obsession is resonating. “It’s a dream for Nikki to feel understood,” she says. “The fact that she is makes me happier than I could ever have imagined.”

Trusting yourself might be the key to making your dreams come true. I know for a fact that my life completely changed when I started doing the things I had been procrastinating about. Up until I was 23, I was a really big people-pleaser. I wanted to make friends, and it was very important to me how I was being seen and acknowledged. When I turned 24, I started looking at life differently, because I didn’t feel good. Something needed to change. So when I went to work on Obsession, I told myself, “I’m not coming here to make friends.” It was the first set I ever went on where I solely walked in as an actor and left as an actor. After production ended, friendships naturally blossomed with the people I worked with, and they’ve turned into some of the best friendships I’ve ever had.

My first audition was for a commercial. I was 13 or 14, and my mom had driven four hours from Fresno to L.A. for me to do it. I ended up getting it, and it was such a cool experience. I remember they had me drive a car, and the brakes went out because I didn’t know you were supposed to pump them to get the brake fluid going—I didn’t even know how to drive. So the car just wouldn’t stop. The commercial never came out, but I remember being on set, looking at the monitor, seeing the lens flares and everything, and just really falling in love with that whole process.

I grew up with a family on both sides that really doesn’t see failure as an option. You just do the work. Having that mindset has really allowed me to take moments in, rather than wishing I had done everything differently. Plus, I think the lack of Hollywood in my family is really, really, really nice.

I love the women in Hollywood who have never let their light dim, like someone as successful as Viola Davis. She’s [given speeches] where she talks about feeling good, believing in yourself, and trusting yourself. Another one is Salma Hayek [Pinault]. Those are two very accomplished women.

Beauty Tip: A matte red lip feels modern with the blurred finish of Dior Rouge Dior On Stage Matte.

Nikki. I would love to ask her so many questions, because I’m trying to write a screenplay right now. It’s so fun and addicting, but so damn hard. I’ve been writing stories forever, but I never really took them seriously. Sometimes it’s really effective just to put them somewhere. Some of them make me laugh, and some of them make me cry.

I brought one up recently in a meeting with a studio, and they were into it, which was really confidence-building. Before that, I never saw myself as a screenwriter, because I never went to college. But it’s a good hobby to have, especially in a world where so much is going on. It’s nice to sit with yourself and your thoughts in a constructive, creative way.

I’m part of a very, very strong community. I think women are such doers. Women know how to get shit done. They’re inherently born with this superpower brain.

I would tell myself nothing, because I think every single thing that I had to go through really solidified where I am now. I would just give her a hug and a solid high five and say, “You’ve got this,” because she did. Keep doing it. Keep going.

I smoked a cigarette with Dave Chappelle at the Comedy Cellar. I sat in the front row for his set, and I was so happy nobody picked on me. I was so nervous, because it was only a week after Obsession had come out. I was grateful that some people had seen it, but not everybody had. I was just sitting there thinking, “Oh, please, please.”

I want to fight for the audience’s trust in me. I want them to see me as someone who can bring them stories that hopefully make them feel seen or entertained. I want to add my perspective and not shy away from the ugly parts of life. I want to have a career filled with movies that are complex. And if anybody wants to do a clothing line with me, that would be so much fun. Hey, designers out there, let me come in and make some things for the shorties!

Don’t let the fear of not being seen as good stand in the way of being understood. Speak your mind, because you know what you mean. And it matters. Don’t worry about the way that other people see you. Let that go first, and never let it back in. Hit the ground running.

#6686. Men Are Outspending Women on Botox. Here’s What They’re Asking For

Guys are going to increasingly wild lengths to achieve their version of the idealized man. Looksmaxxing, as we’ve come to know it, has included surgical procedures to reshape their eyes, taking a hammer to their face to create a more chiseled jawline, and breaking their legs to gain a couple inches. But an OG in cosmetic procedures is seeing a resurgence in men, too.

Chances are you’re familiar with Botox: localized injections to smoothen wrinkles in common areas like the forehead, the eyes, or around the mouth. Long viewed as a treatment limited to the ladies, it’s increasingly becoming another form of male upkeep. Now we’re learning that men are outspending women on the popular procedure. According to an October 2026 report by Guidepoint Qsight, a medical aesthetics data and intelligence provider, men spent an average of $529 per neurotoxin visit in Q3 of 2026, compared with $455 for women. (The figures include not just Botox but also competitors like Daxxify and Xeomin.)

The potential explanation is simple: Botox is an easy way to look a little younger, more well-rested, and even less angry or severe. (As a built-in bonus, it’s virtually painless—especially compared to the barbaric looksmaxxing trends circulating as of late.) According to a 2025 survey of 2,900 aesthetic plastic surgeons, men accounted for over 15% of all Botox cases that year. It was also their top non-surgical treatment by a landslide.

The growing cohort of men opting into “Brotox” believe it’s money well spent. Nancy Samolitis, MD, a board-certified dermatologist in Los Angeles and co-founder of facile, has been treating men for years but has recently seen an uptick in male clientele, aged anywhere from 35 to 70. These days, “they’re more interested in skincare and more open to procedures,” she says. Many also book their first treatment nudged by their spouse or significant other who are existing patients. Others come in simply wanting to look better but not knowing what treatment to get. In many cases, Botox fits the bill.

While the uninitiated might think the injections make guys look surprised or less masculine, good work can be undetectable. Still you, just fresher.

Kyle Waldrop, a 37-year-old product designer in Los Angeles, first started getting Botox three years ago. “I’ve always been good about keeping up with a skincare routine and taking care of myself, so Botox felt like a natural extension of what I was already doing,” he says. His goal isn’t to change his face but to slow down wrinkles before they become obvious. He gets Botox for his forehead lines and crow’s feet, and recently started treating his neck lines, too.

But it’s not always about looking younger. Men are also using Botox in less obvious places. David Kim, MD, board-certified dermatologist and the founder of Soho Dermatology in New York City, treats the chin for more projection, as well as the underarms to combat excess sweating. Bell Yoo, NP, a board-certified nurse practitioner and the founder of Mimo Aesthetics in West Hollywood, adds that she injects the masseter (and sometimes temporalis) muscles for guys who struggle with jaw clenching or teeth grinding.

Aesthetically, men usually aren’t looking for the same thing from Botox as women. For starters, many want to soften their lines without erasing them. Preserving some natural movement is key. “My female patients often love that smooth, ‘glass skin’ appearance, whereas some of my male patients think it looks too waxy or oily,” Yoo says. Men also tend to opt out of a Botox brow lift, which many women request. “Men would much rather maintain a slightly heavier, lower-set brow than end up with an overly arched or ‘Spock’ brow,” Yoo says. Per Samolitis, this requires different injection points and doses tailored for guys. Kim, meanwhile, is careful not to overdo the crow’s feet. “It looks more natural when men have lines around the eyes, and it makes their face look better overall,” he says. These techniques quell the fears that guys have about looking less masculine or overdone. For most, the ultimate goal is to look relaxed and rejuvenated—not tight and taut. “When it’s done well and with the right amount, you look like yourself, just a bit more rested,” Waldrop says. “I still have all my natural movement and expressions, which is important to me.”

All that subtlety comes at a price. Men may end up paying more than women to treat the same areas, but the higher price tag is actually expected: Men often have larger, stronger facial muscles, which require more units to achieve their desired results, Yoo says.

While more men are embracing Botox, some remain tight-lipped about it. Yoo says that most of her male Botox patients are pretty discreet. “I think there’s still some stigma around men receiving cosmetic treatments, and many would rather keep it to themselves,” she says. Waldrop, however, is an open book. “I don’t really see it as something worth hiding or feeling that weird about,” he says. “Guys are already spending money on skincare, haircuts, hair transplants, working out, and all sorts of things to look and feel better, so I don’t really see why Botox should be treated any differently.”

For Waldrop, Botox is less a dramatic intervention than another item on his grooming checklist. He doesn’t see it as something that needs to be announced or apologized for. At the end of the day, “it’s really not that deep,” he says.

#6685. Julianne Moore Never Stops Upping the Stakes

The actress tackles her boldest part yet in The Debut.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Julianne Moore wants me to imagine I’m running late. “You feel like your heart’s going to come out of your chest. Everything’s going wrong. And if you step back, you go, ‘The world’s not going to end if I get there 15 minutes late,’” she says. “Your body doesn’t know that, and your head doesn’t know that. You somehow are like, ‘This seems to be the most urgent thing in the world.’”

There might be no better summation of the way the actress brings unprecedented intensity to even the most quotidian moments onscreen. “I’m really interested in those emotional stakes,” says Moore, who arrives at our interview fresh off the subway with a cheery “Hi, I’m Julie.” Her bright red hair is hidden under a baseball cap, and she sports the downtown New York uniform of a simple black top and track pants.

It’s hard to square this soft-spoken, thoughtful woman, who seems to edit herself in conversation the way a filmmaker edits in camera, with the emotionally labile roles she’s known for playing. Watching her act is like seeing the shell of a building under construction, the interior beams exposed to the elements.

In her new film The Debut, it feels, at times, like she’s playing a Julianne Moore character dropped into the story. (There’s a reason it feels like that: Writer-director Jesse Eisenberg penned the part specifically for her.) When Moore first read the script, she was sitting at her dining room table, her preferred reading spot, and, she tells me, she had to stand up. “I started taking deep breaths, because I was like, ‘Oh my God, I cannot believe how good this is.’”

Her character, Mona, is a meek New Jersey wife and mother who is cast in a community theater musical, her first-ever stage role. As she comes into her own, squaring off with its dictatorial director, played by Paul Giamatti, the stakes become skyscraper-high. The absurdist comedy comes from the way Mona takes the “No small actors” dictum to heart, disappearing into her minor part as an apartment superintendent in ways that confound our understanding of what a performance can be. It feels like a meta-commentary not just on acting, but on Moore’s entire career, from her pharmacy meltdown in Magnolia to her unsettling, childlike turn in May December. Even when they go to extremes, her characters feel rooted in very real and human impulses.

To hear Moore tell it, her career has been less about pursuing a singular passion than following her own interests as they arise. And indeed, one of the first things you notice about Moore is how interested she is. She wants to know everything about me (not a common experience for an interviewer). She tunes in to the frequency of the guy in the booth behind us, loudly wheeling and dealing on the phone. She’s fascinated by human relationships, she says. “All of that stuff seems, to me, really urgent and interesting.”

Beauty Tip: For brighter and smoother undereyes, try Neuraé Harmonie The Eye Contour, which contains hyaluronic acid, caffeine, and watercress extract.

She also has a penchant for playing women, whether from the past or the present day, who find themselves trapped by circumstances. “I’m moved by people and the choices that they make, how they live and who they love and how we’re affected by the society that we live in,” she says. “Particularly for women: What world are you living in? What choices are offered to you? As someone who was born in the 20th century and saw what was offered to the women around me, what changed and what didn’t—I saw what opportunities were afforded to my great-grandmothers, my grandmother, my mother, and then me. My mother was someone whose parents didn’t send her to college, because they didn’t send girls to college. They sent her brother to college. So she went later, after she had kids.”

Moore is following up The Debut with an array of varied roles, including portraying The Joy of Sex author Alex Comfort’s girlfriend in an adaptation of the book, and playing a small part in her friend Tom Ford’s Cry to Heaven. She’s also gearing up to return to the stage for the first time in 20 years, starring in Sarah Ruhl’s Faydra at the Manhattan Theatre Club in February. Why theater; why now? “I think [it goes] back to what I was saying about following your interests,” she says. “That’s all you can do.”

It was three films that all came out at once. Robert Altman had seen me in Vanya on 42nd Street. He cast me in Short Cuts. Then Vanya, which we’d been doing for five years as a theater production, became a movie. And Todd Haynes put me in Safe. They all came out around the same time in the early ’90s, and suddenly I had a profile.

The ’90s were amazing. They were as great as everybody says. We didn’t know it. That was when my whole career changed, with independent film. Suddenly there were all these new voices, because it was the advent of video stores. You could make a movie on a really low budget, and all you had to do was make your budget back in VHS. You could make a movie for a million dollars, and if you made that money back and a little bit more, you’d be like, “Great, we can make the next one.” I think Vanya was $900,000. Safe was a million dollars. Suddenly we had opportunities. You had all of these new voices making these movies, and they could cast who they wanted to, and they [covered] subjects that maybe studios wouldn’t have. Nobody was going to make Safe.

That was very much Todd’s voice. Everything was very scrappy. You didn’t make any money as an actor. You shot it very quickly. The funny thing was, back then we would shoot it in 35 days. Now you have 23. So we felt 35 was short, but then later we got to 23. But it was fun, because you were like, “Okay, we can put this together. We can get a budget. We can shoot it.”

The unsteadiness was easy for me, because I’m not a natural singer. I haven’t been trained. So that was easy and kind of fun in a way—because it’s not like she can’t carry a tune; she sang in church—but she doesn’t have any power, and she has no emotion behind it. I worked with a wonderful vocal coach and with all of our [supporting cast]; they’re all from musical theater. But the day that I had to sing that song [Mona’s big solo moment] live in the room was very early on in our shoot. A lot of people were there—they were in the other room around the monitor, and all of those people I’m singing to are real [Broadway] singers. There was a lot of support for me, and I think a lot of concern. I was scared.

[Mona’s pivotal scene] is, like, eight pages. It’s a lot. And he said, “Listen, I don’t want you to worry about memorizing it. On the day, we’ll have a teleprompter. You don’t have to worry about it. Because I know if it were me, all I would be thinking about is remembering those lines,” and I was like, “Phew, what a relief.” But of course, because he said that, by the time we shot it, I had memorized it. He took the burden away from me emotionally and allowed me to be able to learn it.

You cannot think about it. That’s a narrative unto itself. And I think that obviously the people who are releasing these movies like to have these movies in conversation, because it means more attention comes to the movies themselves, and more people buy tickets and go. So the ultimate goal is for people to see these movies. That’s really what it comes down to. And so of course we feel gratified when people are talking about it that way, because you go, “Oh my God, people really like it and people might really see it.”

When they say “aging gracefully,” I’m like, “What is that supposed to be? We don’t have a choice. We age one way or another. It is a fact. And it’s an uncomfortable fact, because it leads to death.” So that’s where everything gets conflated, because people talk so much about looks, and really at the bottom of all of that stuff is that we all enjoy being alive and we want to function as well as possible and we don’t want to die. So it’s like, “We can talk about that, about what it means to live,” but then cosmetic stuff, you’re just like, “Ah, that’s a whole other deal.”

There’s not a right way or a wrong way to age. So given that we have a limited time on earth, let’s not put that pressure on ourselves that we’re doing it wrong. I read that Helen Mirren said something like, “There’s this idea that somehow the things that happen to you when you’re older will feel less interesting to you because you’re old.” And she was like, “They don’t. They feel just as interesting.” And I think as a young person, you don’t always know that, because we’re always so focused on ourselves, we just assume that when we’re older, nothing will matter. But it does.

Well, put it this way, they’re always with me. I think the worst thing and the best thing about being an actor is that as distant as these people seem from you, you’re able to conjure them from yourself. So oddly, even the most reprehensible are in you. You’ve been able to manufacture even sometimes the worst of them, but yes, they’re always having lunch with you, in a sense.

#6684. Julie Curtiss Captures Snapshots of New York City in Her Paintings

Her latest exhibit, “UNREAL,” is on view at Gagosian

New York City hides its wonders in the folds of everyday life. A crowded deli collage, the quirky decorated interiors of tiny apartments, aquariums lining the windows of Chinese restaurants, and the bustle of crowds all offer small joys for anyone looking closely enough—and artist Julie Curtiss is taking it all in. “I love walking around looking at those big food photo montages that are so gross and grotesque,” Curtiss says. “For painters, it’s such rich material.”

On one of these outings in 2025, Curtiss was walking around the Upper East Side when she caught sight of a peculiar pair: two women wearing fur coats and sporting postoperative compression face masks. The resulting painting, Makeover (2026), features the two mysterious figures standing with their backs to the viewer, one of whom is smoking a cigarette, rendered in Curtiss’s distinctive lurid graphic style. This encounter, which sparked her solo show “UNREAL,” on view at Gagosian through December 19, is a bittersweet meditation on the weight of growing older and the creeping suspicion that life is becoming increasingly uncanny as the city—and the world—changes around her.

“[New York] is always about the facade and constantly rebuilding or changing yourself and about things in a state of disrepair and how you feel on the inside and on the outside,” she explains a couple of weeks before the show in her East Williamsburg studio. Curtiss explains that Makeover marked the start of this New York–focused exhibition, though she needed to shelve the project while completing projects for her show at White Cube in Seoul, focusing on motherhood, and, for Gagosian in Paris, a meditation on domesticity. This new project borrows ideas from both of those shows, distilling them into an examination of her life in New York and how it forged her art and her life over the past 16 years.

Curtiss, now 43, first moved to New York in 2010, after growing up in Paris in a French-Vietnamese household. She worked at Jeff Koons’s studio before moving to work as a studio assistant for KAWS. All the while, she toiled away on her paintings: hyper-stylized, colorful portraits marked by a sharp illustrative sensibility. “You have so much doubt; it’s so full of despair sometimes,” she says of her first years in the city. It wasn’t until 2017 that Hein Koh curated a booth for Curtiss at the Spring/Break Art Show. The show received glowing praise, catapulting her to art-world-darling status and leading to solo shows at Anton Kern, White Cube, and, more recently, Gagosian.

“It sounds cliché, but you just have to persevere and be a little strategic,” she says. “New York is fascinating because it is a place of constant change, and nothing ever feels really secure. Things are always going to move, and you’ve got to adapt to it.”

Life recently changed drastically for Curtiss. She welcomed her first child with her husband, abstract painter Clinton King, in 2024. This newfound motherhood pops up in her painting Kitchen Appendages (2026), a brightly colored illustration of a chaotic household kitchen. The woman is barely present, bent over and nearly out of frame, as a pressure cooker spouts steam and smoke leaves the open oven. This mid-century aesthetic is inspired by Chantal Akerman’s film Jeanne Dielman, 23 Commerce Quay, 1080 Brussels (1972). “[The painting is] a portrait of a woman, but through her kitchen accessories,” she says. “It’s me poking fun at a part of me, the housewife part of myself.”

This playful spirit resurfaces across the exhibition. Intimate reflections are often rendered through magical realism, as in Squid and Whale (2026). This bedroom scene features the two titular animals contorted together in some act of intimacy or violence on a far-too-small bed. “Without really thinking about it, I was making a comment on intimacy and relationship,” Curtiss says, emphasizing how she works by transmuting images she encounters into strange places. This image in particular came from an entirely different place: a diorama at the American Museum of Natural History in New York.

During our studio visit, she is reflective, often mentioning the passing of time and the strangeness of everyday life. “As you get older, things start to feel less real,” she explains to me. “They don’t really go the way you expected them to go. They go off in a weird, surreal place. On a personal level, you look at yourself in the mirror and the way you’ve aged, and you’re like, ‘Is this still me?’ You have this identity crisis because you still see yourself as a young person.” I ask, then, are the faceless black-haired women populating several of her new works—doing gymnastics in Arachne (2026) or nearly carried away by the wind in Before the Storm (2026)—meant to be her?

“They’re always an extension of the self, in a way,” she says. “They are fictional archetypes and characters that embody an experience or side of myself I’m interested in.… I like not giving a face because it keeps people a little frustrated, I’m sure. But at the same time, I find it a more interesting dynamic. It puts the viewer in a voyeuristic position.”

A final glance at the paintings in her studio reveals their purpose: Curtiss wants us in her shoes, to see the world as she does, if even for a moment. In each painting, she crafts a story, leaving us with an occasionally frustrating mid-action snapshot. Each builds a distinct sense of cinematic suspense, as if you might blink and the painting will change.

“I’m as inspired by movies as I am by paintings, [but] I like the ideas that come with the still image,” she proclaims. “You can actually tell a whole story that’s quite complex. There’s a lot going on. People will keep wondering about what happened before the frame and what’s going to happen after the frame.”
