#6683. With the ‘New’ Yeezy, Ye Says He Wants to ‘Let the Clothes Do the Talking.’ But Who’s Listening?

“I don’t have a lot of words tonight,” Ye told me, not long after concluding his Yeezy Season 01 runway show in Los Angeles on Wednesday evening. “I’ll let the clothes do the talking.”

You might read that quote and be surprised to hear that Ye said it warmly, with an all-32-bared smile. But for those still paying attention, his relatively upbeat demeanor tracks with the tame-not-turnt persona that Ye has performed through most of 2026; the one that’s been slowly-but-surely trying to reamass the cultural capital he’s spent most of the last decade either annihilating or reclaiming. Legions of fans have proven they’re still all in; the culture at large remains justifiably dubious. The question this week is, how will Ye’s return to fashion affect the calculus?

Upon arrival, a typical Hollywood warehouse exterior turned into a Frank Herbert-esque interior as soon as you crossed the threshold. Inside, a hundred or so guests sat on two rows of unbroken benches that encircled a large white mound in the center, lit by a heavenly white glow from above. Inside was a mix of the usual cool kids: models (including the runway-favorite teen rapper Nettspend) and recurring characters in the overarching, enduring Kanye Universe. There was Fear of God founder Jerry Lorenzo, who made conversation with Don C, while 2 Chainz was patiently posted up in a hooded black leather coat like ’98 Wesley Snipes. Big Sean, rebuffing the sweltering indoor temperatures in a shearling jacket over a crewneck sweater, caught up with Hit-Boy.

Models on the Yeezy Season 01 runway, which featured a characteristically minimalist set piece.

The 19-year-old rapper Nettspend walked in the show.

Once everyone was seated, the lights dimmed as the unmistakable opening piano note of “Runaway” set the show into motion, with one lone model striding out in a killer black trench. From there, two more models, men this time, walked out in the opposite direction; what followed was a bit of organized chaos with the number of models and paths alternating at random intervals to the tune of a playlist that zipped between new Ye music (UK garage vibes, it would seem) and a gothic orchestra not unlike the scores Danny Elfman used to chef up for Tim Burton.

The fits were crisp, practical and tactical. Most of the menswear was ready-made for basic maneuvers, while the women’s looks were sleek and casual, with a few Milla Jovovich-in-Fifth-Element skimpy ensembles thrown in because Ye can only restrain himself but so much. The most notable thing, about the guys especially, were the relatively streamlined silhouettes: close-cropped coats, bombers and vests, fitted pants and sweats. Where past Ye lines championed and emblazoned the path for the baggy wave, with oversized boots and pants you could swim in, Ye seemed to be brazenly planting a flag back on the opposite end of the spectrum.

Nearly 12 years, and a dozen lifetimes, since his debut Yeezy Season 1 runway show in 2015, the notion of a “Season 01”—his first formal showing since his damning 2022 show in Paris, the one with the “White Lives Matter” shirts—is a conspicuous attempt to clear the slate. All of his previous shows had been produced in collaboration with Adidas, who severed ties with Ye four years ago, after he tweeted a tirade of antisemetic remarks. This time around, to let the clothes tell it, Ye is locked in. I don’t have an image of every single Yeezy Season line seared into my brain, but I feel comfortable saying Ye’s latest was the first time I looked at one of his collections and objectively thought, I could wear that. Most of the gear is quite solid—and familiar Ye's running the same playbook with Season 01 that he’s run with his music, and to some degree, his persona. It’s the Yeezy gear you know and love(d), refined to make it that much more palatable, similar to the way a song like “Whatever Works” puts him back over chipmunk’d soul samples. And true to the title, it does indeed; the fact that it does is maybe a testament to the brilliance that got lost in the insanity. But is playing the hits (quite literally, with “Runaway” opening the show) what we want from one of the most paradigm-shifting—and absolutely chaotic—creative minds of our time?

Historically, Ye’s designs are so focused on an idea of utilitarianism that they ultimately come off as a bit drab, if not downright dystopian. Essentials like hoodies and beefy leather jackets are still central to his vision, but as the models strode around in his usual earth-toned palette—save for a handful of black looks to start, and a bright pop of reds at the end—it became clear that Ye was putting on the same show in a different kind of stadium. The same sci-fi silhouettes, tweaked to their cleanest shape and most pleasing hue, sans screenprinted hate speech. Ideologically, the runway show wasn’t far off from the experience of hearing his 2007 hit “Good Life” all these years later, ringing off stadium speakers, carrying 80,000 people along on a wave of wistfulness— even if Ye himself only performed approximately 75% of the lyrics against a backing track.

In keeping with all of his other moves this year, Yeezy Season 01 is Ye presenting a safer, rule-abiding version of himself: Ye with just art, no antics. Much in the way that his latest album, Bully, eschewed any lyrics that say, shouted out R. Kelly or Bill Cosby (which is more than can be said about 2024’s Vultures 1), it felt like a deep sigh of relief to see him present clothes that don’t feature appalling slogans, at a fashion show with Candace Owens nowhere in sight. But the compromise for a sanitized Kanye is also one that can’t help but feel anodyne as well. The New Ye doesn’t needle, but he’s lost Old Ye’s knack for trying something new. Of course, we’re also well over a decade into the Yeezy experiment—at this point, the present has caught up to the futuristic vision Ye first dreamt up back in 2015. There’s a whole new generation of aspiring designers creating in his image, kids who fancy themselves trailblazers whose paths just loop back to Ye: streamer Kai Cenat just launched his own clothing brand, Vivet, while N3on attended Wednesday night’s show, skipping the Yeezy space gleefully documenting every interaction. It feels as though all of this has happened before, and all of it will happen again.

Mystery. Intrigue. Chaos. This is the typical life cycle for a Ye project, be it music, fashion, or otherwise. An announcement materializes, hype ensues. Then, inevitably, the seams start to show and it becomes apparent that he isn’t inviting you on a pre-planned journey so much as building the plane in real time, seconds before takeoff. And then, through sheer force of will, or maybe even genius, the result ends up so captivating that the speedbumps hardly matter. He’s still a master showman, and all it takes is a strong yearning for the Old Ye to find yourself surrendering to it. The efficacy of that last factor, though, has undeniably waned over the years. For much of the 2020s, in the midst of many a manic outburst or worse, Ye’s messes have hardly cohered into something objectively beautiful. The intrigue curdled into perverse bemusement; for every unwavering diehard fan, there was a rubbernecker tapped in to watch the circus.

The 2026 version of Ye has been an exercise in proving how many people will show up when he shuts up, and whether he can make it back from the brink if he delivers the right spectacle.

The result is the most well-oiled the Yeezy Machine has ever been. An album that more or less dropped when he said it would, for once. A smattering of live shows across the world, each in a sold-out stadium boasting record-breaking rap concert attendance where he leans on his most enduring strengths: visual spectacle and a bulletproof catalog. The only area left to renegotiate is fashion…which brings us back to Wednesday night in LA.

These are the scenes you’d expect at a Ye event, but the first sign that the overall vibe was different and more relaxed was that the man himself was at the door, tucked off into a hallway, immaculately dressed in a fitted all-black leather fit offset by a ridiculously large and ornate gold waist fixture—every bit the Dune-caliber fit as the space we were standing in required. Ahead of the show, he posed backstage flanked by his wife, Bianca Censori, and the four kids he shares with his ex, Kim Kardashian (including 13-year-old North, who was sporting her unmistakable blue-raspberry locks). At Yeezy events past, you’d expect to see harried staff scrambling, while Ye was somewhere out of sight but exuding stress and anxiety out into the atmosphere. But on Wednesday, the 49-year-old beamed as friends made their way past him to their seats. Even a three-piece-suited Kid Cudi came over to say hello.

Ye backstage with his children, from left: North, Psalm, Chicago, and Saint West.

Fifteen years ago, Yeezy Season 01 would’ve caused a massive sea change in the menswear world almost instantaneously, with the wave starting in SoHo then slowly emanating out into the beyond. In 2026, does Kanye still move that needle? The Year in Ye has been one big display of his ability to Don Draper the culture at large, and shock us all by “how much it never happened.” There’s no controversy big enough to keep him away for too long and very few fences he can’t mend.

For example, Sean and Cudi ceased their umpteenth falling out with their old label boss two months ago at a guest-packed, blockbuster homecoming show in Chicago on Ye’s tour stop; their show of support tonight only underlined how deeply the hatchet has been buried yet again. When I spoke to Big Sean after the show, he could only marvel at how much Ye has “given” to the culture across all different categories. One-time GOOD Music COO Steven Victor said the show made him feel like Ye “has his shit together,” noting that Ye admitted to him that he was still working out the model patterns hours before showtime. In past Yeezy Seasons, the cram-effect would’ve been apparent, but here, Victor said he wouldn’t have noticed because it all seemed to go off so effortlessly.

As for the man himself? I spoke to him, but again, he didn’t have much to say, at least on the record. He seemed excited that I picked up on the intentional disharmony of the model routes, and explained that the space we were standing in was a “language I’ve been working on for 10 years” called “DROAM,” which refers to the minimalist design he hopes to apply to stores, urban planning, and a home for himself.

“I got a quote for you,” Victor interjected. “The king returns!” Ye laughed. The question remains, though: Is he welcome?

#6682. No-Knead Pumpkin Focaccia

For those who fall into the pumpkin-should-be-savory camp, let us offer up a new recipe primed to become a seasonal staple: Pumpkin Focaccia. The iconic bread we know and love is ripe for the pumpkin treatment, lending it a golden hue and earthy sweetness. This version doesn’t require any kneading, making it straightforward enough to pull off in a single afternoon. You’ll perform a series of folds as it rises, simply pulling and stretching the dough to help it develop gluten. A showering of fresh rosemary and flaky salt on top is optional, but it takes crisp, plush focaccia from good to great. Serve it with a bowl of olive oil for dipping or a schmear of cream cheese to lean into the seasonal profile.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Mix one ¼-oz. envelope active dry yeast (about 2¼ tsp.), 5 cups (625 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. light brown sugar, and 1½ cups warm water in a large bowl until a dry, shaggy dough forms. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm spot 15 minutes.

Place a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough and moisten hands in water, shaking off excess. Stretch 1 side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat process 3 more times, turning bowl after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Remoisten your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat entire process 2 more times (folding and resting), about 1 hour more. By the last full fold, the dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Pour ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil into a 13x9" metal baking pan. Lightly oil your hands and punch down dough, then transfer to prepared pan. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Turn dough salted side down to coat both sides in oil. Press into an even layer with your fingers. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 450°. Unwrap focaccia and scatter rosemary leaves and more sea salt over if desired; drizzle with oil. Oil your hands and press fingers into focaccia several times to create dimples across surface, making sure to press fingers all the way down to the bottom of the pan. Bake focaccia, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until deep golden brown, 23–28 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let focaccia cool slightly in pan. Using a metal spatula, turn out focaccia onto rack and let cool completely.

Do Ahead: Focaccia can be made 1 day ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.

#6681. Jennifer Lawrence Continues to Embrace Electric Green This Season

It’s certainly not your standard autumn hue

Kermit the Frog once famously declared that “it’s not easy bein’ green,” but Jennifer Lawrence seems to disagree.

Over these past few weeks, the Oscar winner has eschewed moody fall tones for fluorescent, chemical-level greens, putting her stamp of approval on the surprise lime hue for the season. Just the other day, she layered a chartreuse Colleen Allen coat over a matching chartreuse cardigan from Miu Miu, while popping on a neon hair scrunchie to match. Prior to that, she stepped out in a bright-green puffer jacket from Dries Van Noten, with an orange floral jacquard that added even more citrusy power. And as for her new favorite bag? Oh, it’s just a slime-green Hermès Bolide, which would’ve looked right at home in the peak of “brat summer.”

For a dinner at Fouquet’s in New York City over the weekend, Lawrence brought out her statement bag once again, an accessory so bright that it basically doubled as reflective safety gear.

The Bolide bag (which Lawrence also owns in a burgundy croc) sharply contrasted her jet-black, double-breasted Aris coat from the Row, which she layered over a pair of straight-leg blue jeans and a lemony top that peeked out from the front of her jacket.

She complemented her outerwear with a pair of pointy black flats, and popped on a pair of dangly drop earrings for jewelry. Her hair, meanwhile, hung down in tight waves along her shoulders—perhaps a purposeful styling choice as she promotes her new haircare line, Mes.

Whether she’s mixing and matching prints or sporting flip-flops in the fall, Lawrence has simply never prescribed to standard fashion rules. Now, I just need her to really go full-send and put together a lime-green ensemble this Thanksgiving.

#6679. In Her First-Ever Stand-Up Special, Janelle James Sees Through the Dark

In Janelle James: How Romantic, the Emmy-nominated actor and comedian gets right into it.

The hour opens with James’s take on American politics, from the physical attractiveness (or the lack thereof, as the case may be) of the GOP’s key operators to more pointed, cross-party digs at, say, Hunter Biden and Senator Mitch McConnell. (“He died four times. He died so much, it just became a thing.”) There isn’t much about Washington that she doesn’t find “weird.” (The special may have gone a little differently had she taped it after this month’s midterm elections.)

“The show is written in four chunks,” James explains over a Zoom call from Los Angeles on November 2. “My political segment, my fame segment, my dating segment, and a segment on violence—and I can switch them around at will. A day before taping, I thought, I’m going to open on politics and get that out of the way. On the road, actually, I was ending with it.”

James says she developed How Romantic over about 70 sets, with a break last year to film Season 6 of the hit television series Abbott Elementary, in which James plays the endlessly chaotic school principal Ava Coleman. “I built the hour somewhat in that first stretch,” she says. “It marinated in my brain when we went back to shooting. Then when we were on hiatus again, I went on a little mini tour, multiple weekends, Thursday to Sunday, often with double shows.”

James stresses that How Romantic is no “Abbott revue.” “This special is an introduction for a lot of people to me as a stand-up,” she says. A stand-up and, well, a real, raw person behind the outsized television personality. “I start the show out sitting down on purpose, so people get a sense of what the vibe is going to be. I’m not really loud. I’m not really doing act-outs. I don’t really have props. This is me performing as myself, and this is how it’s going to go,” she says. “Those who’ve been following me as a comedian since I started are like, ‘People have no idea how dark you are.’”

Asked whether Janelle and Ava have blended together as Abbott has gone on, James says: “There’s definitely more overlap now. I think that’s true for all of us [in the cast]. Some of the people in the writers’ room I’ve known for years. They know me as a comedian, to the point where I’m like, ‘I’m going to stop talking to y’all,’ because I’ll say something and it ends up in the show. A lot of my colloquialisms—Ava says ‘hot’ all the time. That’s something I say! And that messes with my brain sometimes.”

James’s own brand of humor leans sarcastic and cynical—even a little melancholy (“Everything is funny and nothing is funny,” she says early in the hour). It’s also more explicit than anything an ABC mockumentary sitcom would allow. Just take the sex act James simulates with a microphone. “That part didn’t come until one of my final shows [before the taping]. I just did it one night, offhand, with the club mic,” James says, grimacing. “We went the next day and got me my own, because I thought, I’m going to keep doing that.”

The divide between the version of herself that exists in the popular imagination and the one who shows up onstage in How Romantic feels to James related to the ongoing debate in Hollywood about how comedic performances are received and judged in comparison with dramatic ones.

“What people don’t think about, and the reason comedy is just as important as drama—and harder in certain instances—is that we are performing joy when our real lives can be falling apart,” James says. “I won a comedy contest the night my dad died. I’ve done many stand-up shows straight out of a break-up. That’s very hard to do. Because we make it look easy, people don’t rate it the same as crying on command. I can cry right now! I’m a world of sadness. But it’s about performing joy.”

#6678. 21 Coats and Jackets I Think Are Cool Just Because

No contest, fall is the best season. For a few glorious months, it’s an open bar for dressing and getting your biggest fits off. Tell me what other season lets you go from flannel with cords to a hoodie with shorts to a puffer and jeans all in the same week. You can mix a wild cocktail of textures and colors, play recklessly with silhouettes and experiment to your heart’s content—and your wallet’s demise. But no doubt the best part of dressing for the best season is the outerwear.

And right now, the shelves are stocked with sick pieces, which means my tabs are so more packed than a Tokyo train during rush hour. From dramatic overcoats to slick truckers, artisanal macs and swishy windbreakers, the menswear gods are really smiling upon us right now. But why gab about how great this season’s roster of jackets and coats are when I can just show you? Here are the 21 coolest pieces of outerwear out right now.

Little Red Riding Hood was a menswear icon.

I didn't know you could wax corduroy. Now I do. And now I want it.

After decades of wearing clothes, I'm pretty convinced that reversible jackets are bad. Leave it to Niceness to be the very sick outlier.

This isn't totally my style but I'll figure out a way to make it work because it's just too cool to pass up.

Our Legacy just seems to be getting better and better.

I'm obsessed with Nosapluna, the mysterious and methodical design collective producing antique-inspired designs using artisanal and age-old techniques. Like, who needs Gore-tex when you have this?

Imagine this with a hoodie underneath and crazy faded baggy jeans. Pretty good.

Hoodies aren't normally categorized as outerwear. But then again, hoodies aren't normally as heavy as this, nor are they hand-knit by indigenous craftspeople. So, yeah.

Experiences are great. But if I have to choose between paying to fly to Montana or paying to LARP Montana, I'm going with this RRL jacket every time.

I did a review of Gap's heavy denim Type II jacket a while back and got accused of sponsored content. I meant that shit. And I mean this too: this is a pretty decent jacket that looks good and is reasonably priced.

It appears that the Dries team is doing just fine without Dries.

Boston-based indie label Mark the Tailor has the streets talking thanks to its balance of craftsmanship and a modern lens on tailoring. This playful flip on the humble quarter zip is just one of the things that has menswear fans buzzing.

#6677. Legal Shrooms Are Coming

Could psilocybin offer a breakthrough for treatment-resistant depression?

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

As part of the Future of Beauty Awards, the ELLE beauty team looked ahead at what will be next in beauty and wellness.

Shrooms are passed around at parties as a hangover-free alternative to alcohol. Zoë Kravitz, playing a fictionalized version of herself, accidentally overdosed on them in an episode of Apple TV+’s The Studio. But soon, they may be officially recognized as more than a way to let loose and could be used as a powerful weapon to combat serious depression, with the potential of being legalized in the U.S. by early 2027. Psilocybin is currently legal in some parts of Oregon and Colorado for treating mental health conditions in certain settings; at the federal level, it’s classified as a Schedule I controlled substance, considered to have no medical use and a high potential for abuse. But with biotechnology company Compass Pathways having achieved two consecutively positive Phase 3 trials for its COMP360 psilocybin therapy in treatment-resistant depression, that may change soon. Shrooms could make history as the first classic psychedelic drug (working on a particular serotonin receptor in the brain) approved by the FDA.

In an unaffiliated 2026 study in the journal Nature Medicine, scientists found that people with treatment-resistant depression who were given COMP360’s formulation of psilocybin had lower depression scores than those treated with a placebo. A Johns Hopkins Medicine study published in the Journal of Psychopharmacology in 2022 showed that the antidepressant effects of psilocybin therapy, alongside supportive psychotherapy, may last for a full year. It’s already legal for therapeutic treatment of some mental health conditions in countries like Australia, New Zealand, and Switzerland. Jay Godfrey, co-founder and CEO of Nushama, which is billed as the world’s largest psychedelic wellness center in New York City, uses a familiar psychological construct to speculate about how it might work. “There is a theory that psilocybin causes a quieting of an area of our brain called the default mode network, where your ego is housed,” he says. “Your own righteousness, search for validation, opinions, judgments—all those things are housed in ego. Psilocybin creates what we call ego dissolution: You get to observe yourself in the absence of your judgment, opinions, and all the walls that are around you that keep you safe. It allows you to see your traumas and your life story through a much more loving and compassionate [lens].”

Traditional depression medication, like selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), is typically taken every day to balance serotonin levels in the brain. Psilocybin would likely be different. “You’re taking one to four doses per year,” says Myriam Barthes, the co-founder and CEO of Journey Clinical, the largest psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy platform in the United States. “The experience itself will last about five to seven hours.” Godfrey says that a standard dose of magic mushrooms could likely be 25 milligrams, and both Godfrey and Barthes stress that, unlike legalized marijuana, psilocybin may be regulated as a pharmaceutical drug, with each experience taking place in a clinic under the watchful eye of a medical professional trained in psilocybin therapy. It would be very unlikely that you could have the option to get a prescription for shrooms and take them at home, according to Lief Fenno, MD, PhD, chair of the American Psychiatric Association Council on Addiction Psychiatry. “Patient safety is paramount, so these are highly controlled situations with trained professionals,” Fenno says. “That’s very different than you simply taking a bunch of mushrooms or dropping acid.”

According to the Journal of Clinical Psychiatry, around 2.8 million people have treatment-resistant depression, medically defined by the FDA as having tried two different antidepressants and seen limited improvement (though there’s no prevailing consensus on this definition). Christopher Pittenger, MD, PhD, the Elizabeth Mears and House Jameson professor of psychiatry at Yale School of Medicine, says that there are a few compelling theories for how psilocybin could help them. “One is that it increases brain plasticity,” he says. A healthy brain is more clay than glass, able to be shaped by experience. When someone is severely depressed, their brain is often less able to make new connections and change; psilocybin might be able to make it more pliable. A second theory is that shrooms can alter brain circuits, which control how your mind processes information. One of those circuits is the default mode network that Godfrey mentioned—and Pittenger says that when this network is impacted, you may be able to view yourself differently, which can positively impact your mental health.

Because psilocybin would likely only be available in a clinic under the supervision of medically trained professionals if it gets approved, Pittenger says, there’s little risk of it being abused. “People can use and overuse it, but I don’t think that the medical approval is going to increase the ability to use it recreationally,” he says. The main worry, he adds, is that psilocybin could cause psychosis in people who are already at risk for it, like those with a medical or family history of schizophrenia or bipolar disorder. Headaches, nausea, anxiety, dizziness, and elevated blood pressure have been associated with its administration in clinical trials. The drug may also slightly increase blood pressure, so people with high blood pressure should likely avoid it. A full medical and psychiatric evaluation that covers medical history and past psychedelic use should be done prior to this treatment.

One persistent problem with the trials for psilocybin therapy is that it’s uniquely hard to blind them, which means that patients usually know if they’re being given a psychedelic drug. “Patients in the trials know whether or not they’re getting a compound that creates an altered state of consciousness, or if they’re getting a neutral placebo,” Fenno says. “There are trials ongoing that are trying to understand how much of the very real therapeutic effect we see is due specifically to the psilocybin.”

A recent RAND survey found that public support for legalized psilocybin (currently 23 percent) nearly matches the support for cannabis in the mid-’90s, and Colorado and Oregon have already decriminalized it. But their experience raises caution. “We showed that with decriminalization, the number of adults using psilocybin about doubled in each state,” says Joshua C. Black, PhD, a statistical scientist who recently conducted an analysis of the two states for the American Medical Association. “The size and timing of that increase suggested that many people are using outside of the legal frameworks in both states, at least in the initial years.” The study notes that people in decriminalized states may have felt more comfortable self-reporting psilocybin use, since there are fewer legal repercussions. While this increase might sound alarming, Black says that prescription access will be much more tightly controlled than access under broad decriminalization. “FDA-approved drugs will have substantial controls over manufacturing and distribution, and I don’t think that would generate the same pattern.”

Whether or not psilocybin gets FDA approval, the fact that we’re talking about a different kind of depression treatment makes some experts optimistic. “One of the most exciting parts about all of this research is that it’s got the entire country talking about mental illness, and new treatments for it,” Fenno says. So while shroom chocolates surreptitiously handed out at a dinner party will likely remain illegal and you probably won’t be able to buy them at a dispensary, people with treatment-resistant depression may soon have a new option available under medical supervision.

Editor’s note: If you or someone you know is experiencing a mental health crisis or depression, dial 988 or (800) 662-HELP for emergency help or consult the resources available on the American Psychiatric Association’s website (psychiatry.org).

A version of this story appears in the November 2026 issue of ELLE.

#6676. Pumpkin Cheesecake Muffins

Loaded with pumpkin seeds, canned pumpkin purée, and pumpkin pie spice, these big streusel-topped muffins are every fall lover’s dream come true. And to make things even better, the inside of each muffin is stuffed with a soft, lightly sweetened cream cheese mixture. Make the cheesecake filling and the streusel ahead of time to pace things out if it’s helpful. Don’t, even for a minute, consider using anything other than Libby’s 100% pure pumpkin purée (not pie mix). Nothing is better. We promise.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Whisk ⅓ cup coarsely chopped raw pumpkin seeds, ¼ cup (31 g) all-purpose flour, 2 Tbsp. light brown sugar, ½ tsp. pumpkin pie spice, and a pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl to combine. Using your fingers, rub in 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, until moist pea-size lumps form. Chill until ready to use.

Do Ahead: Streusel can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and keep chilled.

Vigorously whisk 6 oz. cream cheese, room temperature, ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar, 2 tsp. all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. vanilla extract, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl until combined and smooth.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and chill.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Line cups of a standard 12-cup muffin pan with paper liners. Whisk 2 large eggs, 1½ cups (packed; 300 g) light brown sugar, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, ¼ cup whole milk, 1 Tbsp. pumpkin pie spice, 1 Tbsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth, about 1 minute. Whisk 1¾ cups (219 g) all-purpose flour and 1½ tsp. baking powder in a small bowl to combine. Add to pumpkin mixture and fold in with a rubber spatula until just incorporated and no large dry streaks of flour remain (don’t overmix; batter will be lumpy).

Bake muffins until streusel is crisp and muffins spring back when gently pressed, 24–27 minutes. Let muffins cool in pan 5 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack and let cool until just warm or completely.

Do Ahead: Muffins can be made 2 days ahead. Store airtight at room temperature.

#6675. Max Mara Is the Quiet Luxury Blueprint

For 75 years, the brand has put forth the idea that a foundational wardrobe—what we wear to move through the world—is far from boring. In fact, it can offer endless possibilities.

I stepped onto a crowded A train the other day, heading from Brooklyn to Manhattan, and was confronted with a microcosm of people with their different styles: contractors and construction workers (Carhartt and utility jackets), well-heeled, corporate pragmatists (slim suits, printed sheaths), fashion students (wearing their own creations), and art-world peacocks (prints on prints, layers atop layers).

There’s no better way to get a sense of what people really wear than on a morning commute. If you drop in at 8:00 a.m. on the Paris metro, the tube in London, the U-Bahn in Berlin, Singapore’s MRT, or the Shanghai subway, you’ll see a tightly packed sardine can filled with disparate modes of nine-to-five dressing. But recurring motifs appear, particularly on those women who look like they’ve really got it together: a sleek camel overcoat paired with crisply creased trousers and a great T-shirt, or a pair of jeans and a sharply tailored black blazer. This is the no-fail, get-it-done-and-look-good-doing-it city uniform, and much of its history can be traced back to Max Mara, which celebrates its 75th anniversary this year.

This is why the brand, despite its Italian origins, chose to show its resort collection in Shanghai this past summer. “Max Mara has always been a metropolitan phenomenon,” Ian Griffiths, the label’s longtime creative director, tells me on the eve of the show. “After 75 years, that’s what Max Mara is all about. It’s about urban chic; it’s about a woman who really wants to engage with a city.” For Griffiths, just as modernity defines Shanghai, so too does it underscore Max Mara’s longevity in fashion’s rapidly shifting ecosystem.

The show was held at Shanghai’s Long Museum West Bund, an art exhibition space housed inside a brutalist concrete building on the western side of the city. The skies that day were filled with dense gray fog and windy, misty rain, veiling the famously illuminated skyline just enough to look like a scene from Blade Runner.

“There’s something about Max Mara that works really well against the background of brutalist architecture,” Griffiths says. “It’s like the city itself, and Max Mara’s luxury is kind of a foil to this hard city landscape.”

Outside the museum, an entirely new neighborhood was going up. Luxury apartment buildings, restaurants, and gyms were all being erected by clusters of giant cranes placed precariously close together. Inside the Long Museum, guests were time-warped back to Max Mara’s beginnings in 1951, when Achille Maramotti founded the brand with one coat and one suit. He revolutionized sportswear in Italy by mass-producing classically tailored garments at a time when most men and women purchased their clothes directly from independent tailors and dressmakers. In many ways, Maramotti was an early proponent of modern sportswear and one of the first to translate it from its American origins to more distinctly European styles.

One of the most dominant themes on the runways in recent years has been this idea of wardrobing: effortless pieces that can be endlessly remixed, whether it’s a jean and a blazer accessorized with a printed silk scarf, a boxy knee-length skirt suit, or a fluid dress made from cotton jersey. Juxtaposed with recent trends like heavy embellishment, texture, and eccentric shapes and silhouettes, these updated takes on classics offer a way to play with your personal style if the more idiosyncratic stuff isn’t your thing. With Max Mara, though, it has never been about trends. Instead, the brand has held fast to the idea that real taste is inherent, not plucked from the internet, and that clothes should enhance rather than inform who you are or want to be.

It’s why Max Mara has long appealed to women in power who need to be heard and armored. See: Nancy Pelosi in the fiery-orange coat she wore following a confrontational meeting with President Trump in 2018 or Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, looking poised and polished in white jeans and a cashmere camel trench in 2023, a look built to withstand public scrutiny. Katie Holmes said at the show that she loves Max Mara because of its “classic elegance” and its ability to “fit into any wardrobe.” Fashion editor Tonne Goodman, who has styled many Max Mara shows and campaigns, is well known among fashion obsessives for her unimpeachable taste and rigorous uniform; she always wears some version of a chic silk scarf, sweater, and loafers.

“The clothes understand the realities of a woman’s life today,” says society fixture and designer Nicky Hilton, a longtime Max Mara client. “You can put on a beautiful coat or a perfectly tailored suit and immediately feel pulled together. But it never feels overly precious. The feeling of confidence and ease is incredibly consistent. The Teddy coats and camel coats have been staples in my closet for years.”

Max Mara clients wandered the exhibition space alongside newer Gen-Z acolytes like Olympic freestyle skier Eileen Gu and filmmaker and actor Maude Apatow. Laura Lusuardi, who has been the house’s fashion coordinator since the 1960s, was also there, dressed in a tunic, wide-leg pants, and sculptural statement jewelry. “Over 75 years, women’s lifestyles have changed dramatically, and Max Mara has always closely observed and accompanied that evolution, especially through pivotal moments such as the rise of the ‘working woman’ in the 1980s,” Lusuardi explains. “Our incredible archive serves as a constant source of inspiration, allowing us to rethink our heritage through a contemporary lens.”

In tandem with the resort show, the brand staged an exhibition in the same space, curated by fashion historian Olivier Saillard, that re-created its archive in Reggio Emilia, Italy. The space was packed with floor-to-ceiling industrial shelving that featured wooden shipping crates, shoe and hat boxes, spools of thread, and historic ephemera from the Max Mara universe, including Maramotti’s original sewing machines, advertisements dating back to the 1950s, and the original prototypes of some Max Mara coats. Through the archives, Saillard was able to highlight Maramotti’s fashion origins as the son of a mother who wrote sewing manuals and great-grandmother who started a dressmaking school in the 1850s. “Within that origin lies everything fashion has to say: transmission, true elegance, the timelessness of a garment one makes oneself or holds dear,” he says.

The show opened with a nod to streamlined glamour: a sequined ivory trench coat styled with a white turtleneck underneath and a pair of beige T-strap pumps. More monochromatic looks followed, including a boxy black miniskirt suit and a sumptuous white wrap coat cinched with a wide, decorative belt, which would appear in several playful iterations throughout the collection, including with black-and-white-striped sequined short shorts. Griffiths referenced the Bauhaus art and design movement (the original factory in Reggio Emilia was designed in a Bauhaus-inspired style) with dizzying graphic patterns applied to cardigans and pencil skirts, as well as injections of royal blue, mustard, and Max Mara’s signature red.

The Shanghai collection was a reflection of Max Mara’s unique ability to infuse newness and even some novelty (à la the short shorts, sequins, and belts) into its repertoire. As Griffiths explains, “It’s about offering a curated choice that allows every Max Mara woman to find her style, her look, her silhouette.” He adds, “Everyone has a desire for some kind of novelty, so you can’t erase it from the offer, but within the context of a wardrobe or within a collection, there can be one or two pieces, and hopefully those pieces have longevity too.”

Still, the aim, Lusuardi explains, is “not to be just ‘in fashion’ ” but to “go beyond trends.” She adds, “The essence of the Max Mara look lies in its essentiality.”

After the show, walking back out through the exhibition space, you could see their points articulated: young women wearing their ivory silk button-downs and tailored pants with multiple layered belts in mixed metals; older clients dressed in vintage Max Mara skirts and jackets, styled with a cardigan over their shoulders or a decorative minaudière. The brand was all around, but you noticed the people in the clothes.

“Over the years, creativity in fashion has evolved into something tied deeply to personal style,” Lusuardi explains. “It’s how a woman wears and interprets a piece that truly makes the difference. Max Mara offers a versatile foundation that adapts seamlessly to every woman’s unique lifestyle.” In other words, there’s no better—and more modern—uniform than one that’s truly your own, whatever city or subway car you’re making your way through.

Opening image top center: Max Mara Resort 2027. All others, surrounding: “The Max!” 75th-anniversary exhibition and behind-the-scenes images shown at the Long Museum West Bund, Shanghai.

#6674. Cashmere Perfumes Are the Coziest Way to Wear Fragrance

These soft, musky scents capture the plush warmth of your favorite sweater.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Few things are as cozy as cashmere—whether it’s a sweater, scarf, or throw blanket. One unexpected way to wrap yourself in the fabric’s luxury is with a cashmere perfume. These scents capture the best parts of the warm, fuzzy material through an actual cashmere note called cashmeran. The synthetic note, used in perfume since it was developed in the 1960s, adds warmth, woodiness, musk, and spice to a perfume’s layers, giving the overall composition a soft, velvety texture. Grounded in the warm woods and sweet gourmands of the season, or anchored alongside a fresh floral, these cashmere perfumes are the next best thing to a premium garment.

The richness of sandalwood and the creaminess of a milk accord layer seamlessly at the bottom and top of a cashmeran center.

Key notes: milky accord, nutmeg, Iris, rose, cashmeran, sandalwood, Madagascar vanilla bourbon

Customer review: “Santal Calling is divine; on my skin it is magic. Pure comfort in a bottle—creamy sandalwood wrapped in soft iris, warm milk, and the smoothest touch of vanilla. It feels like cashmere against the skin: elegant, intimate, and so addictive that I can't stop spraying myself throughout the day.” - Madrone

Many lavender perfumes capture the essence of the flower itself, but Matiere Premiere took a different approach, encapsulating the atmospheric notes from a lavender distillation factory in Provence. The result is a hybrid of fresh lavender blending with crisper hints of metal that are then softened by musk and cashmeran.

Customer review: “For me, lavender is a tricky scent. It depends how it is paired in a perfume composition. This one opens with a very "fresh" lavender, which will go quiet in the background, and it will reappear in the dry down. Lovely perfume, easy to wear and very good longevity (6+ hours on my skin).” - Ramona D.

One of Maison Margiela’s most popular scents blends the smokiness of burning wood with notes of gaiac wood, cashmeran, and clove oil to bottle the experience of sitting by a crackling fireplace.

Key notes: clove oil, chestnut accord, vanilla accord

Customer review: “My all-time favorite perfume. It smells like sitting by the fireplace wrapped in your comfy blanket, sipping your favorite drink. The scent is perfect for winter!” - MelB

This Mugler classic intensifies as it warms up with your body heat, bringing out the long-lasting notes of white amber, cashmeran wood, and jasmine. It’s equal parts floral and woody, with just the right warmth and sweetness from its amber base.

Key notes: jasmine sambac, cashmeran wood, white amber

Customer review: “This perfume has so many layers and is so sophisticated and wonderful. I really like the notes and how they mature over time. Great longevity as well.” - prespri_7178

Cashmere is the star here, anchoring the scent’s base and owning the dry-down, as toasted coconut, passionflower, and vanilla milk musk notes layer at its heart and on top.

Key notes: vanilla milk musk, toasted coconut, passionflower, plumeria, cashmeran wood

Customer review: “Soft, cozy, sweet, and luxurious. It’s giving cashmere sweater + clean skin! It’s an easy reach that I can’t stop wearing.” - Regina

This intensified version keeps the crisp, linen-like freshness of Byredo’s original Blanche eau de perfume. It takes a warmer turn as black pepper and neroli make way for a floral center, before settling into a base of white musk, cashmere wood, and ambroxan. It wears like a skin scent, although it’s in the floral family.

Key notes: aldehyde, black pepper, neroli, rose absolute, violet, jasmine, cashmeran, musks, ambroxan, cashmere woods

Customer review: “I absolutely love Blanche Absolu, intense aldehydes, clean laundry done to perfection with good longevity on skin and fabric! 10/10” - layla88

Carmina combines sweet and spicy top notes of pink pepper, black cherry, and saffron with a hearty floral center of rose, violet, and peony. To round out the profile, cashmere wood, amber, and musk peak through on the dry down.

Key notes: pink pepper, black cherry, saffron, rose de mai, violet, peony

Customer review: “It's giving 'date night,' to me. It's soft, feminine, and sensual all at the same time. As far as longevity, I sprayed it around 5pm, and I could still smell it on my wrist the next morning.”

Although it’s not quite a gourmand, Esplendor has a sweetness that’s not cloying. Bottom notes of amber and vanilla sit alongside cashmeran. Adding to the warmth at the center is benzoin, a creamy note with a balsamic-like aroma. Classic florals like rose and lily of the valley are stacked at the top to open the scent.

Key notes: lily, freesia, peony, rose, muguet, benzoin, vanilla, amber, cashmeran

Customer review: “Grandano Esplendor drapes the skin in quiet luxury. It is a cashmere sweater, washed in lilies and creamy vanilla, then folded into warm benzoin resin. The sweetness is gentle rather than sugary, and the amber gives it a comforting warmth. It doesn't overly project and lasts 8 hours, at least, on skin. It feels like velvet brushed in slow motion.” - AlchemyAge

Gap’s Om features cashmeran, musk, and amber woods—the trifecta that gives cashmere perfumes their warmth. As the scent develops, hints of spice shine through from coriander flower at the center and ginger to open the blend. Heavier notes of frankincense are balanced with light florals like water lotus.

Key notes: ginger, olibanum essence, water lotus, lilyflor, sandalwood, coriander flower, amber woods, cashmeran, cedar, balsamic musks

Customer review: “If you loved Heaven in the 90s, try the new 2026 "Om". It's smell reminds me of the old Heaven and I LOVE it. It smells like fresh laundry, clean baby clothes, spring flowers, all the calming things. I think I found a new signature scent!” - Samantha H.

Chloé’s Parfum Intense takes you on a journey that hits all the high points of a versatile fragrance. It opens with the sweetness of juicy raspberry and rose, which then shifts into a honeyed element at the center before settling into its intense ending with rich musks and woods.

Key notes: raspberry, rose, ambrox, cashmeran, cedar

Customer review: “Chloé Eau de Parfum is a wardrobe essential for anyone who treasures floral elegance that never feels fussy. It’s instantly recognizable yet versatile — perfect for spring and summer, but cozy enough for year-round wear.” -Beautybae01

Unlike many fragrances on this list that place cashmeran at the base of their composition, this one nestles it right at its heart. The scent experience begins with a kick thanks to a sweet and spicy mix of blood orange, Sichuan pepper, and ginger. You’re then brought right into a cozy heart of cashmeran and a brand-exclusive floral accord before rounding out the journey with a blend of woods, musk, and vetiver.

Key notes: ambrette, baies rose, blood orange, bergamot, Sichuan pepper, fresh ginger, fleuriste fusion, magnolia aroma space, Egyptian jasmine, cashmeran, guaiacwood, cedarwood, blond wood, vetiver, moss, ambroxan, musks

Customer review: “It’s a clean fragrance. Quiet luxury, skin scent that still has a silage that draws attention. Easy wear if you like musk. It’s all you really get. But it’s what I wanted.” - Edward B.

Donna Karan’s Cashmere Mist is quite possibly the perfume that introduced plush, cozy, cashmere-like notes to fragrance. The iconic eau de parfum, which launched in the mid-'90s, features rich florals and sandalwood—and manages to encapsulate all the soft attributes of cashmere without including cashmere wood in its composition.

Key notes: lily of the valley, Moroccan jasmine, sandalwood

Customer review: “It is a soft, sensual scent that has musky overtones. It stays with you all day long, whereas most scents disappear shortly after applying. This is one of the most pleasing scents that works with all occasions and all the different lotions I like to use. I believe I have found a scent that I will purchase over and over again without it getting old or boring. I have had numerous compliments when I wear this scent, which always makes a girl happy.” - Sasicat

#6673. Our 11 Favorite Watches Coming to the Biggest Auctions of the Year

Want more insider watch coverage? Get Box + Papers, GQ's newsletter devoted to the watch world, sent to your inbox every Friday. Sign up here to get it free.

This is the biggest weekend of the year for vintage watches. It’s the year-end watch auctions in Geneva, where many prestigious houses bring their very best pieces to market. And it’s never been a more enthralling time to keep a close eye on what happens in Geneva over the next few days. In the first half of the year, the number of million-dollar watches nearly eclipsed the total for the entirety of 2025. A couple of the pieces listed below, including a unique Rolex and a rare Patek Philippe in stainless steel, have estimates above a million bucks.

Writer Oren Hartov and I pored over hundreds of lots to bring you our 11 favorite watches plus one bonus selection. See them all below.

You know a banger is coming up for sale when the house behind it doesn’t even bother capping its price range. Auction estimates are routinely and famously low to encourage bidders, and this watch’s starting point is still $1.2 million. Why? Well, have you ever seen a Rolex like this before? Before Rolex defined the look of modern watches with pieces like the Submariner, it operated similarly to many other manufacturers in Switzerland, willing to make one-off pieces and experiment frequently with its design.

This square beauty from the early 1940s is “most probably unique,” as Phillips auction house writes in its essay on the piece. This exact piece last hit the auction block in 2004, and no other example has come up for public sale since. It’s crazy to see how much this watch’s case shape resembles Heuer’s similarly blocky Monaco, which wouldn’t be released for another 25-plus years. Unfortunately, as cool as this watch is, it does not come with onyx prayer beads. —Cam Wolf

There’s Patek, then there’s complicated Patek, then there’s stainless steel complicated Patek, then there’s stainless steel complicated Patek made in just a handful of examples, then there’s stainless steel complicated Patek made in just a handful of examples in insane condition. This watch checks all those boxes. A reference 1436, it’s a split-seconds (rattrapante) chronograph, meaning it can time successive intervals of a race or event. One of just two stainless steel examples known to the market, it has an estimate of $2.4-$4.8M, a testament to its rarity and importance. —Oren Hartov

Yet another rare watch executed in stainless steel, this fabulous Lange 1 boasts a gorgeous two-tone dial in blue, with darker subdials contrasting against a cobalt-colored main dial. Dating to 1999 and first sold by the German retailer Oeding-Erdel, it’s one of approximately 30 pieces made in the most utilitarian of metals. Originally fitted with a more standard silvered dial, it received its current navy-blue dial as a replacement and is one of just two stainless steel Lange 1s known in this particular configuration. —OH

Renewed interest in Urban Jürgensen stemming from its recent relaunch under the directorship of Kari Voutilainen, who has since left the CEO position but remains on the company’s board, has seen watches such as this early-’90s ref. 2 garner more attention. A lovely perpetual calendar-moonphase, it’s housed in a classically inspired 37.7mm yellow gold case with cornes-de-vache-style lugs, a stepped bezel, and an incredible dial with the brand’s signature observatory-style hands. Someone tell Timothée Chalamet. —OH

Chopard has a hard-earned reputation for putting out some of the most finely made watches in Switzerland. It’s not just the nerds who are familiar with its work anymore, either. If we (the nerds, obviously) were sending a watch in a bottle to help share that message far and wide, this Lunar One, which looks like something out of Superman’s icy Fortress of Solitude, wouldn’t be a bad choice. This is Chopard’s first watch to combine a perpetual calendar and a moonphase, which is like shaving truffles on caviar. I love that the Roman numerals at 4 and 8 o’clock look like columns nearly buckling under the weight of the center of the dial. This watch also comes with several fun add-ons, like onyx prayer beads plus a ring and a pen set with diamonds. —Cam Wolf

While many younger collectors are obsessed with the Cosmograph Daytona, true “Crown” heads know that other pre-Daytona chronographs sometimes present an even more compelling proposition. This ref. 3525 ‘’Bariletto,’ dating to the 1940s, is not only the first Oyster-cased Rolex chronograph, but it’s also the only known stainless-steel example carrying the signature on the dial of Proud’s, a Rolex retailer based in Sydney. Manually wound, paired to a handsome beads-of-rice bracelet, and measuring a compact 36mm, it comes from the collection of important Italian collector Pucci Papaleo. —OH

While this stainless steel Patek may look like a normal ref. 2509—a beautiful hand-wound dress watch from the midcentury—it’s actually a “school watch” modified by a watchmaking student at the Geneva Watchmaking School. Dating to the 1960s, it’s housed in a 35mm stainless steel case and features a lovely dial with the ‘Ecole d’Horlogerie Geneve’ signature instead of Patek Philippe’s. Open it up, and the hand-wound movement is signed by Norbert Henry, the watchmaking student who assembled and finished it. While it may not attract the attention of more typical Patek collectors, its under-the-radar qualities make it a potential sleeper hit. —OH

It’s tough to argue with the sheer beauty of Vacheron’s mid-20th-century output, much of which is vastly underappreciated compared to comparable pieces from the likes of Patek Philippe. This splendid yellow gold ref. 4072 with a two-tone multi-scale dial dates to the late 1940s—one of my favorite eras of watch design. Powered by the hand-wound cal. V 492 movement and featuring a lovely set of long, contoured lugs, its dial is in fantastic condition, with applied dart and Roman indices, sharp printing, a crisp signature, and legible tachymeter and telemeter scales. It will surely find its way onto the wrist of a collector with excellent taste. —OH

This watch’s dial depicts Saint George, who, according to legend, slew a dragon while on horseback. This is a perfect use for the rich, deep colors you get from enamel. The flames licking at Saint George are beautiful shades of orange and red. He triumphantly lifts his spear as his steed rears its front legs. It’s very cool how much story you can get from this little 35mm timepiece. —CW

Watch collectors might pony up a few thousand for one of independent watchmaker F.P. Journe’s used tissues at this point. However, they’ll have to settle for a host of accessories coming to auction instead this weekend. The maker is so in-demand that, in addition to his timepieces, houses are selling his empty watch boxes and a set of toys that resemble him. This lot is in the middle of those two extremes: a wall clock made to resemble Journe’s Octa Réserve de Marche. Although I’m not gonna lie, flipping this over and seeing the compartment where you stuff in the batteries is a bit of a buzzkill. —CW

They used to make everything look more elegant. This original Longines design was developed in 1931 with famous aviator Charles Lindbergh. It is technically a pilot’s watch, but its elegant, icy-blue dial and Roman numerals would make it the fanciest model on many red carpets in 2026. This is a model from the ‘80s inspired by that original design, and it comes on an absolutely righteous beads-of-rice bracelet. Someone is going to get this guy for around $2,500 if the estimate is correct! —CW

In Rolex world, even the advertisements sell for thousands of dollars. It’s hard to blame people when we’re talking about a rare poster of a GMT-Master wearing a snow-dusted Rolex beanie. Awwww. (Relatedly, imagine if Rolex sold that beanie!? Oh, boy.) —CW

#6671. This Christmas, Harrods Is Doing Things Differently

There are few signs that Christmas has arrived in London quite like the Harrods store lighting up for the festive season. Every year, thousands of visitors descend upon Knightsbridge to see the store’s holiday transformation, and this year, the heritage retailer is giving them even more reason to stick around — and return again and again.

Unveiled on Tuesday, Harrods’s iconic terracotta façade has been revamped once again into a celestial spectacle, complete with 600 handcrafted stars, four kilometers of gold leaf, and more than 17,000 lights. The difference this year, however, is that the holiday campaign, Where the Stars Align, is the first wholly Harrods-created festive concept in several years. This follows a spree of collaborations with luxury houses, including Dior in 2022 and Loro Piana in 2024, which placed the retailer as secondary in its own Christmas storytelling.

This time, Harrods has brought multiple brands under its complete creative direction: each of its 24 Christmas windows feature unique installations from houses including Ralph Lauren, Van Cleef & Arpels, Chopard, Dior, Graff, Cartier, and Chanel Beauty.

“I wanted to create joy, but I also wanted that feeling of childhood — those moments where you stop and just look up, whether that’s with your friends and family,” says Alexander Wells Greco, Harrods’s creative visual director. “There’s that moment to pause in such a busy climate.”

For Michael Ward, the store’s managing director, the façade is also an important gateway to the wider Harrods experience. “Our façade is one of London’s most recognizable landmarks, and at Christmas, it becomes a destination in its own right. It attracts people who may not have planned to visit the store, creating an opportunity to introduce them to everything Harrods has to offer,” he says.

That invitation continues inside. Customers can take part in luxury engraving, leather personalization and bespoke calligraphy, alongside gold-leaf and bauble personalization with Acqua di Parma. A Dior cinema activation will screen a new film from its creative director Jonathan Anderson, while family programming includes snow globe making, arts and crafts, and biscuit decorating. Children can also collect and post letters to Father Christmas from dedicated Harrods post boxes throughout the store.

The scale of the program reflects the commercial importance of the festive period. A 2025 Microsoft Advertising survey found that 60% of small and medium-sized retailers consider the holidays their most important trading period, with 44% expecting it to account for more than a quarter of annual sales. For Harrods, the stakes are particularly high: more than a third of its customers visit during the festive season, according to Ward. The campaign, therefore, is an opportunity to engage existing customers while drawing in visitors who might initially come for the spectacle.

However, success is not measured by footfall and holiday sales alone. Harrods is also looking at the quality of the experience and the longer-term relationships it can build with customers. The aim for every touchpoint, from the windows and the lighting to the restaurants, is to reinforce the wider Harrods proposition. “If someone comes to see the lights, discovers something unexpected inside the store and experiences the exceptional service that defines Harrods,” Ward says, “that is incredibly valuable to us. These are investments in the long-term strength of our brand, as much as in the Christmas trading period.”

Having spent several years investing in the lighting infrastructure that now connects its Knightsbridge façade, windows and surrounding public spaces, Harrods is using this year’s campaign to bring that investment to life. Every evening from 6pm, the façade will host a choreographed light show, repeating every 30 minutes and encouraging visitors to stop by and take in the display.

But while technology provides the scale and the spectacle, the installation is equally defined by the craftsmanship behind it: 600 handcrafted stars, bespoke moons and illuminated elements, brought together by more than 60 specialists and over 40,000 hours of work, with the majority of production taking place in the UK.

“Craftsmanship is fundamental to luxury, and it reflects the same commitment to quality and attention to detail that we expect across everything we do at Harrods. As technology and AI continue to transform the world around us, I believe there is something increasingly valuable about human creativity and the ability to create physical experiences that people can genuinely connect with,” says Ward, noting that recent holiday campaigns from brands such as Prada and Dior have also embraced illustration and craft. “There is a renewed appreciation for the human touch and the sense of wonder that is thoughtfully made.”

For Greco, championing local suppliers was a no-brainer, reflecting both the depth of creative talent available in Britain and the retailer’s responsibility to platform that talent. “We have such huge creative talent in the UK from a production standpoint, across all aspects,” he says. “We have such a vast platform that can really enable and enhance the visibility of these wonderful local crafters.”

“Christmas is such a tactile seasonal moment,” continues Greco. “Irrespective of opening gifts or whatever, you’re with your loved ones, you’re socializing, and I think it’s that tactility that enabled us to make the right decision at the beginning of the year and say, ‘Let’s maintain that. Let’s support the human touch.’”

Rather than concentrating all of its activity around the initial campaign launch, the department store is rolling out a rotating program of retail theater throughout the six-week festive period to reflect the changing priorities of customers as the season progresses, as well as giving them reasons to return.

“In November, we see customers start to prepare for the festive calendar, whether that means finding something to wear for a special occasion or getting their homes ready to entertain. As we move into December, gifting naturally becomes a priority. But gifting today is not simply about buying for others,” says Ward.

Harrods is programming its in-store experiences accordingly. November’s line-up includes live fashion illustration in the store’s Eveningwear and Occasion Room, beauty gifting experiences with Clé de Peau Beauté and personalized Christmas card calligraphy, alongside opportunities to have festive purchases engraved or customized. As the season progresses, the focus broadens to family experiences, with a weekend of snow globe making, arts and crafts and Marcato biscuit decorating on December 12-13. Letters to Father Christmas can also be posted at dedicated Harrods post boxes from November 10 to December 24.

The strategy comes at a time when physical retailers are having to work harder to justify the journey into store. PwC found that 64% of UK festive purchases were expected to take place online in 2025, including home delivery and click-and-collect. Meanwhile, McKinsey’s latest retail research found that 65% of consumers cite immersive environments as a driver when choosing a store for discovery-led visits.

“We are operating in an environment where customers are increasingly thoughtful about how and where they spend their money, and luxury retailers need to recognize that. Customers have high expectations, particularly at Christmas. They are looking for exceptional products, but also for service and experiences that make their time worthwhile,” says Ward. “Harrods is well positioned because we offer far more than a traditional retail experience. Whether someone is looking for a very special gift, preparing for an occasion or simply spending time with family, we can offer something that feels personal and memorable. Ultimately, our focus is not simply on encouraging customers to spend more, but on giving them compelling reasons to choose Harrods.”

There is also a wider ambition to create a sense of community around the store. Harrods has been part of London’s retail landscape for more than 175 years, and Greco sees this as carrying a responsibility beyond its commercial operations. “We are the beacon of Knightsbridge,” he says. “We have a duty of care to make sure that we are delivering exceptional retail theatre, even more so throughout these seasonal moments.”

#6670. The Best Navy Suede Bags to Elevate Your Fall Wardrobe

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

This rich, versatile texture is the season’s chicest alternative to black.

When we’re feeling a little tired of our current clothing situation, sometimes even the most subtle change can bring a total refresh. A new bag won’t overhaul your closet, but it can make everything in it feel new again. We’ll always love our classic black bags, but a navy suede bag is another timeless choice, one that brings a quiet, sophisticated twist to fall dressing.

Suede is made for the season. Its soft, matte texture adds depth and warmth to the layered textures of autumn: chunky knits, wool coats, corduroy, and denim. Paired with navy’s understated richness, it feels polished without being predictable, and it pairs just as easily with camel and chocolate brown as with gray, cream, and black, of course.

Navy suede also has a gift for elevating the simplest outfits. Carry it with a plain sweater and straight-leg jeans, and the whole look suddenly seems more intentional. Swap it in for your usual black tote on a workday, and you’ll notice how effortlessly it softens a tailored look. It’s a small change, but one that makes getting dressed feel fresh again.

Ahead, the best navy suede bags to shop this fall.

This dumpling bag may look small, but it’s roomier than it seems and holds far more than just the essentials. The double-handle design lets you carry it several ways, while the adjustable knots let you customize the fit and wear it exactly how you like.

A little boho and a lot polished, this softly structured tote features a drawstring top, sculptural ruching, and a magnetic clasp. It’s roomy enough for your daily essentials, and the relaxed shape pairs easily with everything from denim and knits to tailored trousers.

So elegant yet so wearable, this pochette bag isn’t just for special occasions. Styled with gray jeans, a crisp white tee, and a tailored blazer, it adds a touch of polish to even the most laid-back outfit, proving that a little elegance belongs in your everyday rotation.

This convertible crescent bag draws much of its appeal from rich, handwoven navy suede. Two included straps let you wear it as either a shoulder bag or a crossbody, so it adapts easily from day to night.

You can’t get much chicer than the Stockholm shoulder bag by DeMellier. A fan favorite, it takes on a new depth in supple navy suede. Consider it your next heavy-rotation bag, the one you’ll grab on the way out the door without a second thought.

Small but mighty, this slim shoulder bag brings polish to any night out. Gold-tone accents add a touch of shine, and a magnetic closure keeps your essentials secure. It holds just enough for the evening, like your phone, cards, keys, and a lipstick, and it looks every bit as good with a little black dress as it does with dark denim and a blazer.

Tiny, but impossible to ignore. This mini crescent trades its usual look for buttery navy suede, and the result is pure charm. There’s room only for what truly matters: your phone, a lip balm, and a card or two. Carry it by hand, the way it was meant to be held.

Modern, practical, and roomier than it looks, this bucket bag is a worthy contender for your work bag, with space for a 13-inch laptop and your daily essentials. The slender buckle is a quiet statement detail that’s as functional as it is stylish.

Sleek, streamlined, and modern, this navy baguette proves that a classic shape can do it all. Carry it on your shoulder for the office, the dinner reservation, and everything in between.

Subtle patch pockets lend this supple suede bag a utilitarian edge, while its generous proportions keep things practical. Here, function and refinement meet in an everyday silhouette that works as hard as it looks.

This velvety hobo bag has a soft, spacious silhouette, a secure bridge-snap closure, and statement hardware that catches the eye. It makes a great everyday carryall, and the matching zip pouch keeps small items safe and easy to find.
