#6668. GQ’s 13 Breakout Stars of 2026

Sometimes it’s fun to be early to the party. GQ launched the Breakouts portfolio in 2014 to celebrate the Hollywood upstarts who were poised to do big things. And not to brag, but we nailed it; that first group included Miles Teller, Shailene Woodley, Eddie Redmayne, and the late, great Chadwick Boseman. Over the ensuing years, we featured plenty more soon-to-be-superstars: Rami Malek. Brie Larson. Daniel Kaluuya. Riz Ahmed. Barry Keoghan. The kids from Stranger Things, when they were still kids. The cast of Succession before Succession became everyone’s favorite show.

In 2017, we put a baby-faced Timothée Chalamet on the list for his turn in Call Me by Your Name. (Our global entertainment director, Dana Mathews, fondly recalls him turning to her during the Man of the Year Party and saying, “This is the best party I’ve ever been to in my life.”) Since then, Chalamet has appeared on three GQ covers, earned four Oscar nominations, and become a household name (and maybe been to a few more great parties).

We took a few years off (okay, fine, seven), but 2026 feels like exactly the right time to revive GQ’s Breakouts portfolio—now through a wider lens. Yes, though we’ve got eyes on Hollywood’s next big things—like, say, Sly Stallone doppelgänger Anthony Ippolito; Gen Z class clown Owen Thiele, of Adults; Misty Green’s astounding leading woman, Rosalind Eleazar—not everyone is working the camera. We’re excited to introduce you to the West Coast’s hottest up-and-coming rapper in AZ Chike and put you on to Fcukers, whose debut album, packed with rowdy electro-pop bangers, made them first in our hearts and on our pregaming playlists. We’ve also got podcaster and journalist Pablo Torre, whose relentless reporting upended a $7.8 billion NBA franchise, and Jordan Firstman, an internet-born comedian who wrote and directed a film that commanded a lengthy standing ovation from Cannes audiences (right after they finished crying).

Point is, our Breakouts class of 2026 brings together 13 fully minted stars who did something that feels increasingly impossible: They captured our attention in a time when it feels like attention is more fleeting than ever. Welcome to their party.

Dress by Dior. Shoes by Jimmy Choo. Mask from Palace Costume Co.

Age: 25Breakout moment: Playing the queen bee on Ryan Murphy’s ’80s glam fever dream The Shards.—————

It’s a different kind of attention that I actually prefer. Because for so long I was getting attention, but not for a specific thing. And that was confusing and kind of messed with my head a bit. I was really young and people knew who I was, but I couldn’t really point to the work that they knew. And so it’s really fun for me to have people [now say], “I watched The Shards,” or “I watched Bottoms,” and then we have something to talk about.

Infinite Jest—no, I’m kidding, they’ve already read it, all of them. A Man’s Place by Annie Ernaux is very good and easily digestible. I think Just Kids is wonderful. What We Talk About When We Talk About Love. That one’s really great. Oh, and this is so classic, but Nine Stories by J.D. Salinger is really good. I know guys—male actors especially—love The Catcher in the Rye.

I got really worried the other day because I started getting a lot of followers. It was two days of so many followers, and I was like, “Oh my God, I’ve been doxxed.” The last thing I logged was Hitch. My top four are A Woman Under the Influence, The Dark Knight, Phantom Thread, and Eternal Sunshine. My Odyssey review has 112 likes. I don’t care how many followers I have on Instagram, how many likes I get. Letterboxd is truly a hit of adrenaline every time someone likes my review. —Frazier Tharpe

Jacket and jeans by Ralph Lauren Collection. Necklace by Chopard. Ring by Chanel Fine Jewelry.

On Wise: Jacket by Isabel Marant. Top by Gucci. Briefs by Araks. Boots by Herbert Levine. Sunglasses by McQueen. On Walker Lewis: Jacket by Balenciaga. T-shirt by Isabel Marant. Jeans by Gucci. Boots by Timberland. Sunglasses by Tom Ford. Jewelry, his own.

Ages: Wise, 28 | Walker Lewis, 29Breakout Moment: The NYC duo’s 2026 debut album, Ö, featuring indie-sleazy hits like “If You Wanna Party, Come Over to My House” and “Beatback.”—————

Wise: That was probably the most surreal thing I’ve ever experienced. We’re like, “This is what it feels to be like Led Zeppelin.”

Walker Lewis: It’s funny—a reel permeated my Instagram from a Brazilian influencer, and it was like, “Who is this controversial band that everyone’s arguing about opening for Harry Styles?” But I think by the last show, people got it.

Walker Lewis: Easy. The Cure. It’s unbelievable, to see somebody still sound that good and be able to play for two hours, and you know every single song.

Walker Lewis: When I was getting a root canal done and the nurse said, “Can I get a photo with you after?” I was like, “You couldn’t have asked before?” —Alex Pappademas

(from l.) On Firstman: All clothing by Tom Ford. Earrings, his own. On Walker Lewis: Jacket by Louis Vuitton Men’s. Shirt and sunglasses by Tom Ford. Tie by Our Legacy. Necklace, his own. On Wise: Top and pants by McQueen.

Robe by Dolce & Gabbana. Pants by Lu’u Dan. Watch by Cartier. Earring, his own.

Age: 28Breakout Moment: The series Off Campus, as the hottest fictional hockey player from this year’s hottest fictional hockey show.—————

I cannot shut up about this, but it has to be throwing the first pitch out for the White Sox. I will remember that forever.

Yeah, it was. And I hadn’t thrown a baseball in a really long time.

I look forward to the moment where I get to really reflect and digest. Next month I have some time off, and I’m going to go home and eat sandwiches at my mom’s house and take my grandma for a walk. “Go on a walk with my grandma”.… That’s a weird way to put it.

I’m, like, an idiot. I’m a full goofball. Garrett Graham is the heartthrob. To me, I’m just like, “I’m Bel.” And in my head, those are very different things. I’m flattered that people can associate me with heartthrob status, but no, I don’t wake up in the morning feeling like a heartthrob.

I mean, I always wanted to play Holden Caulfield, but who knows? —Trishna Rikhy

Jacket and pants by Prada. Shirt by Brioni. Pocket square by Charvet. Belt by Artemas Quibble. Sunglasses by Jacques Marie Mage. Necklace and ring by David Yurman.

Jacket by McQueen. Shirt by Factor’s. Pants by Versace. Boots by Tom Ford. Sunglasses (throughout) by Louis Vuitton Men’s. Earrings (throughout), his own.

Age: 30Breakout Moment: Being the infectiously charismatic friend-to-all on FX’s zoomer sitcom Adults.—————

Sadie Sink knew who I was, and that was kind of cool. I just love her. She’s so talented and so adorable. It’s like meeting the queen before she’s the queen.

I do watch the fan edits. They’re fun. Some of them pick the worst photos of me, and I’m like, “This is a hate crime, but thank you for putting it on TikTok.”

I got two very smart pieces of advice. One was, “Run. Don’t do this. Save yourself.” And then the other person said, “Stick with it.” I’m kind of doing both. I am simultaneously sticking with it and trying my hardest, but also I’m like, Once you have a win, you do have to celebrate it and run as far away as you can and hide.

I bought a bag from The Row…which looks like—and I say this with love—it could be $20, but it’s the most expensive thing I own. And I did this because I went shopping with Hailey Bieber, and when you’re shopping with Hailey Bieber you buy things you think you can afford but you probably can’t…and now it’s too late to return. It’s a beautiful bag—it’s quiet luxury, babe. It’s so quiet you don’t know it’s The Row. —F.T

Jacket and pants by Saint Laurent by Anthony Vaccarello. Boots by Giuseppe Zanotti. Sunglasses (throughout) by Louis Vuitton Men’s. Earrings (throughout), his own. Ring by Bvlgari.

Dress by Bottega Veneta. Shoes by Herbert Levine. Sunglasses by Celine.

Age: 38Breakout moment: Her riveting performance as the title character in Chris Rock’s Misty Green (and her role in Slow Horses).—————

I mean, the first time I watched it, I just thought, Oh—you’re going to be in every frame. [Laughs]

[In an American accent] “Murderer.” Mur-der-rer. I think every Brit finds that hard. I was like, “Can I say ’killer’ instead?” And “mirror.” It’s when you’ve got a double r. But I had a great dialect coach.

I would’ve loved to have been in a scene with Philip Seymour Hoffman. That would’ve been my dream. And I would love to work with Sandra Hüller.

I was onstage with Ralph Fiennes. We finished Misty Green—I did an overnight shoot on Friday into Saturday morning, got on a plane, arrived in London on Sunday, and went straight into rehearsals with Ralph. It was a pretty mad summer.

I was getting ready before the Misty Green premiere [at the Toronto International Film Festival]. And my mom came down. She sat there and she was just sending pictures and she just had tears in her eyes. Just seeing this whole period at TIFF—for her, it’s her little girl. And every now and again, I would just look at her and she was just happy and in awe in a way. It warmed my heart. —A.P.

Dress by Gucci. Hosiery by Wolford. Earrings by Cartier.

Shirt and pants by Brioni. Bow tie and cummerbund, stylist’s own. Vintage watch by Rolex from Foundwell. Vintage cufflinks by Cartier from Foundwell. Earring, his own.

Age: 35Breakout moment: The Cannes hit Club Kid, which he wrote, directed, and starred in as a party promoter navigating unexpected parenthood.—————

I still do, yeah, at the phone call scene at the end. But it feels very distant from me. I feel like I’m watching it more as an observer now, which is nice, and I feel different than when I made it. I was such an open wound.

Cannes was such an emotional experience. I’m 35, and I’ve always known that I had something to say and I knew how to say it, but I’ve never been given the opportunity. So, honestly, to feel like I was being seen and understood was like 20 years of validation that I didn’t get. And so something shifted, that week, in me. I’ve noticed myself not having to use humor as a shield anymore, as much. I’m less afraid to be vulnerable—and not just in my public life but in my personal life too.

Of course, you shouldn’t need the validation of anyone to feel like you’re worthy, but let’s be real.…

What gagged me this year? I would say, honestly, as a statement of ambition, the Javis’ movie [La Bola Negra]. You marvel at it because you’re like, “How the fuck did they pull this off?” To even want to tell that complex of a story, and to just do it and go balls to the wall, is very inspiring.

I was like, “This is too long. It’s embarrassing now.” —A.P.

Jacket and pants by Canali. Shirt by Amiri. Boots by Alessandro Vasini. Tie by Husbands.

Age: 41Breakout moment: Reporting on how the Steve Ballmer–owned Clippers were allegedly funny with money, on his podcast Pablo Torre Finds Out, leading to one of the most severe team penalties in sports history.—————

Two days ago, I walked into this event that The New York Times was holding…it was like the 175th birthday party [for the paper]. I walk out the elevator and literally the first person I see is [NBA commissioner] Adam Silver. I won’t say exactly what he told me, but the tenor of our conversation was like, This is the HBO series adaptation of what this moment would be.

As a first-generation American—my parents are from the Philippines—there’s always been a dream of mine to be cast as a white person. So…Andrew Garfield, come on. Let’s do this.

The funny part is that I’m not even done reporting this story yet. The federal government is now investigating the Clippers, and so I’m now investigating the government’s investigation in the era of Trump too, which is like its own rabbit hole inside of a rabbit hole, which is fucking wild. But at the same time, it feels like now our number is listed in the phone book…actual other NBA owners are calling me up saying, “Can you look into this?”

It’s hard not to be sappy about this, but the lesson I learned is that if you’re telling the truth, you can walk into any room and feel like that as a suit of armor. Even when the person you’re investigating is one of the 10 richest people in the world. —F.T.

Coat by Michael Kors. Vintage pajamas from Palace Costume Co. Socks by London Sock Company. Glasses by Jacques Marie Mage. Necklaces (throughout), his own.

Age: 37Breakout moments: Stealing scenes as a ’70s Provincetown line cook in the Anthony Bourdain biopic Tony, and his stand-up special Uncle Stav.—————

I just did The Drew Barrymore Show. That experience was so magical. I was so nervous to be around Drew Barrymore. I’ve done a lot of cool shit, and that’s the one where I was like, “I am actually nervous to the point where I’m not a professional. I’m just a stammering little boy who’s with the girl he had a crush on from The Wedding Singer when he was a fat 10-year-old, and I’m trying to keep it together.”

Last week I allowed myself an aimlessly wander around New York City day. Got a little stoned, walked around, stumbled into a movie. Walked along the water on the West Side. Sat down to a little random omakase. Rode a Citi Bike around. I call it the hero’s journey, where you leave your home at, whatever, 11 a.m. ,with just the bare provisions, and you’re not allowed to go home. You just have to keep moving and keep doing stuff.

I filmed this Judd Apatow movie The Comeback King, with Glen Powell, Cristin Milioti, Madelyn Cline. That comes out in February. I’m excited to do stand-up—for fun, not to explicitly work on another hour. I’m excited to go back to clubs and just like, “Can I be the funniest person in this club tonight?” And that’s my only goal.

To be honest with you, the last three years, it’s [been] all go. But you got to have these big years, or else GQ doesn’t talk to you at the end of the year. —A.P.

On Halkias: Jacket and pants by Brooks Brothers. Shirt by Many. Shoes by Louis Vuitton Men’s. Sunglasses by Valention. On Torre: Jacket by Tom Ford. Shirt by Factor’s. Pants by Louis Vuitton Men’s. Shoes by G.H. Bass. Sunglasses by Jacques Marie Mage. Ring, his own.

Shirts and pants by Dunhill. Underwear by Calvin Klein. Earrings (throughout), his own.

Age: 31Breakout moment: Storming the West Coast rap scene with collabs from Pharrell Williams and Tyler, the Creator on his major-label debut album, No Rest for the Wicked.—————

Not like I made it, but I have arrived. We went to Magic City on a Monday for the first time. They were playing the fuck out my records in that motherfucker. The DJ played “Look Like My Mama” in the strip club. You ain’t never heard Tyler, the Creator get played in a strip club. We crossing worlds that’s never been crossed before.

The day before the album came out, we were in Area 29 in Houston, doing our thing. Regular night, it ain’t too packed, throwing money. They tap me on my shoulder like, “My boy want to holler at you.” They take me upstairs to this private section, pull the curtain back…it’s Travis Scott.

It was epic, bro. N-gga came out from behind the curtain like Batman. The light hid half his face. He said, “I fuck with everything you got going on.” We go back down to that section, 15 minutes pass, then one of the owners came and grabbed me: “Look, look, look.” Travis was up there, playing [Chike’s song] “Packed Up.” —F.T.

Shirt by Lu’u Dan. Pants by Valentino. Bracelet by Cartier.

Age: 26Breakout moment: Being a dead ringer for Sly Stallone in I Play Rocky, the film about…Sly Stallone playing Rocky.—————

In the thick of prep. I was training at Gleason’s Gym with Stephan James, who plays Carl Weathers. We were beating the crap out of each other and figuring out how to box. I had gained a bunch of weight, and I was trying to actually cut a few pounds, so I was in those sweatsuits, like a garbage-bag type thing. On the way to the gym, I would listen to Stallone and on the way home.… Everything I could find up to 1980, 1985, every piece of Stallone footage that existed.

I [asked] Seth Rogen, “Dude, how do you handle this stuff?” And he said, “Just go with the flow.” It was such a simple answer, but from somebody like him, I was like, He’s got a good grip on this. The simplicity of it landed.

Philip Seymour Hoffman is one. Chadwick Boseman. Christian Bale, Heath Ledger.

[The first Rocky] is the best movie—but when I was younger, the one that caught my eye was four. Rocky IV is nuts. —F.T.

Jacket by Versace. Shirt by 73London. Pants by Umit Benan. Earring (throughout), his own.

(from l.) On Ambrossi: All clothing by Gucci. Shoes by Christian Louboutin. Pocket square by Brioni. Sunglasses by Ahlem. On Calvo: Jacket, pants, and boots by Tom Ford. Scarf, stylist’s own. Sunglasses by Jacques Marie Mage.

(from l.) On Ambrossi: Jacket and pants by Chanel. Shirt by Factor’s. Shoes by Marsèll. Pin by Cartier. On Calvo: All clothing, tie, and shoes by Ralph Lauren Purple Label. Watch by Cartier.

Ages: Ambrossi, 42 | Calvo, 35Breakout moment: Cowriting and directing La Bola Negra, the gay Spanish historical epic loosely based on an unfinished Federico García Lorca play.——————————————

Javier Ambrossi: Very important. We understood that sometimes people expect LGBTQ+ stories to be niche or for a specific audience. We wanted to do a queer story about universal love.

Ambrossi: It’s a way to put in context how different we are. We change a lot, and the story of our grandparents and our story is very different.

Javier Calvo: What do we do with the freedom our ancestors fought for, and died for?

Calvo: Isabelle Huppert. For me, she’s everything.

Ambrossi: I will go with Julia Roberts. My Best Friend’s Wedding is a very important queer story. The relationship between a woman and a gay man—it was the first time I saw that onscreen. And Rupert Everett was so bold, and I could tell in his eyes that he was gay. I was a kid and I was like, “He’s not faking it.”

How did you celebrate when you won best director at Cannes?

Ambrossi: I put the award on the table and went to sleep. And then Javi came over at 8 a.m.…

Ambrossi: “Give me the award!” And he took it! —A.P.

#6667. A Kitchen in Bloom: Inside Miele’s Lush Botanical Oasis Where Art Meets Design

Step inside Art Basel as visionaries Tiffany Howell and Asher Young merge cutting-edge technology with untamed botanical romance, staging an immersive sensory landscape you don’t just see, but feel.

Miele crafts appliances for enduring performance, but they also curate experiences that engage all the senses. Imagine the intuitive precision of a sleek induction cooktop that subtly adjusts temperature on its own; the soft, inviting glow of a French door refrigerator that reveals a curated bounty within ample space; the alluring aroma of a built-in coffee system greeting you each morning; and the calming, almost meditative hum of a steam at work. Each of these choreographed moments elevate Miele appliances beyond a functional tool into something you fundamentally feel. By blending groundbreaking innovation and sustainable features with timeless, minimalist design, Miele frees you to embrace the pure joy of cooking and to savor the intimate, everyday moments that make a house a true home.

For this year’s Art Basel, the ultimate intersection of culture and creativity, Miele brings together two visionaries to redefine the culinary space. Tiffany Howell of Night Palm Design is passionate about creating cinematic homes that tell a deeply personal story. Asher Young is a multidisciplinary artist known for merging art with technology to create immersive spectacle. Together, they have imagined a sensory kitchen built entirely within a lush botanical garden setting. Here, the wildness of the natural world frames the precise German engineering. It is a space where the smooth, handleless silhouettes and cool touch of Miele's Obsidian Black glass stand in striking relief against their organic surroundings, harnessing technology for a design that is both tactile and state-of-the-art. “We used the sleek, matte black Miele appliances as the driving force to bring this to life,” says Howell of the striking visual contrast between nature and cutting-edge machines. “They’re like the perfect little black dress—timeless, elegant, and grounding the entire room.” A deep respect for the environment is also reflected in Miele engineering, which uses innovative technology that preserves ingredients longer—ensuring that the natural world isn't just an aesthetic inspiration, but a core priority for the brand.

Howell’s signature nostalgic romance blends with Asher’s analytical thinking and knack for creating physical, interactive experiences to make the space come alive. Young's touch ensures the installation feels genuinely dynamic, translating the unseen power of Miele’s technology into a captivating physical experience. “How can we create a space that rebalances and also is a place that you can actually engage with? So you can smell the flowers while you're washing your hand. You can feel the cool breeze as you open the fridge,” explains Young. “All these elements is not just for the sake of a visual presentation, but actually to experience and be inside.” The result is an experiential reminder that kitchens should always reflect your personality and passions. “We both said let’s bring our shared language together,” he recalls. The finished design is the undeniable heartbeat of the garden, a space with one foot rooted elegantly in the past and the other stepping boldly into the future.

“A kitchen expresses how you live, what you love and desire, and it’s also where your most cherished memories are made,” says Howell. As the Miami sun sets, the botanical space seamlessly transitions into an elegant, moody enclave for evening entertaining, inviting you to linger just a little bit longer. And in a Miele kitchen, those memories continue into the next day, beginning the moment the fragrant aroma of freshly brewed coffee announces the limitless possibilities of a brand-new morning.

Experience the convergence of culinary art, design, and innovation firsthand. Explore the full Miele collection and begin designing a kitchen that awakens every sense.

#6666. Area’s Toms Collaboration Is Made for the After-Party

Designer Nicholas Aburn on bringing the brand’s signature sparkle to the humble Toms Alpargata.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

“I love designing a big look,” says Nicholas Aburn, the creative director of the maximalist, party-ready brand Area. “But there’s something to be said for making special things that people can actually wear. I want to make the dress that you had the best night in, that you got laid in, that you went home with your partner for the first time in. It has to be fun and special, but also it has to be normal enough that you actually wear it.”

Aburn, who worked at Demna’s Balenciaga and is now in his second year at Area, carried that idea into the brand’s spring/summer 2027 collection. Amid the razzle-dazzle—crystal-covered looks, sculptural silhouettes, and metallic heels that announced themselves with sound—came a surprise: Toms. The humble shoe, part of a limited-edition collaboration available now, received an Area-sized makeover, with the Alpargata style reimagined through the label’s party-inflected lens.

The limited-edition collection recasts Toms’s cult silhouette in five variations. The Crystal Slit, available in white and black colorways, riffs on Area’s celebrity-favorite jeans of the same name, with crystals diagonally tracing the vamp. Balletcore gets two takes in the ballet flat: one with a statement crystal shoelace bow, the other covered in tonal rhinestones. There’s also something on offer for the minimalist: the Sculpture Alpargata, which features origami-like folds. Toms’s molded footbed and plush insoles lend themselves to all-day (and night) comfort, while the embellishments bring an intentional after-party sparkle.

Aburn is often approached by brands about collaborations, but Toms was an easy yes, even if the two might seem worlds apart. “I think even Toms was surprised that I was up for it,” the designer said. “Some of my colleagues were like, ‘That’s the one you are willing to pull the trigger on?’ But Toms is iconic, it’s American, and I like that it comes from this very casual place.”

That easygoing spirit came through on the runway. The shoes were styled with some of the collection’s more relaxed pieces: ink-splattered shorts, a draped cowl-neck top, and pooling white jeans with feather trim. It’s how Aburn envisions them being worn in real life. “At weddings, everyone takes off their heels and puts on those pass-out flip-flops,” he explains. “I like the idea that you bring the Toms in your bag and throw them on when you’re tired. You still have your dress on, your hair is kind of messy. Everything gets a little cooler at the end of the night.”

Aburn, like many, associates Toms with the “indie sleaze” era, when they were ubiquitous with skinny jeans. (He bought his first pair after seeing Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen wear them.) Now, with Area’s signature embellishments in the mix, Aburn already has a few dream wearers in mind.

“[The] Sculpture, which doesn’t actually have sparkles on it, I would be very excited to see guys in. I’d love to see Jacob Elordi in those. Taylor Swift has been a big supporter of the brand; she’d look great in the Crystal Slit ones. And I’d love to see some cool downtown girl like Ivy Wolk wearing the ballet flats.”

#6662. Farmers Market Salad With Miso Maple Dressing

Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

The farmers market is my biggest hack for solo cooking. Instead of committing to a three-pound bag of carrots, you can buy just one, and choose your produce based on beauty or mere curiosity. That’s how I came up with this fall salad, comprising a single head of Little Gem lettuce and some crunchy produce, including that carrot we mentioned, cucumber, watermelon radish, and an Asian pear. Slicing those elements thinly with a mandoline and throwing them in an ice bath for a brief soak helps keep everything cold and crisp.

The dressing is equally important. I start with Kewpie mayo for its richness and savory depth—it’s made with only egg yolks and contains MSG, giving it a fuller flavor than standard mayonnaise. White miso brings even more umami, while rice vinegar keeps things bright. The result is a creamy finger-licking dressing that clings to every bite. Serve with a fried egg (or your protein of choice) and a piece of fresh bread to scoop up the leftovers. Make a double batch of dressing for dipping crudités or marinating salmon, chicken, or roasted vegetables.

Read More: The Farmers Market Is Built for Solo Cooking

Combine 1 small head of Little Gem or other crunchy lettuce, leaves separated, cut into 2"–3" pieces, 1 rainbow carrot, peeled, very thinly sliced lengthwise into ribbons with a mandoline or vegetable peeler, 1 Persian cucumber, thinly sliced, preferably with a mandoline, ½ small watermelon radish, peeled, halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, and ¼ medium Asian pear, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, in a large bowl of ice water. Let soak 10–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 2 Tbsp. seasoned rice vinegar, 2 Tbsp. white miso, 2 tsp. Kewpie mayonnaise, 2 tsp. pure maple syrup, and 1 tsp. toasted sesame oil in a small bowl until smooth and emulsified (or combine in a small glass jar, cover, and shake). Taste dressing and season with kosher salt.

Drain vegetables and run through a salad spinner or pat dry with a kitchen towel to remove excess water. Wipe out large bowl, return vegetables to bowl, and drizzle 2 Tbsp. dressing over. Toss, adding more dressing as needed, until evenly coated (reserve any remaining dressing for another use).

Transfer salad to a shallow bowl or rimmed plate. Top with a fried egg and serve with country-style bread if desired.

Do Ahead: Dressing can be made up to 3 days ahead. Cover and chill.

#6661. ‘Wanted’ Stars Solea Pfeiffer and Liisi LaFontaine on Their Long and Winding Road to Broadway

Solea Pfeiffer and Liisi LaFontaine have been waiting to get Wanted to Broadway since 2018. Back then, the rollicking Broadway musical, which opened Sunday at the James Earl Jones Theatre, was slowly being developed from Angelica Chéri and Ross Baum’s grad school thesis. Though LaFontaine had broken out as Deena in the West End premiere of Dreamgirls two years earlier, as Pfeiffer reminds her, she was intimidated to be costarring with someone hot off the original Hamilton tour.

“Then on our first day of rehearsal, our voices blended like crazy and we had the same sense of humor,” LaFontaine remembers. “I was like, This is going to be my first New York friend.”

Their voices still soar divinely when combined—this is probably the best-sung show on Broadway right now—but the intervening eight years have been as winding as the musical’s inspiration: Chéri’s family lore that her great-great-aunts Mary and Martha Clarke were able to pass as white in Reconstruction-era Texas and might have gotten into some outlaw hijinks.

Wanted has gone through its own transformations, from a title change (it was formerly Gun & Powder) to significant retooling across two different stagings, starring either Pfeiffer or LaFontaine—never together. And the theater landscape itself has completely changed since the pandemic, in ways good and bad. What’s stayed firm is the remarkable talent of these leading ladies, whom time and hard-earned opportunities have made young industry veterans.

A few days before their big night, Pfeiffer and LaFontaine got together to discuss the show’s evolution and how significant it is for them to lead an original musical as performers who, like their characters, are mixed race.

Vogue: Does it feel like you’re in a different industry now from the one you walked into?

Solea Pfeiffer: There’s kind of a shift happening in the industry right now. A lot of development is starting in London before it comes here—a lot of shifting in the gestation process of musical theater at the moment. It’s strange. This season, this moment on Broadway…. I think we’re going to learn a lot about the state of the art in the next few months. There’s so much Black art that’s happening all over New York, and at the same time producers and the discourse are saying, “Broadway is dying, Broadway’s so alive, we’re grossing more than ever.” There are so many statements out in the ether about the state of musical theater and whether it’s doable or profitable or worth it. Depending on how this season goes, I think we’re gonna learn a lot about who’s right about what.

Liisi LaFontaine: The stakes in everything just feel higher. I think we’re all still processing and unpacking the pandemic—and sometimes I can’t believe we have phrases like pre-COVID in our vocabulary. So much has changed, and the need for art and live entertainment has also changed. I think, right now, what we do is genuinely vital to the health of the country, giving people a space to go and feel something.

Pfeiffer: I think making art during a second Trump term feels pretty different. It feels strange to be doing “frivolous art” right now. Wanted is this combination of escapism and a very galvanizing statement about getting out in the world and remembering that freedom is not free. It feels amazing to be part of a show that is platforming such Black excellence and saying, “Look at America.” This little microcosm of a story is the blueprint for a lot of what we are experiencing.

The show hits all of these ideas without ever feeling like homework. I keep telling people that it just feels like a big old musical.

Pfeiffer: One of the first book musicals was Show Boat, which dealt with the exact same themes: a woman who is passing during the Reconstruction era. This is kind of the modern, centennial answer to all the questions raised by Show Boat [which premiered in 1927]. It’s just true to the form—this American story in this American art form—and it’s not pretending to be anything besides a big old musical. At the same time we get to really dissect these American traditions of assimilation and sacrifice. It feels like we’re contributing to the canon.

The show’s been in development for so many years. How have conversations around race changed in the room?

LaFontaine: Oh my God, the reckonings. I think the best part is that our writer is a Black woman, so naturally the conversations will be different than if it was anyone else in that lead role, a little more sensitive. Having a Black woman tell a story that is specifically true about her family, having a Black director [Stevie Walker-Webb], mixed race people starring in the show, our choreographer [Chelsey Arce] is mixed race…. It’s a very brown room, a very female-heavy room, and all the men in the room are very receptive. A lot of the men that we’re around these days, we say they feel like they’ve been written by women.

Solea and I have learned how to talk about our race and things we never even realized we needed to talk about. Last night at the stage door, we met a woman in her 50s who is mixed race. She was crying to us, talking about how complicated it is, how each generation, older and older, had less and less language. Us ’90s babies were born in this golden era where it was like, America’s on the up and up and race? We’ve never even heard of her. Obama’s coming. But I think about the Mariah Careys and the generations above us who had to either hide their Blackness or completely assimilate into one side or the other.

Pfeiffer: Miscegenation was literally a crime during our parents’ lifetime. Doing the show in 2018 and 2020, I remember it felt like an important development in feeling whole as a mixed person and that I didn’t have to dissect myself to make sense of myself. Now, as we’re seeing people have their citizenship questioned in the street based on look alone, there’s something really important about naming American whiteness. The Reconstruction era is when this American identity of whiteness was codified into law. Now, we have slave catchers in the streets doing this again—it’s like the American playbook. It’s nothing new, and we don’t get taught this, or it’s getting written out. That’s what I think is so exciting about telling this story in 2026. All the roadblocks that pushed our timeline of getting the show to Broadway…. Like, Oh my gosh. But we get to do it now. We get to say something not just for the Black experience but for anyone who doesn’t fit into that clear “American identity.”

You’ve both spoken about how meaningful it’s been to work on a show that acknowledges your own mixed race identities. Has that been a grounding experience?

LaFontaine: This is the first time I’ve played a specifically mixed race person. Any other time it’s been kind of open to interpretation. Dreamgirls is a very Black show. In Moulin Rouge!, I was considered the first Black Satine. There’s always this feeling of leaning into one side or the other, dependent on how people perceive you. I feel, in my adult life, there’s even less language for being mixed. As a kid, my parents made up words to help us identify ourselves and it felt a lot more like there was space for both. But as I entered the real world, I was like, Okay, I’m just—I am a Black woman. It’s the one-drop rule: If you look Black, if you have a Black parent, then you are Black. And I’m down for it. I love being Black, but there is an erasure that happens to half of you. My dad’s white, my mom’s Black, and he passed when I was 14, so I really only had my Black parent around for my whole adult life. I didn’t realize how much I needed something like this to be able to fully self-realize.

It’s making me feel like a whole person instead of someone who’s been fragmented down into what makes the most sense. It is incredibly grounding and really special. It’s amazing to meet other mixed race girls at the stage door who say, “This really got me.” Even if certain things aren’t being said, certain conversations we wish we could lean into a little bit more…. Just seeing it on stage, there’s so much that makes people see themselves. I think for anyone with a biracial heritage, there’s a very complex feeling of, Where do I fit in? The show asks that question over and over and allows us to find the answers. Being inside of it for so many years, it’s been amazing and complicated and hard sometimes, like maybe I want to stop thinking about this a little bit. But it’s really special to be able to play myself fully.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

#6660. Spiced Beef Baked Potatoes

Baked potatoes may not seem like a dish that requires much technique, but there’s a difference between a good baked potato and a great one. Wrapping them in foil can lead to a tender interior but render the skin too soft. For the most crisp skin, bake them right on the oven grate at quite a high temperature. (To make it taste almost like a potato chip, rub those scrubbed russets with vegetable oil and season with plenty of salt.) Shockingly, this doesn’t prevent a fluffy interior—that comes down to the internal temperature reaching at least 212°. Sure, it may seem strange to take your potato’s temperature, but it’s a fail-safe route to the most enjoyable potato.

Some, including the Idaho Potato Commission, swear that the way a baked potato is opened affects the texture, eschewing a knife for a fork to gently poke a plus sign into the surface. Others, like beloved food writer Nigel Slater, prefer to strike the potato as though it were part of a martial arts competition. “Bring your hand down fast and sharp as if you were doing a karate chop but only hard enough to crack open the potato skin,” he writes in a piece for The Guardian. (Whether or not to attempt this feat is literally in the hands of the potato-baker.) We found a single fork-pricked line down the length of the spud is the most effective.

Once opened, a baked potato can be filled with anything from tuna salad to cheesy baked beans. Here, it’s a picadillo-inspired mixture with ground beef (packed with protein, iron, and creatine—though ground turkey or chicken work nicely too) adorned with golden raisins and stuffed olives. A spicy tomato sauce will slowly soak into the potato, further seasoning it with every passing minute. Make sure to use a chili powder that’s a mix of spices like chiles, cumin, oregano, garlic (not just dried ground chiles).

Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares feel-good recipes for any day of the week. Read more: White Potatoes Are Not Empty Calories. They’re Actually Great for You.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 425°. Prick 4 large russet potatoes (about 10 oz. each), scrubbed, patted dry, all over with a fork, then rub all over with 1 Tbsp. vegetable oil and sprinkle with 1¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Bake directly on oven rack until skins are crisp and flesh is very soft (an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center should register 212°–220°), 55–75 minutes. (If thermometer registers 210° before beef mixture is finished, turn off oven and leave potatoes inside until ready to use.)

Meanwhile, pick enough leaves from ½ bunch cilantro (about 2 oz.) to measure ½ cup; set aside for serving. Finely chop remaining leaves and all of stems (you should have about ¾ cup); set aside separately.

Heat remaining 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium. Add 1 medium red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 5 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is softened, 8–10 minutes. Add ¼ cup double-concentrated tomato paste and cook, stirring constantly, until deepened in color and slightly tacky, about 2 minutes.

Increase heat to medium-high. Add 1 lb. ground beef, 2 Tbsp. chili powder, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Cook, stirring and smashing often with a heatproof rubber spatula to break up meat, until cooked through, about 4 minutes.

Reduce heat to low. Add ½ cup golden raisins, ¼ cup sliced pimiento-stuffed green olives, reserved chopped cilantro, and 1 cup water. Cook, stirring occasionally, until sauce thickens slightly and flavors come together, 8–12 minutes. Taste beef mixture and season with more salt if needed. Remove from heat and cover. Let sit until ready to use.

Transfer potatoes to a platter or plates and let cool 5 minutes. Using a fork, prick a 3"–4"-long line in the center down length of each potato, leaving 1" unpricked on each end. Using your hands, firmly press ends down toward platter to split potatoes open. Smash flesh as desired, then season inside of potatoes with salt. Divide beef mixture among potatoes and top with reserved cilantro leaves.

#6657. All the Gifts GQ Editors Want This Holiday Season 2026

As the desk at GQ that handles all things shopping, the GQ Recommends team has developed a rather motley assortment of wants, needs, and highly specific desires. We have good taste, if I may say as much, and no shortage of opinions about what makes a thing worth owning. So this holiday season, I asked everyone to set aside the usual assignments and show me what's on their own wishlists. What follows is an eclectic grab bag of A1 gifts, straight from the folks who spend all year finding the good stuff.

Still got names to cross off? Peruse our gift guides and sign up for the GQ Recommends newsletter for more good stuff worth giving (or keeping).

Years after getting married, I can say with confidence that the best thing about marriage is my wife. But a close second is the set of Sabre Bistrot flatware we received off our registry. A pleasure to hold and behold. And now they make chopsticks, which is unfortunate news for someone afflicted with my particular strain of completism. I have no choice but to finish the set. —MN

I couldn’t in good conscience ask for everything I want from Camiel Fortgens, which is, uh, everything. But this heavy-knit beanie, with the melange yarn and signature raw edges, feels like a reasonable place to start. —MN

It's true, the best radio station on the internet deserves its own hardware. Made in collaboration with tech company Atonemo, this dedicated player has big, tactile buttons for tuning into NTS 1 and 2, a dial for wandering through the Infinite Mixtapes, and the ability to plug straight into my amp. I feel so alive, and I've never been more excited to turn a dial. —MN

Nosying around other people’s bookshelves is a favorite pastime, and I can think of only a few libraries I’d rather rifle through than Luis Barragan’s. I’ve made the pilgrimage to his home and studio in Mexico City, and this new book offers a new look at the peerless architect’s life and influences through the personal collection he kept on his shelves. —MN

You may already know that we love Lady White’s top-tier white T-shirts, but we’re also massive fans of their sweats, especially this superweight hoodie. And when they say superweight, they mean it. I’ve own the zip-up version, and it's basically a winter coat. This will become my dog-walking hoodie, my 6 A.M. stroll to the bodega hoodie, and the late-night walk back from the cinema hoodie. —JB

Back in high school, some homies and I thought of ourselves as future producers. The music was terrible and thankfully is lost in the ether somewhere on SoundCloud, but despite those early attempts, I still find sampling a fascinating part of music. It’s a way to shut off the brain and think about songs in a new way. I doubt the music will be any better than it was back in the day, but I’ll have fun acting like Jamie XX or Nicolas Jaar, at least. —JB

I’m a pen-and-paper guy. You will often catch me feverishly jotting down thoughts in the middle of a meeting. I’ve recently needed to retire my old Moleskine notebook and found myself doing a deep dive into reusable leather-bound book holders that you can treat like a modular journal. You can add in different types of notebooks, calendars, and daily planners—the possibilities are endless. —JB

There comes a time in every man's life when he fancies himself a barista and thinks he should dedicate some time to learning how to pull a damn good espresso. I am that man, and the delusions are more errant than you would expect. Because I drink so much coffee, I’ve convinced myself I might as well get good at making it. —JB

As much as I don’t want to admit that I overindex on outerwear, my closet tells the truth. It’s so full that I can’t even shift any of the hangers without taking one of them out first. But that won’t stop me from eyeing this gorgeous coat from Auralee. It’s everything I want in a coat: dramatically long, artfully faded, and a deep black colorway. Now I’ll just have to find a new coat rack. —GO

I saw this bad boy in a shop and was so drawn to it. The colors are just right, the size is great, and the material is ultra-sturdy, but on this day, the devil on my shoulder told me not to get it that day. I came to my senses and came back the next day only to find that the tote was sold out. Hence why I’ve got it on my wish list because I believe in second chances and miracles. —GO

This little thing is a clever ear warmer that can be worn as is or can be slipped over the bill of your favorite hat. It’s silly and weird and cool and totally unnecessary. And yet, I would not be mad if this made its way into my stocking. —GO

I’ve always wanted a true Neapolitan-style jacket and getting to try on some of Natalino’s pieces in person during a pop-up in NYC has only stoked the fire. From the hand-stitched entails to the soft shoulders to the absolutely supreme fit, there’s no better jacket in my mind. —GO

No, I am not a ne'er-do-well Italian playboy loath to step into a leadership position at my dad's sprawling imports company. Yes, I would like to dress like one. —AG

Leave it to the vintage fiends in Japan to turn up a version of JCPenney’s canonical Big Mac flannel—the greatest flannel ever made, FYI—that might actually be worth the asking price. —AG

Okay, okay, okay. Once the sticker shock has worn off, think about how good of a boy I’ve been this year… —AG

You could drop $100K on leg-lengthening surgery and then rebuild your jeans rotation from scratch. Or you could just buy La Botte Gardiane’s naturally height-enhancing boots, which look great with the jeans you already own. —AG

I used to question whether the Eadem hype was another fad born of bloated influencer budgets, but dude. This balm is legit. I want every single color. You should get this for your girl for the holidays. If you’re scared of picking colors for her, opt for “Butter Mochi” (clear! unscented!) or “Sakura Shaved Ice,” a light pink that complements nearly every lip combo under the sun. —MH

I was treating my guy to his first ever foray into Buck Mason when I clocked a store employee wearing the Roper Jean and immediately lost the plot RE: which T-shirt the boy was trying on next. The silhouette! The wash! The contrast stitching! The complimentary Buck Mason tailoring for my stubby little legs! A girl can dream. A girl is still dreaming. Someone please gift this to me. —MH

Confessions of an adult seasonal allergies sufferer: I open the windows to air out my apartment despite knowing that that’s just welcoming the allergens into my home. Practical people might say I should address the issue at the root, but where’s the whimsy in that? Wouldn’t capitalism prefer that I purchase a solution to my problem instead? —MH

It took only one year at GQ and one “welcome to the team” bottle of D.S.&Durga to turn me into a fragrance fiend. For my bank account’s sake, I made a No New Fragrances vow earlier this summer … but gifts don’t count as breaking that pledge. Also, I really need a winter scent; my beloved Eau Splendide is more of a summer gal. —MH

I already own a bottle of Naked Dance, and it’s dangerously close to empty, which is the highest compliment I can give a fragrance. Well, the second highest. The first is how often I’m asked what fragrance I’m wearing, and I’m not ready to give that up. It’s a cult pick from a tiny niche house, right down to the cap, which is handmade from wood scraps and resin, exactly the kind of detail I can’t resist. —AH

I’m a vintage obsessive at heart, and this bracelet has that worn-in, one-of-a-kind look I’m always drawn to. Pyrite is also known as fool’s gold, and frankly, I’d be a fool not to want it. —AH

A good belt is the most underrated piece in any outfit, and my studded belt collection could always use one more. I’ve reached the point where I pick my outfits around my belts, not the other way around, and this one already has a few looks planned. The most practical gift on my list? I think so. —AH

All fall I’ve been hunting for the perfect pair of cords, mostly because I’m notorious for wearing the same pants almost every day. These feel like they walked straight out of a ’70s record sleeve, with that soft, slouchy fit. They’d slot into my current wardrobe perfectly, and finally give my usual pair a break. —AH

I love a gift you can give and secretly steal for yourself. This bathrobe is a “thoughtfu” gift for your partner that you’ll get to commandeer when they’re not looking. Two for the price of one really. You’re welcome! —LP

It’s a cliché, but the best gifts are the ones you wouldn’t buy for yourself but desperately want. And who doesn’t want a chic, soft, luxurious, well-designed towel? No one, is the answer. Tekla has a knack for unexpected color combinations that should feel wrong but somehow feel so right (this pink and brown combo is excellent)—a mood booster for any bathroom. Oh, and they’re unisex, making them a handy option when you have a last-minute gift to give. —LP

There is a myth that shower gel, or “smellies” as we call them in the UK (I’m British), are thoughtless gifts. I disagree. A luxury shower gel will add a little something extra to your morning routine, or someone else’s, and is a crowd pleaser for secret santa. This specific wash I can attest also smells incredible. —LP

Last holiday season, I treated my mother to a pair of Jenni Kayne cashmere socks. Since then, she’s never looked back and now has an expectation that Christmas = cashmere. She deserves it, so I’m happy to oblige (I may as well buy myself a pair at the checkout whilst I’m at it). They make a great gift for anyone who loves a cozy weekend at home or wants something luxurious to slip into after a day of hiking or skiing (my personal favourite time to treat my feet). —LP

A couple of decades ago, Helmut Lang was the place to go for a more city-minded denim jacket. And while those pieces still do numbers on the second-hand market, I’ve always found them a touch too fitted. So imagine my relief to discover this roomier Kaptain Sunshine take, which still feels special (and office-appropriate) due to its pleats, dark color, and smart single pocket. —LC

As a teenager, I was completely taken by this scent. Then, throughout my twenties, I tried all of the nicher body washes I thought I was meant to like. The ones that smelled like herb gardens, cedar forests, or sometimes… nothing at all. But following a recent, delayed flight-induced spin around Duty Free, I was reunited with Re-Charge Black Pepper. Please, kind gifters, reunite me with even more of it. —LC

Not just a stunning book about jazz and America in the 1960s, but also hundreds of pages of incredible style. I’m hoping to deepen my understanding of the music over the holidays, and know it would only help to be leafing through this as I do so. —LC

As with the Molton Brown above, I’m done surveying the market: I feel my best in these! And I’d wager the men (and women) in your life likely do too. —LC

Genetics haven’t exactly done some of us any favors in the under-eye department (me, I'm talking about me), but this eye cream levels the playing field. It works beautifully for me, and it’s exactly the kind of splurge that makes a great gift. —EH

Experiment is one of the most exciting skincare brands I’ve come across lately, with a thoughtfully edited lineup that doesn’t try to do too much. Its new mini set is a great introduction, featuring what I think is an underrated ingredient: glycerin. It helps skin hold onto moisture, which is exactly what my thirsty skin craves in these drier times. —EH

Vitaly has been on my radar for years, and I’ve had my eye on more than few of its chains and rings. It just launched an Art Deco line, which is a glorious mix of classic style and signature industrial Vitaly edge. While a lot of the larger statement pieces are on my wishlist, the Tier Chain feels like a daily driver and a statement piece at the same time. —EH

Once we get through the joyfully chaotic holidays, the new year calls for rest and relaxation. While cozy socks and a soft throw are always welcome gifts, this blanket feels like an ultimate upgrade. Weighted for gentle relaxing pressure and heated for warmth even in the chilliest rooms. Sounds like a recipe for the sweetest of dreams! —EH

#6656. Three Prada Obsessives Unpack Miuccia’s Defining Decade

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Bazaar’s Lynette Nylander and Camille Freestone join Laia Garcia-Furtado for a roundtable on her new book, Prada in the Nineties

Prada is as much an adjective as it is a noun. My colleagues and I often describe wardrobe twists, like a bejeweled brooch on a Peter Pan collar or an embroidered sock peeking out of a Mary Jane, as “very Prada.” But what is it about these little notes of character that signals “Prada” in our brain?

That’s one of the questions Bazaar’s deputy culture director, Laia Garcia-Furtado, answers in her new book, Prada in the Nineties. (Published by Batsford, it drops today.) Her deep dive into one of the brand’s most pivotal decades reaches far beyond the heroin-chic label we tend to slap on ’90s fashion. From runway reviews to cultural anecdotes, Garcia-Furtado takes us backstage, into the life and personality of Miuccia Prada, the industry’s north star of intellectual fashion.

Mrs. Prada’s arsenal of off-color prints and skirts have inspired generations of women to aspire to an ugly-chic kind of cool; looking at her today, it’s easy to find ourselves lost in her world. But in harkening back to the nascent stages of her career as a designer, Garcia-Furtado reminds us that the throughline of her genius lies in her sense of self.

It’s a story that began with nylon, an unexpected choice for a member of the Prada family, with its legacy of selling bespoke leather goods to royal clientele. Yet Mrs. Prada’s choice to bring nylon totes and duffels to the luxury market was not merely driven by rebellion—it was a manifestation of her own desire for a well-designed bag that embraced utility. And the groundbreaking success of the bags demonstrated that her dreams were shared by other women—a hint of where Prada would take the brand.

Garcia-Furtado understands this lore firsthand. After all, she’s spent a lot of time in Mrs. Prada’s shoes—well, the ones she designed, at least. She began building her own archive of Miuccia merch in college with a pair of woven leather Mary Janes by Prada’s little sister, Miu Miu. A lucky eBay find from the spring 2001 collection, they were marked by interlaced checks of leather with pops of plum purple and canvas buckle straps. She has continued to build her collection ever since.

Writing the book gave Garcia-Furtado carte blanche to dig into the nitty-gritty details that unite women of varying tastes and lifestyles as proud members of Prada’s hive. Below, she gathers with Bazaar’s fellow Prada obsessees, executive digital director Lynette Nylander and senior fashion writer Camille Freestone, to unpack all the things that have placed Mrs. Prada in a league of her own, from the ’90s to now.

Prada in the Ninteties by Laia Garcia-Furtado

Jennifer Jenkins: What inspired you to go on such a deep dive on Miuccia Prada?

Laia Garcia-Furtado: There are very specific images that we go to when we think of Prada in the ’90s, but all of those collections are from the late ’90s. So I thought, "Wait, what about the early '90s?" When I started looking up those collections, I realized that what I was really doing was tracing how Prada went from almost an independent, fledgling designer to an icon in a period of ten years, which is really crazy. I love to go down a research hole; that's actually my favorite thing. It was just great to have an excuse.

Lynette Nylander: One of the things that struck me about going through Laia’s book, and my own personal understanding of Prada in the '90s, is that it was really foundational. A lot of the signatures and markers of what Prada is today were made in that formative time. One of my favorite things about being part of the Prada hive—and I think we all identify as that—is that she has carefully constructed a brand where you can mine from its past. She's very okay with the idea that something is a rehashed idea from a '90s collection in the 2000s, in the 2010s, in the 2020s. Everything is meant to be in dialogue with everything else. That's really refreshing in a world where designers are making very distinct collections and basically almost asking you to do away with whatever you bought last year and buy into what's “now.” She very much respects the past, which is why I think a book on the '90s is brilliant.

Camille Freestone: Also, the designs are so pared back. We think now of much more heavy-handed embellishment when we imagine Prada. Part of it was that it was the '90s and it was just a simpler time. Runways have just gotten more megawatt altogether. But the Prada collections are quite pure. The design is quite simple in the best way, so they let her creative touches shine in such a way that feels very present.

LGF: I mean everything old is new, et cetera. Going back to what you were saying about the simple shapes, even when things are heavily embellished and there's a lot of beading and sequins, it never feels like putting on a bunch of stuff for the sake of putting on a bunch of stuff. Even if it's super over-the-top, you think, “It's exactly what it needs to be.” It feels very real. One of my favorite things I read while I was doing research is a quote where she's saying how in movies and in art, you're allowed to bring in real life and it's allowed to be ugly and regular, but fashion was a place where you weren't allowed to do that, and she wanted to change that. When I read that, everything from those old collections made so much sense.

But even now, I think you can read a collection, even if she and Raf are saying that it's about one thing, and you look at it, you're like, "It's really about something else."

LN: Yeah, and that's always been a part of that duality. And I mean, even in the inception of Miu Miu, she talks about it as this other side of her personality. She's someone who is really in dialogue with her more fantastical, imagined self. And I think what was interesting about going through the '90s collections was that it was fantastical, but again, more real.

But I want to talk about what you learned. They always say hindsight is 20/20, but I don't think we were lucky enough to understand what a unique time the ‘90s were. It was pre-social-media. Celebrity culture had hit this apex, and Miuccia was there as this brand that carried and collected a lot of celebrity in a way that is not how it is now.

LGF: It wasn’t grody! And I think that was especially evident when she launched menswear, and John Malkovich was her model or Willem Dafoe—I mean, now we all love Willem Dafoe, of course, but it was very different from what everyone else was doing.

And another thing that's really interesting is that we have a vision of the ’90s, but the first couple of years of the ‘90s are still the ’80s. It takes years for the prevailing aesthetic that we all remember to rise up. Going back, Prada was a heritage label, but she launched ready-to-wear in the late ‘80s. And it wasn't like when Vuitton launched ready-to-wear, when everybody understood it as a major brand. Prada was by no means in its flop era, but it wasn’t as well known as Vuitton. It was not the same.

So when she started, critics were writing things like “Prada also showed a collection.” There wasn't even a long review. And then she sort of started getting talked about in the same breath as Martin Margiela or Ann Demeulemeester, like, “These people are the plucky new designers.” We think she's so untouchable now and it's like she almost can do no wrong, but you can go back and see how it all started and see her be like, "I hated this collection actually, and I'll never do that again." I mean, my kingdom for any designer that would say that now—to just be that honest.

JJ: You touched a lot on her unapologetic way of expressing herself, even while taking in different cultural references and touchpoints. Was there anything in particular you were most surprised to learn about her?

LGF: My favorite trivia is that she got married on Valentine's Day.

LGF: She's a romantic. I feel like that says so much.

CF: It's amazing. She was in the Communist Party of Italy, and so not of the fashion world at all, but so endlessly fascinated by it.

LGF: It's so funny because it's very much like her parents said, "Okay, you've had your fun. Now, come back home, join the family business.” And she wanted to be an actor—the mime thing! In one interview, she said, "My favorite part was when we had to do really specific body control stuff." And you can totally see her just being so good at that.

LN: Well, I think that she's so good at it because I can't think of a designer, at least in more modern history, that really sort of mines from herself. Have you ever noticed, if you read a part of a review, or you’ve seen those videos of her backstage, it's never like, "I was looking at the art of Georgia O’Keeffe”?

LN: She doesn't even mine it from a place. She isn't even saying, "Oh, I was walking down the piazza in Milan." It's not about that—it's this higher sense of self. I think about the fall/winter 2026 collection, with Bella Hadid and the four rounds of looks. And of course she did that because she's the only person who would do that, because those are the things that ticktock around in the caverns of her mind when we're all fast asleep.

CF: Well, she's oddly practical. She's kind of utilitarian. And I think now I'm just saying a different thing in different words, but you think of a crystal embellishment when you think of Prada, you think of a quirk, but it's all rooted in a really utilitarian approach. I feel like this is clothing, not art.

LGF: It's also because that's how she dresses. I mean, yes, are her high heels too high for us to walk and not get blisters? Yes, but we still wear them. It's fine. But she designs clothes that she wants to wear, and we always look at what she's wearing at the end of the show to see how she's styling.

LN: She's the model that we're looking for at the end of the show.

CF: Then it's funny to put her back in dialogue with a Martin Margiela; they both were subversive in their own ways, but hers was lensed through an idea that these are just clothes. You need to get dressed in them!

LGF: There is something about the two of them. Margiela never wanted to be interviewed, but when you look back at a lot of the profiles of her, there will be editorials where it's designers with their muses, and she's almost always by herself. She's her own muse.

It's just her. It's like her looking in a mirror. It's her and her son, or it's her by herself, but it's such a clear vision. And I mean, I think it also makes a difference because a lot of the male designers need a muse…but for her, it's always her.

CF: I'm also always fascinated by the “designer uniform.” There are so many examples. Phoebe Philo, Michael Kors, Jonathan Anderson: everyone takes their bow, and it's almost like they're the antithesis of their clothes. So obviously, we are always talking about a woman designing for women, but in that particular context of those big houses, she's one of the few who is just dressing just like her collection.

LGF: And it's amazing the few times she's come out wearing pants.

LGF: It's so rare! You're like, "Oh my god, the slim cigarette.”

LN: I have two things I want to say to the idea that she doesn't really have a muse. The muse is herself, but somehow that doesn't come across as arrogant. It's not the opposite. It comes across as, “I just do what I know I’ll respond to and hopefully other people like it.” And I think there's something really earnest about it.

CF: There's also no ideal of the perfect woman, either.

LN: Yes, in fact, I don't think she even really deals or trades in ideals.

I also want to talk about the colors. I mean, if I think about Prada, I just think about this kaleidoscopic universe of color. She can go anywhere. She can put any color combination together. It's kind of genius. But particularly in the '90s… they're all quite muted. You have this line from Robin Givhan in the book, “The greens hovered somewhere between shades of slime and mold. The browns were”—I mean, this is the beauty of the Robin Givhan written line—“the browns were murky, the color of water as it stagnates over a long, steamy summer. The dizzy and crisscross patterns were reminiscent of UHF static or an old-fashioned labyrinth in rusted plumbing.”

LGF: It's funny though because Miuccia Prada hated all of those collections.

LN: I think if there was ever going to be a brand that's going to respect the fact that Robin Givhan ripped her to shreds, it's going to be her. I think she believes in the idea of free thought, and that was Givhan’s thought and put so beautifully.

But I do want to talk about the colors, because I just think it's so specific of how I think about Prada, but also how I think about my own relationship to color. I don't know if you feel like that, but probably in an inadvertent way, she has given me the confidence and the permission to put together these really disparate color combinations.

LGF: I mean, I think that collection that Robin is talking about, from spring ’96 (which is the root cause of my everything; I had a slime green room—I love slime green) is really interesting. Even before she got into the cool color combinations that we know her from, those early '90s collections, even when it was like, “Here's a bunch of beautiful white dresses,” suddenly there would be weird goldenrod silk and a weird orange. The color thing was always there from the beginning. And when you look at the collections throughout the years, you see how she gets a little bit more confident in that and starts mixing it. But that punch of weirdness was present from the beginning.

CF: But somehow, I think, "Why do I like this slime shade? Why do I like this brown? Why do I like this purple?" But all of a sudden, she's made me want purple.

LN: I hate purple in any other context than hers—I need purple.

CF: All of a sudden I want purple. And there's these weird plaids that all of a sudden make me think, "Oh, I need that."

LGF: Also, in the late '90s, she does collections with things embellished with mirrors, and she was like, "Well, everyone is being a hippie and doing this, so I also did it,” but she did it extra crazy. And I love when she is engaging.

Going back to what you said about her being probably one of the few designers that is like, "This review panned me, it's fine,” I feel like she really was engaging with what was being written about her.

One season editors were like, "There are no suits. This is outrageous! Where are all the suits?" So then the next season she opened the collection with a suit and it's very like, "You're welcome. Are you happy now?” I like to see her engage, not that she doesn't do that anymore, but I think in the ’90s, it was a little bit more obvious.

LN: And now she kind of hovers above it all. I want to talk about 1998. Her ascent was complete, you say, in 1998, when she was now at over a half a billion dollars in sales. She landed at 15 in Vogue’s list of the most influential brands. Other women at the top 20 were Donna Karan, Angela Missoni, and Mariuccia Mandelli, and Miuccia is one of the only working designers left. What was happening in 1998, and what collection is that?

LGF: It's the one with the cool red-and-white boots that are space-age. It's all very space-age mod. ‘98 is the time when she went all-in on the millennial aesthetic that everyone was into, when she did her sports thing.

CF: I also think she doesn't deal very much in volume. That's not really her game.

LN: Thank god. I don't know if I'd want a poofy Prada.

LGF: Yeah. But it's so crazy—in a decade you go from reviews that say, "Oh, Prada also showed a collection," to, "Everyone is focused on whatever she does."

LGF: I think she just became more confident in her vision, which was different from everyone else. And I mean, Tom Ford was also doing something at Gucci; there was that vibe shift, and she was part of it, but it was different. From the beginning, she was always the thinking woman's sex-appeal designer, and that just stayed. She was very in tune with the culture, but she wasn't just doing reproductions of what you could see. She was injecting it with her own aesthetic.

You can look at something and say, "Oh, this was her way of doing grunge," but it was not grunge. It was her own thing.

LN: What was that thing? I mean, do you look at broader context and get a sense of the music she listens to or the boys she kissed or the movies she liked?

LGF: Yeah, I think it's very much a movies thing. I feel like you get a sense of her upbringing. The Mary Jane—the shoes she wore as a little girl—were always a thing. She got married in a dress and a coat made by a childrenswear designer. The little socks—you start seeing those reflections of her life, and they're more apparent the more that you know her, but I don't think it's the kind of thing where you need to know what it is in order to like it. And I think there is something about it where it's for grown women. Young people also like it, but her clothes are not clothes for young teen girls.

LN: Was that also something you learned from your research?

LGF: I mean, technically, I think Miu Miu was supposed to be the younger brand, and the vibe did feel a little bit younger, but Prada always felt a little bit adult. Even when you look at the suits or the proper little silk dresses, you're like, "These are clothes for adults."

CF: I feel like that's also where the styling sneaks in. You’ll see the childlike Mary Jane with the suit and maybe one little brooch or something that is so subtle…but it's not hitting you over the head.

LGF: Yeah, because I think there's also a thing where you always look up to something. You know how you read Seventeen magazine when you're 12? And I think there is something about Prada where no matter how old you are, it still feels just beyond where you currently are.

LN: Every time I buy a piece, it still feels, in a weird way, unattainable, or I question if I'm mature or smart or cool enough.

LGF: And then you look in the mirror, and it feels like it feels exactly where you should be.

CF: It is like, "Am I a woman? Am I a glamorous woman?"

LN: Yeah. Maybe it's just because we think about her so much as the likeness of that.

CF: Well, we have made her the ideal almost. She is the one to be judged against, for so many people, but then that makes it hard to articulate what she actually is.

LGF: But even her glamour—there is something attainable about it. She doesn't wear crazy makeup, and she doesn't style her hair in any kind of way. It's just her holding her little scarf, and you think, "I need a scarf to hold!" Going back to her interest in real life, it's just so her. And who doesn't want to just be like themselves? You want to be her, but you really just want to be you.

#6655. Chic, Thoughtful Gifts That Will Delight the Woman Who Has Everything

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Spoil her with little luxuries she didn’t know she needed.

Shopping for the maximalist woman can feel trickier than shopping for anyone else on your list. Her beauty routine is set, her wardrobe is filled with pieces she adores, and her home is precisely curated. So how do you surprise someone who seems to have it all? As a maximalist with a circle of fellow maximalists, I’ve taken the guesswork out of it and rounded up presents she’ll be delighted to receive.

Look for thoughtful, personal gifts that won’t take up much space but will hold plenty of sentimental value, like a petite signet ring engraved with her initials, a silver frame holding a favorite photo of the two of you, or laundry detergent infused with her signature scent. Everyday luxuries are another lovely option, from an electric wine opener to ultra-cozy slippers or pajamas embroidered with her name. Ultimately, focus on meaningful little treasures or luxurious upgrades to the things she already uses and loves.

Ahead, discover the gifts she’ll remember long after unwrapping.

A dainty, personalized signet ring is sure to earn a permanent spot in her everyday jewelry stack. Choose from 14K yellow gold, sterling silver, or gold vermeil, and make it uniquely hers with an engraved monogram, initial, or meaningful date.

This hand soap smells divine and works like magic to whisk away lingering odors from garlic, onions, and the like, thanks to its gentle exfoliating beads. It’s quickly become a permanent fixture by my kitchen sink, and I haven’t looked back.

Bombas may be best known for its stylish, ultra-comfy socks, but the brand also knows a thing or two about making cozy slippers. And how sweet is this fleecy pair in a neutral check pattern? Whether she’s lounging around the house or stepping out for a quick errand, she’ll have a hard time taking them off.

With so much attention devoted to skin and hair care routines, lashes and brows often get overlooked. So why not treat her to Cécred’s cult-favorite Lash and Brow Builder, a little luxury she can easily incorporate into her daily beauty regimen.

Make the often-dreaded laundry routine feel a little more luxurious with detergent and dryer sheets that infuse her clothes with DedCool’s dreamy fragrance. With notes of bright bergamot, soft vanilla, and warm amber, the scent is reason enough to fall in love, but these laundry essentials go beyond smelling irresistible, helping lift stains and soften fabrics, too.

Eberjey is beloved for its buttery-soft pajama sets in the chicest colorways, and I’m a firm believer that one can never have too many pairs of luxurious PJs. Make her gift feel all the more special by adding a personalized monogram—complimentary, might I add.

There’s always room for another gorgeous pair of earrings in a jewelry lover’s collection, especially when they’re as exquisite as Fope’s designs. For a truly unforgettable gift, spoil her with the brand’s gold Prima earrings, embellished with glittering diamond accents.

Whether she loves hosting or just enjoys unwinding with a nice bottle of wine, an electric corkscrew makes opening her favorite vintage a breeze. No more struggling with a traditional bottle opener or wondering whether the screw is in far enough. Plus, it’s much easier on the wrists.

Elevate her winter wardrobe with an elegant, supremely soft cashmere poncho she can effortlessly slip on for an extra layer of warmth, whether she’s lounging at home, out and about, or braving the office air conditioning.

I’ve been raving about Gemi’s serum-infused hand sanitizers, which keep hands clean without leaving them feeling dry or stripped. This adorable keychain version clips right onto her handbag or keys for easy access, making it a practical yet charming gift for the woman on the go.

For a gift she’ll adore showing off on date nights and at glamorous evening affairs, look to couture designer Zuhair Murad’s new collaboration with footwear brand Aldo. Known for avant-garde creations and intricate embellishments, Zuhair Murad brings a couture-inspired touch to Aldo’s stylish, affordable designs in a collection of party-ready accessories. Among the gorgeous pieces is this patent bag, finished with Murad’s signature logo detailing.

These glimmering studs have earned a spot on actress and style icon Claudia Sulewski’s Nice List at Mejuri, and it’s easy to see why. Not only are they dainty enough for everyday wear, but they’re also available in every birthstone, allowing you to personalize her pair with a gem that corresponds to her birth month—or simply choose her favorite stone.

If you’re looking to make a major impression, a designer handbag is a surefire way to earn yourself the title of her favorite gift-giver. Gucci is known for its sumptuous leather, and this understated shoulder bag is destined to become her new go-to for work and beyond.

A luxurious silver photo frame holding a cherished memory is a sentimental present she’ll be proud to display. For an extra-personal touch, have it engraved with a meaningful date, sweet message, or heartfelt sentiment.

ELLE beauty director Kathleen Hou praises this tortoiseshell hair pin as “an elegant adornment to any updo,” noting how its silver accents catch the light and enhance hair’s natural shine. And considering how often hair ties seem to mysteriously disappear, this chic alternative makes a useful gift for any stylish woman who loves keeping her hair swept out of the way.

Here’s a little luxury guaranteed to make her smile: a Chanel travel fragrance spray housed in a sleek case finished with a limited-edition, jewelry-inspired chain.

When in doubt, a gourmet box of chocolates is a gift that’s unlikely to last long once unwrapped. Compartés is a name to know in the world of luxury confections, and this generously sized gift box is brimming with chocolate-covered nuts, fluffy marshmallows, dipped fruits, and more.

If she takes her makeup routine seriously, she’ll love Simplehuman’s 5x magnifying mirror, which folds up for easy travel and makes perfecting every detail easy.

Transform her bathroom into a five-star spa retreat with this plush, fluffy robe. Whether she’s slipping it on after a shower or wearing it while getting ready for the day, she’ll feel like she’s enjoying a luxurious hotel stay without even leaving home.

Myles Price’s super-soft pull-on pants make an ideal gift for the woman who’s always on the go or simply appreciates lounging in style. I can personally vouch for the comfort—I own a pair myself, and between the exceptional quality and flattering fit, it’s hard not to want to wear them everywhere.
